I don't quite know why this wasn't just a piece of Hungle Bungle fodder that I left running in the background for Steam cards, but for some odd reason, I spent a good portion of this weekend hauling tonnage from Frankfurt Am Main to Rostock in Euro Truck Simulator 2. The experience was... mixed. My first attempt was a rocky one. After setting up my company and picking the driver that most looked like a tiny pope, I started up the tutorial and learned my way around the inside of a big rig. So far, so good, but moments into my first actual job the truck got caught on seemingly nothing and glitched out spectacularly, forcing me to cut power to the computer to get the damn game to go away.
Hesitantly, I ran it again, and thankfully it worked much better this time around. Using my trusty GPS and occasionally checking the Options screen for controls (How do I headlights? How do I windshield? What the hell's an Ausfhart?), I was burnin' my litres of petrol, cruising past countryside, intimidating other drivers with my apocalyptic girth, and agonizingly crawling up steep on- and off-ramps, ignorant of the screams of the jerks in cars around me. The discovery of the radio was delightful; the game offers a default selection of live European stations to run through, all completely indecipherable, all pretty fascinating, and all of which drop F-bombs with cheery regularity. If that's not your style, you can import whatever audio tracks you want and just shuffle through those (because all truckers love haulin'♥♥♥♥♥to One-Winged Angel and Dancing Mad Tier). Admittedly, all I was doing was driving at moderate speed down some fairly low-res highways, but there's something meditative about the experience. The road called, and I answered.
Over time though, things soured. I decided I was done being a mere professional trucker, employed by others and making a fraction of what I could working on my own. I discovered several recruiting agencies and truck dealerships, so technically, becoming my own boss was now an option. Then I saw the price tags. Getting my own truck, even the worst of the worst, would run me upwards of $100k. As I was making a mere $2-3k per job (assuming no Headlight Violations or Vehicular Collisions take a chunk out of the profits), and each job takes a good chunk of real-world time to complete, I could see I'd be grinding for a while. And then another glitch hit, this time simply freezing the game for a good thirty seconds, then unleashing everything I missed out on all at once as the game caught up with itself. So many car crashes. So much fines. I'd managed to completely undo all my hard work up to that point in a single, underwhelming 40 car pile-up.
On top of that, the game had some other less than stellar traits. Rather than being a faithful recreation of the European highway system, everything is shrunken down to scale. You clear kilometers in seconds, and even the biggest cities seem to be composed of a couple industrial sites, a gas station, a hotel, and maybe a dozen odd generic structures here and there. The pastoral scenery fares no better; I'd say it's maybe a touch better than PS2 quality, but that's pretty jarring for a 2012 game, especially when scenery is such a critical part of the game. I was briefly okay with the attention to detail paid to the truck interiors, but there are no personal touches added, no fuzzy dice, no dancing Hawaiian girl, no litter on the floor, no beaded seat cover. A little flair could have gone a long way here. Finally, (and this may be an understandable limitation to keep the game from becoming a demolition derby) all car crashes do is jostle the screen a bit and dock your pay. No matter how much more massive you are than your prey, all you manage to do is bump them, and off they go on their merry way. I'm not out for blood here, but I'd like the repercussions to be a little more significant than that.
There's definitely an audience for this game. I myself came close to finding it worth the time - perhaps not as a source of fun, but as an interesting and relaxing title to come back to now and again. Unfortunately, the bugs and the budget both hamstring it more than I'd like. If you're deadset on buying it, go ahead, and you'll likely enjoy the experience. For everyone else, wait for a bargain or keep your expectations in check; it's a hell of a bumpy road out there.

•	Online hacking
•	Lack of privately hostable servers
•	Perpetual early access, standstill development

There really isn't a whole lot of game here.  Mostly it is a driving simulator.  It looks reasonably good but ultimately it is a simulation of something that is quite boring to do.  It can't simulate the best things about driving like the smell of the road, the wind in your hair when you open the window, or the social aspect of interacting with people on the job or over your cb radio, but if you turn on the internet radio player built-in to the game while you play you can get a similar experience to driving down the road and listening to the radio.  It can be a pleasant and soothing experience, but I think most gamers (younger ones especially) would not find enough action to want to do this for long.
I personally play and enjoy this for what it is -- an excuse to listen to internet radio from Europe and tune out -- but I can't recommend it to others because I think many people would not enjoy it for more than a few hours.  You could just save your money, tune into internet radio for free, and do any other slow-paced activity (or just lie down and relax while you listen) to achieve the same thing.

If you are debating whether or not to buy this game, buy it. If it has sparked your interest enough to come down here and look at the reviews, it is worthwhile for you to own.
The graphics are simply stunning, the UI is very understandable, the career system functions well, the tutorials are thorough, and the who simulation is beyond fantastic. Everything is there and feels real: the power lines, the other cars, the boats, the hot air balloons. The weight is perfect for each truck, and you don't feel cheated when you screw up. Every mistake is your fault.
That's what a simulation game should be. It shouldn't be hard because it is poorly designed, and it shouldn't be clunky. This game doesn't provide a well rounded experience, if only because each area so far exceeds the standard (seriously, Dice needs to look at the graphics and take a few lessons.)
As with any game, there are a few issues. While the UI is clear, it is ugly. You feel as though Euro Truck Simulator 2 lays with the rest of the crappy, awful "simulators' pushed out by obscure developers. Don't let that fool you; the actual game is fantastic, and you can get used to the UI. The other issue comes from the grammar. Honestly, it feels like Engrish (I know it's not an Asian game.) That doesn't hinder the clarity of the language in anyway, however.
So, if you've been interested enough to look at reviews or to even visit the page, you should get Euro Truck Simulator 2.
[EDIT]: Ooh! Let me add this: if my review didn't persuade you, look at the latest news from the developers. They're redoing all the sounds. That's an important part to making the game better, but there's no real problem with the sounds as they stand. The devs just got access to better methods, so they're redoing most of the truck noises. What other game do you know of where the devs would be that devoted?! BUY this game.

Assuming that everyone know what Borderland is by now, I am now merely reviewing the Linux port.
And I am happy and relieved to tell that the Linux version is an excellent piece of port. There are a few framerate dips, but they are so few, short and far between that I really don't want to hold that against them at all.
More importantly is it to notice I've not seen any screen tearing, something that unfortunately is a quite common thing on Linux ports today. But not here. Nope. A steady, and (with the few exceptions mentioned) solid framerate picture backs up what easily is one of the very best coop games on the market today.
Also, everything works. That includes ingame voice chat support and controller support. I've played this game exclusively on a Logitech F710, and only in coop with buddies on the internet.
So if you are a Linux gamer like me, this game is a nobrainer. Even if FPS is not your genre, buy it. Buy it, cause it's games on this level and from these kind of distributors that will be the key to establish Linux as a gaming platform.
So get a buddy or three (buy'em a copy each!) and enter the wonderful world of Pandora. Just go crazy in a shower of loot and colourful, fresh and cheerful graphics for a few hours. It's so definitely worth it.

I find it difficult to articulate the exact reasons why I find Euro Truck Simulator 2 so enjoyable. By all rights, the game should be tediously boring; who wants to spend fourty five minutes in real world time driving a semi loaded with lumber from Scotland to Poland? Interestingly enough though, this game is somehow able to make that journey not only bearable but also oddly satisfying. I think it has to do with how polished the game feels. There is no "Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing" going on here but instead, solid driving and handling mechanics that make it seem like you are actually driving a massive truck carrying fifteen tons behind you. I find myself going back to this game every once in a while because the driving becomes oddly relaxing after a while: you get your cargo, turn on some SomaFM, and start your journey. That is until you forget that you can't drive like you do in GTA and get into massive accidents. Additionally, it is rather satisfying to move up from taking lower end jobs with rented trucks to purchasing and upgrading a home base, hiring other drivers, and building your own trucking empire.
All in all, I am thoroughly surprised at how engrossing this game can be. It won't appeal to everyone, or even most people for that matter but if it piques your interest, pick it up on a sale and see if it is as enjoyable for you.

Some good points, but a moronic savegame system spoils it.
The top line says it all, really. This is a nice-looking game, and the gameplay is generally good. However, the save game system is an absolute deal-breaker for me and, if I'd been warned about it, I'd never have wasted my money on the game. Simply put, there is no facility to "save right here, right now", although the quit menu gives the impression that that's what you're doing. You're not; the game gives you the option to save, and you might think that that would mean when you come back to the game and choose "continue", that's where you start. Wrong; the game remembers what you've done: what xp you've accumulated, what items you've picked up, what ammo you've expended; however, it drops you right back at the start of that section, with all new enemies in your way again. This is, frankly, shoddy, and reminds me of old console games with their limited save points. Apparently it's something to do with multiplayer games, but I have no particular desire to play this as anything other than a single player shooter. Why is there no option to start a game as single-player only, and save wherever you want? There should at least be an option to restart your game at one of the many checkpoints you've reached since the start of the level.
End of the day, this game looks good, but unless you've got the time to run through entire sections from start to finish, the savegame system means you'll see the same terrain, and the same mobs over and over again. They, of course, will be at full health and fully armed, while you've already fired off a load of ammo getting through it initially. Glad I bought it when it was on sale, wasting my money on full-price would have been even worse.

Summary:  The amount of grinding time versus the amount of time it takes to lose it all; not worth it. (Read bottom for update)
On one hand, spending weeks grinding for supplies, making the perfect base, hidden from other players, good gear, haven't even seen another person walking by, and then getting shot in the face by someone you couldn't even see and having them destroy everything you have strived for does not influence you to play the game again. I wouldn't be upset if this was a once in a while thing. I get it, PvP is a big part of the game, but it seems that no matter what I do or how much better my gear is, I die almost instantly. I disconnected and was eaten by a wolf that phased through my stone walls and lost all of my best gear and gun that I worked hard for. The game itself is beautiful, and functions really well (aside from that animal AI and how hard it is to defend yourself) and I had a good time with some friends, but when it all boils down to who has more friends the game starts to feel redundant.
I did not feel like I really wanted to respawn and start again. I'd leave the server and find a new one, just to have the same concept happen again. This went on for at least twenty something servers I could connect to. Not to compare this game to Minecraft or anything, because I know it sounds stupid, but if this game functioned more like it then I feel like the game would have a better community and people wouldn't feel the need to give up so often. (Can't wait to get roasted for this)
Bottom line is if you have a lot of friends and the game is on sale, buy it. If either of those aren't applicable, don't.
(Edit 10/1/17) I have recently tried playing on a x100 server and I've got to say, this is the way the game should be played (or at least x10 or something.)
I don't see why the base game isn't just this, because who the hell wants to grind for 300 hours? This doesn't instantly give you everything you need but it makes it SO MUCH LESS frusterating and tedious. You actually have somewhat of a chance against someone who's been playing for 9000 hours. Base design actually matters.
After all of this I'd say the game itself is a fair 3/10 but in a x10 server it's 8.5ish/10.

There really isn't a whole lot of game here.  Mostly it is a driving simulator.  It looks reasonably good but ultimately it is a simulation of something that is quite boring to do.  It can't simulate the best things about driving like the smell of the road, the wind in your hair when you open the window, or the social aspect of interacting with people on the job or over your cb radio, but if you turn on the internet radio player built-in to the game while you play you can get a similar experience to driving down the road and listening to the radio.  It can be a pleasant and soothing experience, but I think most gamers (younger ones especially) would not find enough action to want to do this for long.
I personally play and enjoy this for what it is -- an excuse to listen to internet radio from Europe and tune out -- but I can't recommend it to others because I think many people would not enjoy it for more than a few hours.  You could just save your money, tune into internet radio for free, and do any other slow-paced activity (or just lie down and relax while you listen) to achieve the same thing.

If you are debating whether or not to buy this game, buy it. If it has sparked your interest enough to come down here and look at the reviews, it is worthwhile for you to own.
The graphics are simply stunning, the UI is very understandable, the career system functions well, the tutorials are thorough, and the who simulation is beyond fantastic. Everything is there and feels real: the power lines, the other cars, the boats, the hot air balloons. The weight is perfect for each truck, and you don't feel cheated when you screw up. Every mistake is your fault.
That's what a simulation game should be. It shouldn't be hard because it is poorly designed, and it shouldn't be clunky. This game doesn't provide a well rounded experience, if only because each area so far exceeds the standard (seriously, Dice needs to look at the graphics and take a few lessons.)
As with any game, there are a few issues. While the UI is clear, it is ugly. You feel as though Euro Truck Simulator 2 lays with the rest of the crappy, awful "simulators' pushed out by obscure developers. Don't let that fool you; the actual game is fantastic, and you can get used to the UI. The other issue comes from the grammar. Honestly, it feels like Engrish (I know it's not an Asian game.) That doesn't hinder the clarity of the language in anyway, however.
So, if you've been interested enough to look at reviews or to even visit the page, you should get Euro Truck Simulator 2.
[EDIT]: Ooh! Let me add this: if my review didn't persuade you, look at the latest news from the developers. They're redoing all the sounds. That's an important part to making the game better, but there's no real problem with the sounds as they stand. The devs just got access to better methods, so they're redoing most of the truck noises. What other game do you know of where the devs would be that devoted?! BUY this game.

I believe some issues still remain in the game to this day 3 years on from the release, after playing the stanadlone for over 400+ hours I still believe that with work from the team it could be a extremly good game, I am not a Bohemia developer so I do not know about their time frame but I see some great updates every few months / year and then it becomes stale with little to no progress.
There are still issues in the game I saw when first purchased that are still very much relevent to this day, a big worry is that I remember Dean spending countless hours in the ping-pong suit moving to get perfect crispy animations for characters and yes they do look good, but the actual finished cut we have today is awful zombie animations which are out of time (desync is possible) I still see character animations bugged unfinished and having to go prone or quit the server in order to get out of a certain animation your character is stuck in.
I believe the next 6-12 months are crucial to the progression of this game the game could very well be dying out a rapid speed but I have no statistics to show, instead of spending time introducing new features, the core features of the game must be right first in order to progress on.
I would love to be able to go to DayZ in a years time and spend countless hours playing.

Some good points, but a moronic savegame system spoils it.
The top line says it all, really. This is a nice-looking game, and the gameplay is generally good. However, the save game system is an absolute deal-breaker for me and, if I'd been warned about it, I'd never have wasted my money on the game. Simply put, there is no facility to "save right here, right now", although the quit menu gives the impression that that's what you're doing. You're not; the game gives you the option to save, and you might think that that would mean when you come back to the game and choose "continue", that's where you start. Wrong; the game remembers what you've done: what xp you've accumulated, what items you've picked up, what ammo you've expended; however, it drops you right back at the start of that section, with all new enemies in your way again. This is, frankly, shoddy, and reminds me of old console games with their limited save points. Apparently it's something to do with multiplayer games, but I have no particular desire to play this as anything other than a single player shooter. Why is there no option to start a game as single-player only, and save wherever you want? There should at least be an option to restart your game at one of the many checkpoints you've reached since the start of the level.
End of the day, this game looks good, but unless you've got the time to run through entire sections from start to finish, the savegame system means you'll see the same terrain, and the same mobs over and over again. They, of course, will be at full health and fully armed, while you've already fired off a load of ammo getting through it initially. Glad I bought it when it was on sale, wasting my money on full-price would have been even worse.

I have been having quite a lot of fun playing this game, even though I admit, there isn't much going on.  I guess that's why it has "Relaxing" as a tag.
You start out by driving trucks, and making deliveries for other companies until you are able to save up enough to purchase your own truck.  You can customize it to your liking, and do upgrades to it by pulling into a garage.  Then you can purchase Garages, and start your own trucking company buying trucks, and hiring employees to drive them.  The one problem with the Company part is there is no degree of difficulty.  Just keep buying garage spaces and trucks, to get a pile of drivers earning you money.  Unless you do something silly like totally maxing out the bank loans, you can keep this up endlessly.  Another problem.  You can mod up your NPC Drivers trucks, but you will never see them on the road.
The company does seem to be quite dedicated to building the game up yet, adding new content, and fixing alot of things.  And there is a huge modding community, although I haven't downloaded and used any mods yet, and not sure if I will.
The games UI seems to be quite decent.  Cars will let you in if you have you signal light on, but occasionally they will ignore your wishes, much like real life.  The only problem, occasionally on underpasses, the UI will screw up and cause huge traffic gridlocks, and the only way out seems to be driving in the ditch around the area which can cause collisions (Which you have to pay for), damage to your vehicle and the load, ect.

Another nice little option they added.  They have a Radio in the semi's that are set to play local (Euro) radio stations via the internet.  So as you're running your load through Berlin or Paris, you have the option of switching to an actual radio station in the area to make it seem even more authentic.
Lastly, I will warn.  This game will be boring to many.  I am use to playing racing games, or am always expecting to see a deer or something jump out in front of me when I am driving at night.  Instead, the game is more about scenery, getting the loads to their destinations within the time limit, ensuring you don't run out of gas, crash, roll your heavy load by taking a corner a bit to fast, watching the speed limit (yep the police in game do have photo radar everywhere) as well as red light cameras and they even give fines if you don't have your headlights on as the game starts going into dusk.   The game is made in such a way that you can actually tell what type of load you are carrying by how your semi reacts on the road.  You can actually feel it straining to pull many of the heavy loads, especially when you are starting off, and have semi's with engines that have lower HP.

I find it difficult to articulate the exact reasons why I find Euro Truck Simulator 2 so enjoyable. By all rights, the game should be tediously boring; who wants to spend fourty five minutes in real world time driving a semi loaded with lumber from Scotland to Poland? Interestingly enough though, this game is somehow able to make that journey not only bearable but also oddly satisfying. I think it has to do with how polished the game feels. There is no "Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing" going on here but instead, solid driving and handling mechanics that make it seem like you are actually driving a massive truck carrying fifteen tons behind you. I find myself going back to this game every once in a while because the driving becomes oddly relaxing after a while: you get your cargo, turn on some SomaFM, and start your journey. That is until you forget that you can't drive like you do in GTA and get into massive accidents. Additionally, it is rather satisfying to move up from taking lower end jobs with rented trucks to purchasing and upgrading a home base, hiring other drivers, and building your own trucking empire.
All in all, I am thoroughly surprised at how engrossing this game can be. It won't appeal to everyone, or even most people for that matter but if it piques your interest, pick it up on a sale and see if it is as enjoyable for you.

DayZ is such an amazing game. The PVP aspect is the most heart pounding experience ive ever had. The possibility of losing hours worth of gear in an instant makes for really intense moments especially in military areas. The graphics i have to say are pretty god dam good and areas of the map can look stunningly beautiful at certain times of the day or night. The character customisation is also pretty good there are loads of differant cosmetic items to choose from depending on how you wish to portay your character in the unforgiving land that is DayZ. Weapon customisation is also good for some weapons but others i feel are lacking in some attachments. especially optics. Drivable vehicles have recently been reimplented into stable branch and for me DayZ is an entirely differant game with these present. Running for hours across the map does get very boring and sometimes you think' what's the ******* point' but now that you can travel the map far quicker than before i think its a good step in the right direction. Now yes there are some bugs that can get very frustrating at times and even cost you your life. Personally the most annoying in my experience is items falling threw the map. And when its the only gun you have ammo for! yea it needs fixed. There are some server crashes here and there and yes i dont experience some pretty bad fps drops at times. Desync isnt too bad when it comes to real up close and personal gun fights but it still needs some work.
Overall i would recommend this game as DayZ provides an experience of survival that no other game comes close. However as you probably know this is an alpha and has been for some time. There are many things broken and it does have a rather steep learning curve.
Personally I feel most dont appreciate what the developers are trying create. Its a game of massive scale with such depth to so many mechanics that some just dont respect the fact these games are difficult to make. And that its also a learning process for the Dev's to. It has took several years to develop Dayz and some would argue its hasnt come that far really since its release but i can assure you. If Bohemia Interactive didnt think it was possible to create this game they would have stopped development a long time ago. When this game releases in full it will be the best survival game out there.

Dayz is easily the most immersive and at times heart-throbbing game I’ve ever played. The eeriness of the huge Belarussian open world is truly one of a kind and every encounter you get is real and unscripted, you never know what you’re going to get and that is a feeling other games just don’t give me.

Concluding: Great game, unique feeling. Try it out if you are into games that do effectively force you to use your head instead of mindlessly shooting at everything. Even though a game like this is quite slow-paced, you can and will truly get an adrenaline rush out of it at times.

You know, you see a ton of negative reviews for this game, and I get the reasoning, but take them with a grain of salt. Most of the negative reviews are from people who have spent 400, 500, even saw a few 1400 hour gameplay times paired with negative reviews. People who have enjoyed far more hours with Dayz yet afforded positive reviews to games with less than 20 hours played. This is just the mindset of the millennial cupcake's gimme moar thought process.
Yes the game is still in alpha.
Yes the game is a running simulator with survival aspects.
Yes people still play thousands of hours on it because it's incredibly addicting.
What the game lacks in fast progress it makes up for in intense player interaction, one of the most exhilarating exercises in the game, (second to being chased by a pack of bloodthirsty wolves with nowhere to run). Spending hours gathering loot to either lose it being robbed or murdered by a mob of fellow raiders, or gaining top of the line military gear by killing a fully geared trio with a mosin at a helicopter crash site. There's a lot of disappointing ways to die in this game, which is probably why there are so many negative reviews, but they are met with equal opportunities of achieving greatness paired with an epic story.

Let me start by saying that you can play Borderlands 2 alone. It's just going to get boring. Fast. But if you have a few friends to play it with? Things start getting extremely interesting.
Highly customizable with lots of replayability for new loadouts, skillbuilds, even leveling new characters, a world expansive enough to sometimes merit just fooling around on, and extremely challenging New Game + modes, Borderlands 2 gives you a lot of tools to play with. The humor is its own unique brand, and it seems that there's a character for everone. And despite the emphasis on silliness and humor, you can easily find yourself growing attached to characters. Or, at least, getting really angry at certain ones. Stab you in the eyes angry.
If you like comparing stats and optimizing your unique style of play, this is for you. If you like silly, often juvenile humor, this is for you. If you have a bunch of friends willing to die repeatedly for the glory of a new shiny gun, this is for you. And if you're the type that wants to push said friends in an incenerator just so you can have first dibs on the loot that spews forth...then how could you. (But it's still the game for you.) Just don't plan on being engaged for more than one playthrough if you're running solo. It's possible...just not the same.

This game is an almost near perfect game. The graphics are a great and unique style that just keep looking and finding new things you missed every time you play through. The style of graphics for this game are the kind that will age very well.
The gameplay is solid. A First person shooter at heart mixed with excellent RPG style that allows you to uniquely make you're own character different then others. You can customize your characters with different skins and head styles. These are limited but still enough to give you a feel of your own unique character.
The main attraction of the game is the guns (loot). The amount of guns that they available is great. You will never feel that the guns are getting stale. Plus there are many different rarity levels that it will keep you hunting more and more.
The music in the game is absolutely stunning. With a few returning tracks for the first game, there are many new tracks in the game and they are perfectly placed. Music that plays during the boss battles will have you really into the game and give you a great feel of the atmosphere which the developers were going for.
With unique characterization and great replayability, this game is a definite must own for any RPG fan or Loot fans!

Euro Truck Simulator 2 (ETS 2)
The Good:  The developers did a good job of immersing the player to want to expand and make safe deliveries and even go into the delivery business.  I for one made many attempts at a perfect delivery.  I'll let you know when it actually happens.  There are many options that will engage the player from who to hire, to the types of deliveries to specialize in, to shopping or customizing the perfect truck.  Seriously, the customization alone has taken a good percentage of my time.
The Bad:  While ETS2 is in fact a simulator, the developers did too good of a job of simulating the occassional stretch of boredom on driving long routes.  This is after all a game and IMHO, would have been better if some of those routes didn't take as long as they do even if the route spans from the UK to Poland.  While the different delivery routes offer variety, gameplay can become repetitive.
The Imaginative:  IMHO, I see potential especially if the setting of this game were placed in the future where we had hover vehicles, more scenic routes and even more severe weather.
While I happily give this game a thumbs up, I wonder if this game is too specialized to a particular audience.

I remember when I first heard about DayZ.
It was over my christmas break in 2012 when I watched Rooster Teeth's video introducing DayZ Mod for Arma 2, talking about the concept of the game and how incredible the idea was. At the time, it was Rooster Teeth's most popular featurette video of its kind, and for good reason. It got me instantly hooked, and I bought a copy of Arma 2 and downloaded the mod instantly. And for about 200 hours or so, that for some reason were not recorded on steam, I loved my time with it. I played on primarily Lingor and Chernarus, both of which were incredible maps that I can still recall many great memories on.
When DayZ standalone dropped seemingly out of nowhere in December of 2013, I bought it instantly. I knew I had to support the devs and this great (idea of a) game, because imagine how wonderful it would have been to see a standalone DayZ, the world of Chernarus fully fleshed out, a community of players both friendly and unfriendly making the game a diverse experience of survival, cooperation, and PVP. Maybe we could build bases on islands off the coast, where we could take helicopters and fly off to fight battles at the three airstrips over rare loot that just spawned, maybe our friends would have gotten kidnapped and it would have been our responsibility to help them. Perhaps an entire server could have gone to war, a war of morality vs. banditry. The possibilities were endless.
I played for quite a bit throughout 2014. Not as much as I did DayZ mod since the standalone was missing many features, but about fifty of the hours I have were at launch. I had a lot of fun with DayZ, doing the same things I did in the mod, except this time without many of the guns, vehicles, and zombies (you heard me right) of before. It was basically Wasteland from the Arma series with some zombies sprinkled in and more of a morality system, but I had fun. Loot, join up, PVP, die, repeat. It was a fun game, for a while.
Over time, the development slowed. Over time, the cycle I just said got boring. Over time, the frustrating glitches where I would regularly phase off ladders and fall of buildings for no reason other than a poor engine and devs who don't know basic game design became infuriating. Over time, DayZ was no longer the ambitious game Dean Hall, the meme of the gaming community with his constant "It has to be done by the end of the year" BS, envisioned. It was a lifeless shell of Chernarus, a fictional country I wanted to spend a portion of my life in, fighting zombies and morally corrupted players. It was the inspiration for many of Steam's most popular games, including H1Z1, Ark: Survival Evolved, and Rust, all of which have now taken on lives of their own and have their own dedicated communities. DayZ, however? One of the most ambitious games of all time? The spawner of dozens of rip offs, the game so many people hopped on board, the game so many people wanted to love? It is now a failed experiment with more people playing Arma 3's version of DayZ than the actual game, an example of how not to handle overwhelming hype, how not to handle an early-access build, and how not to invest your money in an Australian man in-over his head so much that he wouldn't even finish a development that hasn't even entered beta four years later, departing relatively soon into the lifespan of his pet project.
This game is infuriating. This game is a chore. And it depresses me, because I'm the reason so many of my friends got into playing DayZ. I defended it for so long, tried so hard to love it and give it the benefit of the doubt, but every time I start it back up, it's as if nothing has changed.
I find a crowbar, eat some beans, and fall off a ladder.
Repeat.
I'd rather press a wet plastic bag to my face and breathe in than play this.

I hope you have nothing better to do with your time because once you start playing, you will not want to stop. I currently have three garages set up across Europe and a fleet of trucks, but nothing is more relaxing than taking my Globetrotter, turning on Manchester Real radio and taking an oversized load from the UK to Russia.
For as much of a bad reputation the word Simulator has gotten for all of these other "Simulators," ETS2 has gotten it right. A decent ammount of trucks you can pick and customize gives you plenty of choice when making your office your office. There are a good 30+ cities you can set up in all across Europe and take one by one and even expand on to add trucks and hire drivers to bring in revenue. The upgrades system starts off fast and does seem to drag out in the later levels so I suggest upgrading your distance perk first which allows you to make longer trips.
Now, the biggest issue in sims is the physics engine. Fortunately this game got it right. Collisions are soft or hard depending on how bad the impact is, you cannot ping off into space uncontrollably (unless you find one of the extremley few points to make your way out of the map. Place is sealed like a ziploc bag) and if you take corners too quickly your truck can roll over or steering becomes harder to control like it should. 10/10 physics in this game.
Other great notable features:
-Weather and working wiper blades
-Various fog patterns
-Some really effin' smart AI
-No seriously, these are the best AI I have ever seen.
-Truck customization
-Payouts and rewards depending on how well of a job you did
-The menu text isn't out of place or leaves white space!
-Enfoced speed limits (I'm happy for that though because some of those bends have tossed me onto my cab before)
-A large variety of jobs
And last but not least,
-The modding community
If you want more ETSII content, then look no further than the mods. DaSquirrelNuts over on youtube reveiws a truck-ton of them from US trucks to oversized loads and map add-ons.

You can customize your characters with different skins and head styles. These are limited but still enough to give you a feel of your own unique character.
The main attraction of the game is the guns (loot). The amount of guns that they available is great. You will never feel that the guns are getting stale. Plus there are many different rarity levels that it will keep you hunting more and more.
The music in the game is absolutely stunning. With a few returning tracks for the first game, there are many new tracks in the game and they are perfectly placed. Music that plays during the boss battles will have you really into the game and give you a great feel of the atmosphere which the developers were going for.
With unique characterization and great replayability, this game is a definite must own for any RPG fan or Loot fans!

The DayZ team is currently at its lowest point in the history of its development. Disengaged from the community with less patch releases than ever before - it truly is close to the end for what could have been a fantastic game.
I've got a few hours in this game, and truly enjoyed myself when I first started. The problem became when it started to feel like a task to play the game. The limited content available became dry very quickly, and the saving grace was the occasional PVP encounters. That's really all that kept me (and a lot of my long term DayZ playing friends) engaged.
But lately (probably 12+ months now), even the PVP has become sparse and unrewarding. There was a period of 4+ months where in %90 of PVP encounters you couldn't loot the person you just spent all of your resources killing. I get that these bugs happen, and it's alpha. I can handle dealing with these type of game breaking bugs, because I accept the state the game is in.
What I cant accept is the extremely poor response to these many many many many bugs (gamebreaking or not). The DayZ dev team takes MONTHS to release patches, and when they do, they often either break more integral parts of the game (such as extremely low item spawn rates or unable to hear gun shots near you - RIP). These patches often don't even fix the loudest concerns this community has. It's like the dev team is 2 people and Brian Hicks, working part time.
I'm not angry. I'm just extremely dissapointed. It's taken 4 years to get to what we have now ... and its just not worth it. Whoever is financing this team needs to do a reassessment of its operations, because, as a business operator myself, there are some very clear, very serious, management concerns on this team.
The game *may* launch one day, but unfortunately, the extremely amateur development process will have destroyed any loyal fanbase that once existed.
2 years ago I would have said "give it a shot!". Today, I actively tell people to avoid it and save their money & time.

Bout time I reviewed this game. This review is coming from over 2000 hours of game time (Steam and xbox combined) so i know the ins and outs of nearly every part of the game.
To start with, its a great solid game in which will provide plenty of entertainment for you and friends, solo or in a full team of 4. Yes the game is a blast solo, though alot is said about its co-op experience however that doesn't mean it isn't fun for single players, but obviously you can get more (or less in terms of loot) from playing with friends. This game is addicting, you just want more and better loot and to level up, kill the raid to get loot to kill the raid again, run arenas, play slots, chest farm, boss farm, toilet farm... well those aren't that lucrative. The fast paced gameplay and tense combat is great fun and when you get through without dying or going down you get a real sense of achievment, or relief if you did happen to do down or die. A first playthrough is always a blast and that alone is worth its cost, then if you REALLY enjoyed yourself you get to do it at a higher level, with more challenge, but more reward.
This game for me is about gameplay, not the story telling, yeah there is a stronger story than BL1 and more narrated side missions it still isn't up there with the likes of halo, GoW or other top, story focused games. So don't go in expecting to have a brilliant campaign story, go in expecting to have fun, and to have a good laugh.
There are plenty styles of play that Borderlands supports. Like being the center of attention, taking fire, tank it all and kicking out lots of dps at close range? Gunzerker. Like sitting back and sniping? Zer0, who isn't affraid to go ninja and stab enemies in the back. There is the siren, a support character for that team player. Then there's Axton, well, axton is a tricky one, tough to play at the top levels however early game, he shines with his huge tank, area of effect (the nuclear kind) and crowd control. then there are two bonus to provide lots more hours of fun after you get bored of the other four.
Yeah the game has its downs, its buggy, the scaling of certain skills, mechanics such as damage over time and certain types weapons just lose out to level. At top end level the game almost becomes unfair to the player forcing them to use only the best gear in the game, specific builds and so on, but then again, it is the top level. Its easy to break certain parts of missions forcing you to reload your game which can be very fustrating, also the AI has some weird quirks but overall isn't too game breaking.
Overall this is a game I would recommend even now just before the pre sequel as this is a game that will never grow old, will allways be fun to pick up and play, yes it has some flaws but to a flawless game is nearly impossible and well this is a game that triggered the looter shooter genre and so it must be good!

An incredibly fun game to play.  Although I may not have many hours on Steam, I also own the game on PS3 that I play often.  Single player is a lot of fun on its own, but the most fun will come from playing with friends.  The best part of playing with friends is how immensely challenging the game becomes.  A lot of games become too easy when you use group synergies, but I feel that borderlands properly scales the enemy difficulty.  No matter how many people are in your group (assuming you are all similar levels), you will likely feel challenged.
There are currently 6 different classes that all feel very unique to play, each with three skill trees to choose between.   Each skill tree makes the class feel at least moderately different, and being able to redistribute your skills allows you to try out new styles of play even within the same character.  Class Mods add even more customization, allowing you to create a fairly unique character.  You won't be a completely special snowflake, but you have a solid chance that nobody else in your group of four will build the same way.
TL;DR Great game, lots of customization, try to play with friends.

I'm going to tell my story in this section so if you don't want to read it then skip over this part. Ever since I was 10 years old playing minecraft (I know that's cringy asf) I have wanted to play a game that lets you build your own base, PVP, and interact with other players. Now I just didnt want this, I dreamed about this. The idea of this kinda game was always in my head and I would not rest until I found a game like the one in my dreams. Now little did I know I would later find this game with my friend. I remember going over to my friend Daniels house and playing legacy with him for a little bit, but at the time I didnt really like the look of it. From what I gathered the graphics wernt the best at the time and it looked a little boring. (But keep in mind I was a little younger and didnt really know how to play the game, let alone move around. So as friends do I bought the game to play with my friend. So we played and damn were we♥♥♥♥♥♥ So we changed over to games like Gmod and csgo. Then for the next couple of years the games just sat in our inventories as we waisted our time grinding the ranks of counter strike. I got the noble rank of Global and daniel got to around LE. So we decided to change our main game to something else, we tried a bunch of differnt games like Rainbow, which no offence got boring quick, to Arma and h1z1. But then I was watching a youtuber that I liked and he metioned something about a "New Rust" just coming out. So I told daniel to download it and that we should try it out. So he downloaded it to his ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop and I put it on my computer. Right when we got in it was nothing like we saw a couple years ago in legacy, it was a whole new world (This time with some more modern and IMO better looking graphics). So we began our journey in the rust world. Of Coarse the begining was extremely rough. Loging out and wondering why we lost our stuff, to building wooden windows on our bottom floor. But as time went on I noticed that this was it, the game I was looking for, the perfect balance of everything I wanted (Not to mention amazing updated coming out almost every week). Fast forward to now, me and daniel are still friends and play every single day after school. Rust is all I think about in school, wether it's if we got raided or whats happening with the server or new base designes. I have racked up a good amount of hours in this game and dont mind adding thousands more. I look forward to wipe days every week. I love to PVP and I think ive gotton pretty decent at it. The message I am trying to get out of this story is that rust is the absoulte best game I have ever played.
-Constant updates every week
-A ingame report system that actually works
-A almost close to perfect crafting system
-Very fun early game and late game
-A Component system that seems to be working
-A active reddit that has many anthusiests.
-AMAZING GRAPHICS
-Very big problem with roof campers
-bears that can ♥♥♥♥ even late game people up
-Some small skin glitches
-rather toxic people in game
Rust will always be close in my heart, even if it has some problems. But as i said in my story this is the game that I have always wanted to play ever since i was young, and it will just keep getting better.
If you are thinking about buying this game, I think my recommendation is pretty clear. Buy it. I promise if you have patience and some friends to play it with, it will be an amazing gaming experience.

I hope you have nothing better to do with your time because once you start playing, you will not want to stop. I currently have three garages set up across Europe and a fleet of trucks, but nothing is more relaxing than taking my Globetrotter, turning on Manchester Real radio and taking an oversized load from the UK to Russia.
For as much of a bad reputation the word Simulator has gotten for all of these other "Simulators," ETS2 has gotten it right. A decent ammount of trucks you can pick and customize gives you plenty of choice when making your office your office. There are a good 30+ cities you can set up in all across Europe and take one by one and even expand on to add trucks and hire drivers to bring in revenue. The upgrades system starts off fast and does seem to drag out in the later levels so I suggest upgrading your distance perk first which allows you to make longer trips.
Now, the biggest issue in sims is the physics engine. Fortunately this game got it right. Collisions are soft or hard depending on how bad the impact is, you cannot ping off into space uncontrollably (unless you find one of the extremley few points to make your way out of the map. Place is sealed like a ziploc bag) and if you take corners too quickly your truck can roll over or steering becomes harder to control like it should. 10/10 physics in this game.
Other great notable features:
-Weather and working wiper blades
-Various fog patterns
-Some really effin' smart AI
-No seriously, these are the best AI I have ever seen.
-Truck customization
-Payouts and rewards depending on how well of a job you did
-The menu text isn't out of place or leaves white space!
-Enfoced speed limits (I'm happy for that though because some of those bends have tossed me onto my cab before)
-A large variety of jobs
And last but not least,
-The modding community
If you want more ETSII content, then look no further than the mods. DaSquirrelNuts over on youtube reveiws a truck-ton of them from US trucks to oversized loads and map add-ons.

I give this a "yes" recommendation, but there are a few things to say...
This game improves on Borderlands 1 in the story department and it also adds some excellent characters. Handsome Jack is an outstanding antagonist, and the voice acting for the character is tops. There is quite a range of environments as well. And there are a lot of guns with a lot of styles.
But there are weaknesses as well. To me, a lot of the guns don't "feel" as good as they did in the first game, especially the Jakobs sniper rifles, which don't feel as solid. Also, while there are a lot of new and different weapon designs, a lot of them just seem silly looking; more form than function. Also, it seems that loot-farming is (deliberately?) broken. Drop rates for decent weapons is really low, and weapons become obsolete rather quickly as you level up, so you often end up having to make do with mediocre junk rather than weapons you want to play with. When you do finally find one you really like, it becomes useless sooner than similar situations in BL1.
Also, it seems that this one is even more geared towards co-op than even BL1 was. There are several loot-bosses around in the game and DLC that are absolutely impossible to attempt alone, which means we single-players are basically locked out from some parts of the game. Contrast to BL1 where there wasn't a single thing that couldn't be done alone.
The game is fun enough though. Story-wise it is a step up from BL1. In other ways I feel it is a step down. Overall, worth playing.

I haven't yet played this game for a time long enough to give at a completely accurate review, however, Rust is an excellent game from my experience. The only things that I dislike about it don't come from the game, but from the devs themselves.
The devs of Rust are oddballs. They will add a cool feature like the experience system and all of a sudden remove it in the next patch. They also add unecessary items like vending machines and so on (I guess it's cool for players to be able to make their own shops).
If you are looking for realistic combat and firefights, this isn't a very good game for that. Though the weapon sounds are pretty cool and sound quite realistic, combat is a little bit odd for a survival game. IBullet drop is extremely exaggerated and unrealistic and players can heal generally quickly through the use of syringes and medkits. I don't have many complaints besides those (it's annoying to lose a firefight however, because someone pulled out a syringe faster than you). The game can also get pretty intense when helicopters controlled by NPCs come hovering around your base looking for trouble, or when a plane brings in an airdrop and you can hear the massive amount of gunshots which are being fired by the people fighting to the death to see who can claim the rewards of the drop.
The firearm crafting doesn't make much sense either, you need to find certain 'bodies' of a weapon (as of win.1172.69) and then you just need pieces of metal, springs and pipes. In reality, you would need not just a 'body' but a reciever (I guess the weapon's body could include the reciever), an action, a stock, a barrel and all sorts of screws other parts to hold the gun together. Firearm bodies can only be found in certain places, for some reason you can't make them but you can made a working codelock with some metal scraps and wood.
This game is generally good, but only truly fun to play with a group. I would recommend it if you could find a group to play it with.

I'm going to tell my story in this section so if you don't want to read it then skip over this part. Ever since I was 10 years old playing minecraft (I know that's cringy asf) I have wanted to play a game that lets you build your own base, PVP, and interact with other players. Now I just didnt want this, I dreamed about this. The idea of this kinda game was always in my head and I would not rest until I found a game like the one in my dreams. Now little did I know I would later find this game with my friend. I remember going over to my friend Daniels house and playing legacy with him for a little bit, but at the time I didnt really like the look of it. From what I gathered the graphics wernt the best at the time and it looked a little boring. (But keep in mind I was a little younger and didnt really know how to play the game, let alone move around. So as friends do I bought the game to play with my friend. So we played and damn were we♥♥♥♥♥♥ So we changed over to games like Gmod and csgo. Then for the next couple of years the games just sat in our inventories as we waisted our time grinding the ranks of counter strike. I got the noble rank of Global and daniel got to around LE. So we decided to change our main game to something else, we tried a bunch of differnt games like Rainbow, which no offence got boring quick, to Arma and h1z1. But then I was watching a youtuber that I liked and he metioned something about a "New Rust" just coming out. So I told daniel to download it and that we should try it out. So he downloaded it to his ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop and I put it on my computer. Right when we got in it was nothing like we saw a couple years ago in legacy, it was a whole new world (This time with some more modern and IMO better looking graphics). So we began our journey in the rust world. Of Coarse the begining was extremely rough. Loging out and wondering why we lost our stuff, to building wooden windows on our bottom floor. But as time went on I noticed that this was it, the game I was looking for, the perfect balance of everything I wanted (Not to mention amazing updated coming out almost every week). Fast forward to now, me and daniel are still friends and play every single day after school. Rust is all I think about in school, wether it's if we got raided or whats happening with the server or new base designes. I have racked up a good amount of hours in this game and dont mind adding thousands more. I look forward to wipe days every week. I love to PVP and I think ive gotton pretty decent at it. The message I am trying to get out of this story is that rust is the absoulte best game I have ever played.
-Constant updates every week
-A ingame report system that actually works
-A almost close to perfect crafting system
-Very fun early game and late game
-A Component system that seems to be working
-A active reddit that has many anthusiests.
-AMAZING GRAPHICS
-Very big problem with roof campers
-bears that can ♥♥♥♥ even late game people up
-Some small skin glitches
-rather toxic people in game
Rust will always be close in my heart, even if it has some problems. But as i said in my story this is the game that I have always wanted to play ever since i was young, and it will just keep getting better.
If you are thinking about buying this game, I think my recommendation is pretty clear. Buy it. I promise if you have patience and some friends to play it with, it will be an amazing gaming experience.

What's it like to be a Badass? Well, it's bad♥♥♥♥♥ You see, this game has a bazillioner guns than the first game, and each type of gun feels different due to the wonderful randomized loot. Loot feels great, combat feels great, and you just feel like a badass killing a flood of ineffective enemies and the occasional hard hitting badass who hits you for all your HP.
All six classes (two of which are paid DLC) are great fun. The Psycho and Mechromancer are by far the hardest, and turn the mechanics of the game upside down. For example: Psycho's middle tree (Mania) wants you to be taking health damage and have your shield not recharge, his fire tree wants to set himself on fire so he has improved stats and deals more damage. The Mechromancer's hardest tree (Anarchy) wants her to never reload manually, only by taking her clip empty. At the same time she won't care about regen speed or delay on shields because the way her kit is set up. This sets up two classes that play completely different from the other four.
Playing it with friends makes the game more fun, but the matchmaking is pretty great thanks to steam. Even years after release it still has active players playing at all levels. Pick it up, I dare you.

Unlike most simulators where you can experiment without consequence, ETS2 makes you want to excel at every task and get through every trip without damaging your equipment or disappointing your customer.
Driving takes a lot of concentration and awareness but is ultimately relaxing. The scenery is beautiful even if it doesn't render cities anything like their real-world geographies. Being able to tune in to local European internet streaming radio stations adds a lot of flavour, making you feel you're right there as you listen to DJ chatter in French or German or Polish while playing local favourites.
Vehicles control well enough on an Xbox gamepad but I've watched people on Twitch with steering wheels and head trackers play the game in all its glory. Mouse and keyboard are viable as well and are superior to the gamepad when it comes to looking around, but it's more precise driving with an analog controller of some sort.
I was surprised at how much I enjoyed this game. I bought it with low expectations but quickly became completely immersed in the moment and in managing my little company. It's an excellent simulator and a fun tycoon game as well.

There isn't really anything that I can say about this that the other (currently) 66,000+ positive reviews here haven't already said, so I'll point out this: it took me over a year to finally play the game because I thought that I wouldn't enjoy it, but I downloaded the demo to show to my twelve-year-old sister, who loved it, and I ended up buying it on a whim to play with her. That is genuinely one of the best decisions that I've ever made; it became her favourite game of all time, we played through it three times as a pacifist alone (all of my time clocked into this game on Steam was from playing it with her) and, as someone who's been playing games all his life, playing it through with her was one of the best experiences that I've ever had with a video game. If you have a younger sibling or child in their early/mid teens (who won't turn their nose up at pixel graphics),
make sure that you play this game with them. The story of the game is almost tailor-made for that and I can't possibly recommend it enough. Of course, if you
have a younger sibling or child, play it anyway, because it's one of those games that can absolutely be enjoyed and loved by all ages, and appreciated for very different reasons by people of different ages. This is not a "kiddy" game at all, never assumes that the player is an idiot and touches on some rather grown-up themes in very tasteful ways, and in a much better way than a lot of games do.
Undertale is a game with an incredible story with important, thought-provoking messages topped with surprisingly great humour, a beautifully realised world and what is honestly one of my favourite game soundtracks of all time. Even though the gameplay is a little more reserved than in most games, the gameplay that you do get is surprisingly innovative and very unique; I do not like typical RPGs or SHMUP/bullet Hell games
, but, here, they are combined in a way that eradicates everything that I dislike about both genres, the biggest being the relatively hands-off approach of typical turn-based combat and the relentlessness and nauseating visuals of bullet Hell games for someone like me. Even though I've been playing video games all my life, getting to experience it in person and introduce it to someone who loves it possibly even more than I do has genuinely been one of the best gaming experiences that I've ever had.

There isn't really much too say about Undertale that hasn't already been said, it's basically the juggernaut of indy games by this point.
Cons
-Way too much combat in the first area for how little story happens and that's on top of it being very bland looking, I've seen more than one person almost give up thinking the whole game would be like this.
-Not very controller friendly, there seem to be a fair few annoying issues when using the analog stick.
Either way
-Some people, such as myself, find the graphics overall charming, other people find them to be just plain bad.
Pros
-On the surface, combining traditional turnbased RPG combat with bullet hell dodging is lunacy, but it actually made for a very unique combat system, the fact that nearly every major boss switched up the mechanics meant each boss fight was memorable.
-The characters are fantastic and the world is charming, Undertale is one of the few games that seems to realize that in order to care about the world as a whole you need to have a player who wants to be part of it. Far too many games just assume the player will automatically care about the game world despite it being a bland grimdark craphole filled with unlikeable snarky jerkbags.
-One of the few games where "Moral" choices actually have some weight too them, you actually need to be consistant in how you treat everone, rather than just making a single choice when you shoot a boss character enough times.
All in all, this is my favourite RPG of all time, with its memorable cast of wonderful characters and a world I was completely absorbed in from start too finish.

I haven't yet played this game for a time long enough to give at a completely accurate review, however, Rust is an excellent game from my experience. The only things that I dislike about it don't come from the game, but from the devs themselves.
The devs of Rust are oddballs. They will add a cool feature like the experience system and all of a sudden remove it in the next patch. They also add unecessary items like vending machines and so on (I guess it's cool for players to be able to make their own shops).
If you are looking for realistic combat and firefights, this isn't a very good game for that. Though the weapon sounds are pretty cool and sound quite realistic, combat is a little bit odd for a survival game. IBullet drop is extremely exaggerated and unrealistic and players can heal generally quickly through the use of syringes and medkits. I don't have many complaints besides those (it's annoying to lose a firefight however, because someone pulled out a syringe faster than you). The game can also get pretty intense when helicopters controlled by NPCs come hovering around your base looking for trouble, or when a plane brings in an airdrop and you can hear the massive amount of gunshots which are being fired by the people fighting to the death to see who can claim the rewards of the drop.
The firearm crafting doesn't make much sense either, you need to find certain 'bodies' of a weapon (as of win.1172.69) and then you just need pieces of metal, springs and pipes. In reality, you would need not just a 'body' but a reciever (I guess the weapon's body could include the reciever), an action, a stock, a barrel and all sorts of screws other parts to hold the gun together. Firearm bodies can only be found in certain places, for some reason you can't make them but you can made a working codelock with some metal scraps and wood.
This game is generally good, but only truly fun to play with a group. I would recommend it if you could find a group to play it with.

The feeling of driving a real truck is captivating. Just to name a few, it´s really fun to take right turns carefully because your load is about to hit the sidewalk, and the graphics are excellent + charming. Also, highway driving is super-relaxing, and the game has got a little system that lets you manage your own garage. Did I mention that you can tune your truck in a gazillion ways? I spent countless hours driving my FH16 Classic 750 Globetrotter Exclusive 6x2+4 R VOLVO at midnight, watching the stars go by, listening to my favorite podcast <3
But... as soon as you reach level 15 you pretty much have infinite money and the game loses half of its charm. Besides, after a while you start taking shortcuts out of boredom (e.g. ignoring red traffic lights) and you realize the AI is not as intelligent as it looked. Sadly, at this point the game stops being a "cool simulator" and becomes a "mmmeeh game" without much to do in it but installing random mods.
Anyways.... overall I really liked the game and I recommend it if you wanna get into trucks and/or realistic driving. At the very least, it´s worth 20+ hours of fun. Buy it in a sale or when it goes below 10 euros, though. Otherwise you're better off buying something else.

Mechanically, Undertale is an RPG-lite adventure game with a battle system based on mundane-to-zany menu interactions (like Earthbound) and bullet-hell defensive segments (like Touhou).
Narratively, Undertale is about a lost child who falls down a hole in a mountain and finds themselves trapped in a kingdom of monsters. Their journey to return home seems simple at first, but of course becomes increasingly complicated as the cast and history of the kingdom are introduced over time.
Thematically, Undertale is about friendship, mercy, humor, self-doubt, regret, hatred, bigotry, sacrifice, love, anime, and spaghetti.
Meta-thematically, Undertale touches on ludo-narrative dissonance and harmony, cycles, mercy, what it means to interact with characters in a game, and determination.
Meta-meta-thematically, Undertale ... is.
Undertale is not for everyone. The internet hype machine has inadvertently polarized potential players into people who will love the game to death, and people who will reject it outright as insufficient or insulting.
You will know whether the game is for you or not after the end of the first area, the ruins. It will take you less than an hour to get there and find out. I recommend you try, and don't give up if it seems tough at first.
For myself, Undertale was so good it made me never want to play it again.

There isn't really anything that I can say about this that the other (currently) 66,000+ positive reviews here haven't already said, so I'll point out this: it took me over a year to finally play the game because I thought that I wouldn't enjoy it, but I downloaded the demo to show to my twelve-year-old sister, who loved it, and I ended up buying it on a whim to play with her. That is genuinely one of the best decisions that I've ever made; it became her favourite game of all time, we played through it three times as a pacifist alone (all of my time clocked into this game on Steam was from playing it with her) and, as someone who's been playing games all his life, playing it through with her was one of the best experiences that I've ever had with a video game. If you have a younger sibling or child in their early/mid teens (who won't turn their nose up at pixel graphics),
make sure that you play this game with them. The story of the game is almost tailor-made for that and I can't possibly recommend it enough. Of course, if you
have a younger sibling or child, play it anyway, because it's one of those games that can absolutely be enjoyed and loved by all ages, and appreciated for very different reasons by people of different ages. This is not a "kiddy" game at all, never assumes that the player is an idiot and touches on some rather grown-up themes in very tasteful ways, and in a much better way than a lot of games do.
Undertale is a game with an incredible story with important, thought-provoking messages topped with surprisingly great humour, a beautifully realised world and what is honestly one of my favourite game soundtracks of all time. Even though the gameplay is a little more reserved than in most games, the gameplay that you do get is surprisingly innovative and very unique; I do not like typical RPGs or SHMUP/bullet Hell games
, but, here, they are combined in a way that eradicates everything that I dislike about both genres, the biggest being the relatively hands-off approach of typical turn-based combat and the relentlessness and nauseating visuals of bullet Hell games for someone like me. Even though I've been playing video games all my life, getting to experience it in person and introduce it to someone who loves it possibly even more than I do has genuinely been one of the best gaming experiences that I've ever had.

There isn't really much too say about Undertale that hasn't already been said, it's basically the juggernaut of indy games by this point.
Cons
-Way too much combat in the first area for how little story happens and that's on top of it being very bland looking, I've seen more than one person almost give up thinking the whole game would be like this.
-Not very controller friendly, there seem to be a fair few annoying issues when using the analog stick.
Either way
-Some people, such as myself, find the graphics overall charming, other people find them to be just plain bad.
Pros
-On the surface, combining traditional turnbased RPG combat with bullet hell dodging is lunacy, but it actually made for a very unique combat system, the fact that nearly every major boss switched up the mechanics meant each boss fight was memorable.
-The characters are fantastic and the world is charming, Undertale is one of the few games that seems to realize that in order to care about the world as a whole you need to have a player who wants to be part of it. Far too many games just assume the player will automatically care about the game world despite it being a bland grimdark craphole filled with unlikeable snarky jerkbags.
-One of the few games where "Moral" choices actually have some weight too them, you actually need to be consistant in how you treat everone, rather than just making a single choice when you shoot a boss character enough times.
All in all, this is my favourite RPG of all time, with its memorable cast of wonderful characters and a world I was completely absorbed in from start too finish.

Background:  I started playing Rust around the Holiday season of 2015, approximately in December of 2015.  In a year I had clocked in almost 2000 hours.  I saw the shift from the blueprint system, to the XP system, to the Component system.  I've played solo and in a large group.  Almost all my time is spent on vanilla servers (unmodded).
The game:  Rust really draws on a person's desire for building, progressing, accomplishing goals, interacting with players, survival, and motivation.
-Building, customizing, and defending a base you can call home.  Getting raided can be truly heartbreaking, but defending it can be exciting and rewarding with a well-designed base.
-Acquiring, organizing, and maintaining items.  This fuels the desire to raid and Kill-on-site; you get stuff.  Stuff has value, some things are rare, some are common.  It feels good to get things like High-Quality Metal, Rifle Bodies, Springs, etc.
-Social interactions are unavoidable, but add to the game.  Negative reactions create a desire for revenge and add to the excitement of raiding a rival.  Positive interactions can create long-lasting friendships.  It should go without saying, but teamwork is purely beneficial. Solo survival can be fun, but long-term, groups are the only way to go.
-There are a variety of servers. Vanilla progression too slow? They have modded, increased-gathering servers.  Want to cut straight to the chase and shoot?  There exist battlefield, combat tag, and embankment servers for that.  Sick of large clans steam-rolling all the smaller guys? Many servers are available with group-size limits.
Misc:
Active developers: there are weekly Devblog posts that give insight on what's to come and what has arrived.  These are well-written and fun to read.  The developers are constantly progressing, and oftentimes, they listen to the community.
Death, betrayal, and loss are all inevitable.  You win some, you lose some.  You can shift some factors in your favor if you play it right, but it really is just a balance.  The community is toxic, offline-raiding sucks, and roof-campers are cowards.
That's all I can think of for now.  Just buy it now or wait for it to appear on Humble Bundle for cheap, as it frequently does.

Mechanically, Undertale is an RPG-lite adventure game with a battle system based on mundane-to-zany menu interactions (like Earthbound) and bullet-hell defensive segments (like Touhou).
Narratively, Undertale is about a lost child who falls down a hole in a mountain and finds themselves trapped in a kingdom of monsters. Their journey to return home seems simple at first, but of course becomes increasingly complicated as the cast and history of the kingdom are introduced over time.
Thematically, Undertale is about friendship, mercy, humor, self-doubt, regret, hatred, bigotry, sacrifice, love, anime, and spaghetti.
Meta-thematically, Undertale touches on ludo-narrative dissonance and harmony, cycles, mercy, what it means to interact with characters in a game, and determination.
Meta-meta-thematically, Undertale ... is.
Undertale is not for everyone. The internet hype machine has inadvertently polarized potential players into people who will love the game to death, and people who will reject it outright as insufficient or insulting.
You will know whether the game is for you or not after the end of the first area, the ruins. It will take you less than an hour to get there and find out. I recommend you try, and don't give up if it seems tough at first.
For myself, Undertale was so good it made me never want to play it again.

There isn't really anything that I can say about this that the other (currently) 66,000+ positive reviews here haven't already said, so I'll point out this: it took me over a year to finally play the game because I thought that I wouldn't enjoy it, but I downloaded the demo to show to my twelve-year-old sister, who loved it, and I ended up buying it on a whim to play with her. That is genuinely one of the best decisions that I've ever made; it became her favourite game of all time, we played through it three times as a pacifist alone (all of my time clocked into this game on Steam was from playing it with her) and, as someone who's been playing games all his life, playing it through with her was one of the best experiences that I've ever had with a video game. If you have a younger sibling or child in their early/mid teens (who won't turn their nose up at pixel graphics),
make sure that you play this game with them. The story of the game is almost tailor-made for that and I can't possibly recommend it enough. Of course, if you
have a younger sibling or child, play it anyway, because it's one of those games that can absolutely be enjoyed and loved by all ages, and appreciated for very different reasons by people of different ages. This is not a "kiddy" game at all, never assumes that the player is an idiot and touches on some rather grown-up themes in very tasteful ways, and in a much better way than a lot of games do.
Undertale is a game with an incredible story with important, thought-provoking messages topped with surprisingly great humour, a beautifully realised world and what is honestly one of my favourite game soundtracks of all time. Even though the gameplay is a little more reserved than in most games, the gameplay that you do get is surprisingly innovative and very unique; I do not like typical RPGs or SHMUP/bullet Hell games
, but, here, they are combined in a way that eradicates everything that I dislike about both genres, the biggest being the relatively hands-off approach of typical turn-based combat and the relentlessness and nauseating visuals of bullet Hell games for someone like me. Even though I've been playing video games all my life, getting to experience it in person and introduce it to someone who loves it possibly even more than I do has genuinely been one of the best gaming experiences that I've ever had.

There isn't really much too say about Undertale that hasn't already been said, it's basically the juggernaut of indy games by this point.
Cons
-Way too much combat in the first area for how little story happens and that's on top of it being very bland looking, I've seen more than one person almost give up thinking the whole game would be like this.
-Not very controller friendly, there seem to be a fair few annoying issues when using the analog stick.
Either way
-Some people, such as myself, find the graphics overall charming, other people find them to be just plain bad.
Pros
-On the surface, combining traditional turnbased RPG combat with bullet hell dodging is lunacy, but it actually made for a very unique combat system, the fact that nearly every major boss switched up the mechanics meant each boss fight was memorable.
-The characters are fantastic and the world is charming, Undertale is one of the few games that seems to realize that in order to care about the world as a whole you need to have a player who wants to be part of it. Far too many games just assume the player will automatically care about the game world despite it being a bland grimdark craphole filled with unlikeable snarky jerkbags.
-One of the few games where "Moral" choices actually have some weight too them, you actually need to be consistant in how you treat everone, rather than just making a single choice when you shoot a boss character enough times.
All in all, this is my favourite RPG of all time, with its memorable cast of wonderful characters and a world I was completely absorbed in from start too finish.
