If you don't actually do your own research to see what happened to the game and just hop on the dayz hate bandwagon then I probably can't change your opinion.
In a nutshell though, Dean Hall pretty much slapped together a different version of the dayz mod on release and left with the money. The engine that Dayz ran on at first was literally just some variation of the arma engine. I don't quite remember the name but it was either some kind of aviation engine or even unity so I've heard. Anyways, After Bohemia bought it, they practically replaced 80% of Dayz's content. They replaced the engine,
, server browser, and added a bunch of unique stuff from
to cholera and brain prion disease. The current engine is actually a custom one because other engines
the features that the Dayz devs are trying to implement. Of course, you guys probably didn't hear about this because most people put it under the category of "too little too late".
Honestly I do think that Dayz has taken a very long time to release but if you view all the progress Bohemia has made, you'll begin to realize that they actually started to develop the game when it released. And so it's been about 5 years. I don't know about you but that sounds like a pretty average time considering how small the Dayz team is right now. As you can tell from what I previously said, they pretty much scrapped all of Dean Hall's originial design with more efficient software.
Honestly, the majority of the community is cancerous. Most people I've come across just kill on sight or take advantage of you when you're vulnerable (like when you're bandaging). There are a few people who have been nice to me and even gave me stuff and I try to do the same. My current policy with strangers is kill those who can easily kill me but that's just me.
There is no set goal of Dayz. No objective besides just staying alive. Heck, the game doesn't even tell you where the good loot is. I and many of the players that still play Dayz feel that Dayz is a way to simulate for ourselves how we would survive in a apocalyptic situation. Obviously, there are some jerks that act like commandos but maybe that's how they would actually act if they lived in a environment that did not punish them for their actions. Dayz is a way to also express how people act in interesting situations.

A year or so ago, I spoke, via social media, with a representative from Bohemia interactive about the development of this game, its early access release, the lack of PR and poor customer relations shown by Brian Hicks. Having been blocked from Hicks' social media account for merely questioning the progress of this game, it occurred to me that there was a disconnect between the promises made not only about the actual progress of the game but the level of real player involvement in this progress.
As early access buyers we were told that this early investment was not only a way to save on the cost of the game, but was an investment in its future as these must needed funds would help in its development and allow the community to help shape the development process. The speed at which Mr. Hicks banned me and others along with the withholding nature of his tweets and attitude prompted me to bring this to Bohemia’s attention directly. They responded with the usually denial of Hicks’ withholding demeanor, and that patience is needed in the process as they too wish the game was coompleted. I then questioned them regarding the level of community involvement and the investment made by all those who purchased early access to the game as many of my friends felt at the time as if they were not being treated as investors, which we are, but more like annoyances. After all, they said early on that they needed our money to fund this project. Their response was quite telling.
They admitted that the game was fully funded prior to the early access launch, so they didn’t need our money, and that essentially they launched the game unfinished because people wanted to play it, which is corporate for, they had to capitalize on the demand no matter what. While there is nothing wrong with capitalizing on the demand for a product or service, it is wrong for a firm to mislead the buying public for its own gain. When I presented that contradiction to them directly I was given a canned answer and thanked for my input after an extended period of silence.
Sadly this game is the quintessential example of the, “First Penguin” analogy. Being one of the most anticipated games in the early access arena, DayZ unfortunately was forced to navigate relatively uncharted waters and continues to struggle to keep their head above the surface. The perception remains that this game has been miss managed in every way. From technical decisions to marketing to customer relations, DayZ has become an example of what not to do when developing a video game.

What it is:
You are a truck driver in Europe.  You start out taking jobs as they are available and drive various trucks from place to place delivering a variety of cargos.  Eventually when you have enough money saved you can buy your own truck.  When you have even more money saved you can buy garages and start hiring employees to drive other trucks and earn you even more money.  You'll use fuel so you'll need to stop and get gas periodically.  Also you might need to stop at a repair shop occasionally, and you'll also need to stop regulary to sleep.
The base game comes with a map that stretches from Scotland to Slovakia, Poland to northern Italy.  The developer is creating map extentions you can buy.  Currently there's one available that extends east to Hungary, and I understand they are working on one that will extend it north into the Baltic countries.
This is the latest truck game from the company that brought us the 18 Wheels of Steel series, German Truck Simulator, UK Truck Simulator, and Euro Truck Simulator 1.  Everything is better in this one.
Pros:
Huge map for its genre.  It does use simulated distances, so you could drive from Switzerland to England in a half hour or so, so if you're expecting a map as big as Flight Simulator X you'll be disappointed, but I know of no other ground transport game that has this many miles of road.
Lots of detail, especially in the trucks.
Weather changes.
Full day/night cycle.
This developer is constantly coming out with updates to make the game even better.  It's refreshing to see a company support their product to the extent that SCS does with this one.
If you choose to listen, the game comes with a selection of real European radio stations that stream over the internet that you can listen to in the truck as you drive.
Cons:
Physics is a little simple for my tastes, though I understand they're working on an update to adjust this.
Business model is a bit simple too.  You eventually get to the point where you are making money hand over fist, but there are no other competitors to take your market share from you.  (Plenty of other trucks on the roads, but that's all you see of them.)
No snow.  (Hopefully they'll add this later.)
Though your truck can be damaged and the game keeps track of this, no damage visually appears on the body of the truck itself.  I've read that due to licensing agreements with the truck manufacturers that they can't add this later.
Overall:
8.5/10 and rising with each update.

People at first may see this game as a horrible, cruel, violent, psychopathic, rage inducing, sleep preventing, pornographic, time inducing game. But really, it's a fun environment for the whole family to enjoy from the age of three upwards!
Don't be thrown by reviews and videos of naked men and women running about with rocks, for this is only part of the fun. Plus, if you like (which I doubt you would) you can enable a blur to be placed in front of the naked men and women's genitalia.
Of course there will be the occasional hacker, just like with every game out there; but Facepunch are doing their best to eliminate these people from the toxic rust community with weekly updates. Did I just say toxic? I meant friendly.
This game takes a lot of time to master, it also takes a lot of time in general to do anything within the game. So this game is for people with a lot of time on their hands and have reached the patience equal to that of a monk.
The base building is also a pain to master also, ranging from a twig material to an armoured one. Over time you'll find yourself being raided a lot, but also being able to learn from where you went wrong and how to improve on your base design. The base building in this game is literally a trial and error but there are some very good tips for new players on YouTube.
The optimisation of this game isn't the best, but what can you expect from an early access game? Besides, even at the most basic graphic settings, the game still looks beautiful.
Did this game make me rage? No.
Did this game cause me to break things I own? No.
Did I die a lot? No.
Did I make new friends? No.
Did I have fun throughout the whole Rust experience? Of course.
Overall, this game is not for the faint hearted. You will die, a lot. You will rage, a lot. But this game is honestly, in my opinion, a 1/10 and I can't get enough of it.

I like survival games, I'm a dolt like that. I've had good fun with ARK, Rust, 7D2D and even Miscreated. But DayZ eludes me for a few reasons, and I'd like to share them. Perhaps this will influence you, dear reader, on whether you should get this game (hint, no).
1) DayZ performs REALLY badly. I have an i7-6700, 16gb DDR4 ram, the game is installed on an SSD and my gpu is a GTX1080. Running most modern games should be a cakewalk. DOOM gives me stable 150-160fps on max graphics, hell even ARK is somewhat stable and runs at around 50-60 with everything maxed out. But DayZ you ask? Constant microstuttering, framedrops, wild framerate fluctuations and the game still looks like utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ The textures are low quality, the lighting is sub-par, the animations are wank. Only the view distance is probably ok here. So why does the game perform so abysmally? I can't fathom why it can't handle a stable framerate, since stuttering when fighting just means that you will die.
2) Dying and respawning. When you respawn, it's in the middle of absolutely nowhere. And there will be no food to be found and barely any items. There are no vehicles, so you run. And run. And run. And you are starving. And there's no food. And you eat worms and apples. And there are no animals. Compared to any other survival game where you spawn in, DayZ has a brutal learning curve that just discourages starting the whole thing. Sure, it's "hard core survival"  - the feeling of being royally screwed sets in really fast, but it doesn't mean it's FUN. Even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ food/drink system in ARK feels great compared to this.
3) No loot. Since the game is all about looting, it's weird how bad the loot is. Sure there's clothes and shoes and random guns, but it's not interesting. And apparently in the 0.61 version it's bugged too. The coastal areas have very little loot even on empty servers, and definitely no food to go around. The feeling I get is "why bother", and I just go and play something else.
4) Overall feel. DayZ is built on the foundations of ArmA, and it shows. The game feels sluggish, archaic and convoluted for the sake of being that. I'd like to compare the control scheme to say...Rainbow Six Siege. Both games have simlar movement options available to you, but Siege is smooth, whilst DayZ is arthritic. Everything stutters, has innane amounts of delay - and I'm not sure if it's intentional or just bad performance and you mostly and up clipping into something. Melee feels really bad, since hitboxes are♥♥♥♥♥♥ the delay makes calculating hits hard, and it's punishing as hell. Yeah, you aren't supposed to fight the zombies in melee, but give me a break. I want the zombies to be deadly, and not because the game sucks.
Overall, this grand dad of the survival game genre has been vastly outperformed by every single contender out there. It's just that bad. It's just not fun. There are no reasons to pick this up, especially given the pricepoint, since you can just get a better game. Want that gritty realism - Miscreated is better (even though it's janky as fuark). Want zombies - 7 Days to Die. Crafting is better in any friggin other game too. Gunplay goes to Rust. Why bother with this.

300 solid hours on this game over the past couple of years and I can safely say I've mostly enjoyed it. I give a recommendation for this game BUT there are some things you should know and be prepared for before you buy.
1. The Early Access Alpha has been going on for 3+ years now and despite the Dev's best effort to make the game a solid experience it is still plagued with bugs that you will have to deal with. I can understand some people's bad reviews bc of this frustration, but for me it was always about how you can get around those bugs and still have a fun time.
2. The learning curve is pretty steep initially. The Map is ♥♥♥♥ing huge and you will be lost forever unless you have a 2nd monitor to look at an online map like Izurvive or DayzDB. You also have to run everywhere so getting from one end of the map to the other could take hours if you stop to loot along the way. Everything, including directional signs, in game is in Russian you will have to translate and get the common abreviations for towns/cities/locations (which most vet players can tell you). You will have a really hard time finding edible food/drink and will probably either starve or get sick drinking pond water without using purification tabs. You'll have to research which ammo type can go in which gun, if it rains a lot and you get wet you have to build a fire and dry off or you will die of hypothermia, etc., etc. Most of these things you can look up online or get help from other players (if they are friendly enough to not kill you on sight). It's a lot to figure out but if you find a friend to teach you these things, it makes the game much easier to deal with. That brings me to this next point.
3. The game is much more fun when you play with friends or if you meet up and play with randoms who are friendly. You will learn so much more about the game if you find a friendly player who knows their♥♥♥♥♥♥and is willing to teach you a few things. Human interaction in general is often what makes this game worthwhile.
4. PVP and Unique encounters. Speaking of human interaction, this probably the biggest point I can emphasize besides learning the mechanics of the game. Be prepared to die. A lot. Be prepared to get knocked out from behind and have all your gear stolen. You will get sniped out of nowhere. You will have someone pretend to be friendly and the second your guard is down with them, they will smash your face in with a sledge hammer. You will get out played and killed by a guy with a garden hoe when you have a pistol with ammo. You will want to kill yourself (by pressing F11). This game is brutal as hell when it comes to PvP. Basically, git gud scrub. But it's also where funny and ♥♥♥♥ed up♥♥♥♥♥♥can happen. Someone will take you captive, break your legs, have their way with you, and then give you a loaded pistol to kill them with only for you to find out the ammo is ruined and the gun jams. Sadistic ♥♥♥♥s.
5. RP. So this is something that can be a fun break from just killing and looting. There are RP servers both heavy and light and its generally a more fun experience if you enjoy that sort of thing.
That's a few things to consider before purchasing this game. IMO this game still has a long way to go, and while it's easy to criticize the devs for what they haven't done to fix the game, it's important to remember what they have done. Zombies were improved, the new renderer improved optimizing the game, the new sound engine, etc. The progress is slow but if you aren't concerned about it and just want to enjoy what is there, then go ahead and give it a try.

Is Euro Truck Simulator 2 fun? I'm not sure. What I am sure of is that I've spent more time playing it than any other game I picked up during the summer sale thus far. But why is it that when I should be riding techno dinosaurs in Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon or building a group of survivors in State of Decay I am instead carefully driving a load of logs through the English countryside, listening to French radio and checking my mirrors every time I want to change lanes? I have no real way of putting it into words. I guess because it evokes a sense of calm. If you've got the right music playing and you're in the groove on the highway, it suddenly becomes easy to fantasize about the simplicity and peacefullness that is being a trucker.
Maybe an easier way of putting it is to compare it to the game Zen Bound. Do you remember that game? It was an iOS game in which you turned a piece of wood around and around in an effort to wrap a paint covered string around it. The developers advertised it as a cathartic experience because while there was a "win condition," the game didn't time you or really penalize you for losing. It was all about focusing your brain without applying stress to it. That's what Euro Truck Simulator 2 is. Its funny that such a meditative experience hides behind something so apparently boring as driving a truck, and maybe the developers themselves didn't really understand the effect experiencing their game would have on the player. In that sense, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a happy yet unlikely twist of fate. After a busy day I like the idea of driving through a sun dappled countryside listening to the radio over stressing about whether or not I have enough ingredients for a fire before nightfall in Don't Starve.
Of course this is a assisted by the tremendous level of nuance applied ot the game that begins to expose itself the more you play (although these will all sound pretty dumb to someone who's not already on this game's level). Constructions sites will come out of nowhere, there will be heavy traffic in areas where there shouldn't be. The AI has its flaws certainly, but on the whole its extremely intelligent. One time I got to an intersection where another guy stopped to my right at pretty much the same time. I tried  to give him the right of way, but he just sat there waiting for me to go. I inched out, and oh he inched out at the same time. Inch, inch. Part of me wished I could just wave to my computer screen "go ahead, go ahead." The subtle realsim in a moment like that is incredible, and its compounded by the fact that the radio that you're listening to (if you're listening to one of the game's streams) is real. You're not getting some recycled GTA radio tied to the game, RTL 2 is actually streaming from France, including commercials, traffic updates (I think, I don't speak French), morning zoo bits making fun of politics and their very own jingle ("Rrr tee lll duuuuu!"). Its constantly changing with the times and feels current, and you have no idea what kind of spell that can cast in a simulation game. It actually makes me want to try it with the Oculus Rift, if the gods of Zuckerberg ever decide to grace the unwashed nondeveloper masses with it.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

This game confuses me for two reasons.
First off, I do not know how, why, or through what it has accomplished this (and cannot explain it either), but somehow... I like it. Somehow, I like driving a truck across Europe to deliver things from one place to another, trying to make sure I don't damage the truck (and still wind up damaging it anyways). Somehow, this fascinates some remote area of my mind and makes me want to play more of it. I do not know how. I do not know why. All I know is that this is the truth.
Second, I'm a 'murrican who barely knows the rules of the road in America (still working towards getting my license :P), and this game sorta throws you straight into the lions' den of not just driving a truck, but driving a truck in Europe. It won't hold your hand for long: after a very brief explanation on how to move forwards and backwards, it will expect you to be proficient in delivering cargo for a pretty decent distance. It will expect you know the rules of the road, how to read signs, and how to drive a truck without crashing it into stuff. I know few of these things, so I often find my balance littered with fees from crashing into other cars, not turning on/off my headlights at appropriate times, etc. It will also expect you to be perfectly capable of driving in the pitch dark after a few game hours or so of driving.
It's a challenge. But I like a challenge. And maybe that's how this game somehow managed to make me enjoy it.
And I can tell that the game itself was very well worked on. The simulation is pretty much perfect, as far as I can tell: controls are smooth and work great, AIs work pretty much how one might expect (although, something tells me road rage isn't as bad in Europe as it sorta is in California, US: with some of the unsafe driving maneuvers I was using, I expected honking, swearing, and an occasional one-finger salute, yet they remained completely silent XD), loading across towns and whatnot seems practically seamless, stuff like that. They've done a great job simulating the game.
So, all in all, it's a good game that somehow turns out to be very enjoyable. I don't think I'll find it relaxing like it's been reviewed until I have a couple bajillion hours into it, but it's enjoyable nevertheless.

All around me, my social life is surrounded with people of the age 15 and 1/2. They rocket away and study the DMV to get their permits as fast as the wind allowed. They acheive their permits, and in 6 months they eagerly earn their licenses, and laugh of their driving adventures and mistakes, while also giving me, another friend, a ride when he needs it.
I never had much desire to drive, it just felt like a dangerous chore to me. Study a painfully long book (which I was doing but with little commitment and speed, took me nearly a year to actually finish it) take a hard test, go onto the road and just be pressured all the time. I was far too lazy to even get through the book and tests, it was tedious and boring. As time went on, I was nearly 16 and 1/2, even lacking a permit. And so many situations would have been made easier if I got it earlier, but I had usually had to take advantage of someone who could drive, in some shape or form. A lot of times it was my parents, which just felt worse depending on the distance.
One day bored, I decide to play Euro Truck Simulator 2 out of boredom, starting up I realize I know most of the basic driving laws at this point let's try this game out. I was hooked. The goals of striving for a new truck, or a new business upgrade kept the game alive. But a lot of fun wasn't the only thing that got me, I had gained the desire and confidence to drive.
I skimmed through the rest of the book, took the practice test, passed, and then went to the DMV and passed the real permit test first try (barely). At this point I still have my permit, but if it wasn't for Euro Truck Simulator 2, there is a very good chance I would still be slacking off and hardly touching the book, thank you Euro Truck.

In depth

As a military game DayZ is very hard because of switching 3rd person and 1st person cameras, reloading your gun, healing yourself and it should be challenging. However it was too challenging for me as I was too slow to draw my weapon and I easily pressed wrong button during the attack or smth. Something odd kept happening almost every time I was in the battle situation. Sometimes it's because of bugs or features that aren't working as intended and sometimes it was simply stupid player panicing because this game makes your heartrate at least 250bpm. If just you knew who is enemy and who's your friend... On the other hand I really liked the looting and running in the woods. PVE isn't actually hard in this game. Alright. Ahem...     UNDERTALE.
A game where you play as a kid name Frisk, who acidentally fell down a mountain, leading into "The Underground" filled with insane monsters (that are somewhat funny and friendly).
I knew this game when my friends (almost everyone) on skype recommend me to play undertale. I seen people play it like PewDiePie or JackSepticEye and people make songs out of it like DAGames. So after I see that there are alot of undertale on youtube, I might aswell play it. Did I waste my money on a crappy game? No, and its NOT CRAPPY. This game is worth your money.
I love playing games like these. I never fell in love with game characters other than this game. This game can really touch your heart. It has that kind of feel to it that makes you want to keep playing and not wanting to stop. You can always reset and start again or keep going and all. There are many theories and mysteries behind some of the characters in the game like Sans and theories about the underground and the game itself. Its crazy trust me. I tried to figure things out myself and it put my brain in a knot. But I do not want to talk about that. What I wanna review is the game characters 1 out of 10 and the story line 1 out of 10 aswell as the game overall (In a summary) 1 out of 10.
Characters:
Frisk: This character is who you are. Your a kid who fell down a mountain and is to find their way back but meets monsters on the way. I really have nothing to say but that this kid would not be me at all. If I was Frisk, I WOULD SO STAY UNDERGROUND WITH THE MONSTERS! 5/10
Flowey: The mystery creature. This flower has alot of dang problems I must say but he can be a badass at times. Flowey is a flower who can know you reseted the game at one time or another (But of course doesn't know after a true reset) and can actually CLOSE YOUR GAME BACK TO YOUR DESKTOP. He also gains a form known as OMEGA FLOWEY (Neutral Ending). And boy is he creepy or is it just me? 8/10
Toriel: The goat lady. Toriel was the queen of the underground but left his husband for the reason of taking the souls of humans that fell down (to break the barrier that keeps the monsters underground). Toriel, the guardian of the Ruins meets you after flowey attempts to kill you in the beginning of the game and make you welcome in her home in the Ruins. Sadly you leave her after her battle and of course yeah. Overall, 6.5/10
Sans: Sans is a skeleton that is a funny, joke loving... skeleton? I honestly dont know what to say other than this guy needs to be *pun*ished cause his puns are so *tear*able that we have to sit and do nothing but write down all the skele*tons* of puns he makes per day. Also he can cause you to have a bad time and all. 10/10
Papyrus: Papyrus is the brother of Sans who really badly wants to join the royal guard but attempting to capture Frisk but instead befriends you. He is a really fun guy I have to say. He isn't my favorite but hes on the list of awesome characters in games. 9.5/10
Undyne: Undyne is the leader of the royal guard who tries to kill you and steal your soul for the king of the underground. Later on you kinda befriend her. Friends with a fish? Never thought that was possible. Oh in Undertale you can be friends with a fish lady? Oh... makes sense. 8.5/10
Alphys: Doctor Alphys is the (royal?) scientist working for the king. You meet alphys who her lab and you be friends with her and... lets say she is insane on social media. As you walk around, you have to stop to read her spam of social media updates and all.    ... Honestly get twitter. That is where I get all my best trends at. 8/10
Mettaton: Mettaton is a robot made by Alphys. MTT is a the a popular person in the underground if somewhat. Its like... I dont know. You fight Mettaton and you fight them again but more intense and... I just gotta love Mettation for the legs. Im gonna get my arms removed and replace them with legs. 9.5/10
Asgore: The king of the underground. You meet asgore in his throne room and as he wants to have a seat with you and have a cup of tea with him, he says "You know how it is down here" pointing to the fact he has to kill you and steal your soul to break the barrier keeping the monsters underground. He is a nice guy and I just love his personality. I would so go for tea right now infact. Im going to QT now. 9.5/10
Asriel: The son of Asgore and Toriel. Asriel died and became a flower (Flowey) but returns in a form. Asriel tries to kill you but your soul refused to die. As your fighting Asriel, you save your friends from whatever curse they were under by Asriel and eventually, save ASRIEL. He turns back into a kid (Which is his main self ya know?). He eventually gave his souls up and all the souls he got broke the barrier. It was sad for Asriel to leave cause he would turn back into a flower without a soul. I love Asriel and his personality. This is my most favorite character in Undertale. 11/10
The Story Line:
You play as Frisk, a kid who fell into the undergound and try to return to the surface. Along the way, you meet friendly monsters. You face dangers, you make friends, heck... you can even date a skeleton. Will you make it out alive and return to the surface? That is for you to find out. I give the story line a 9.5/10
SUMMARY: Overall this game I would recommend to this to everyone I know and dont know. This game can really touch your heart and you can connect with some of the characters too. I never fell this much in love with a game EVER! Toby Fox did a really good job on the soundtrack aswell and the character ideas and stuff. Same props go to Temmie Chang.
Overall... This game is a 10/10 for me.

This game confuses me for two reasons.
First off, I do not know how, why, or through what it has accomplished this (and cannot explain it either), but somehow... I like it. Somehow, I like driving a truck across Europe to deliver things from one place to another, trying to make sure I don't damage the truck (and still wind up damaging it anyways). Somehow, this fascinates some remote area of my mind and makes me want to play more of it. I do not know how. I do not know why. All I know is that this is the truth.
Second, I'm a 'murrican who barely knows the rules of the road in America (still working towards getting my license :P), and this game sorta throws you straight into the lions' den of not just driving a truck, but driving a truck in Europe. It won't hold your hand for long: after a very brief explanation on how to move forwards and backwards, it will expect you to be proficient in delivering cargo for a pretty decent distance. It will expect you know the rules of the road, how to read signs, and how to drive a truck without crashing it into stuff. I know few of these things, so I often find my balance littered with fees from crashing into other cars, not turning on/off my headlights at appropriate times, etc. It will also expect you to be perfectly capable of driving in the pitch dark after a few game hours or so of driving.
It's a challenge. But I like a challenge. And maybe that's how this game somehow managed to make me enjoy it.
And I can tell that the game itself was very well worked on. The simulation is pretty much perfect, as far as I can tell: controls are smooth and work great, AIs work pretty much how one might expect (although, something tells me road rage isn't as bad in Europe as it sorta is in California, US: with some of the unsafe driving maneuvers I was using, I expected honking, swearing, and an occasional one-finger salute, yet they remained completely silent XD), loading across towns and whatnot seems practically seamless, stuff like that. They've done a great job simulating the game.
So, all in all, it's a good game that somehow turns out to be very enjoyable. I don't think I'll find it relaxing like it's been reviewed until I have a couple bajillion hours into it, but it's enjoyable nevertheless.

All around me, my social life is surrounded with people of the age 15 and 1/2. They rocket away and study the DMV to get their permits as fast as the wind allowed. They acheive their permits, and in 6 months they eagerly earn their licenses, and laugh of their driving adventures and mistakes, while also giving me, another friend, a ride when he needs it.
I never had much desire to drive, it just felt like a dangerous chore to me. Study a painfully long book (which I was doing but with little commitment and speed, took me nearly a year to actually finish it) take a hard test, go onto the road and just be pressured all the time. I was far too lazy to even get through the book and tests, it was tedious and boring. As time went on, I was nearly 16 and 1/2, even lacking a permit. And so many situations would have been made easier if I got it earlier, but I had usually had to take advantage of someone who could drive, in some shape or form. A lot of times it was my parents, which just felt worse depending on the distance.
One day bored, I decide to play Euro Truck Simulator 2 out of boredom, starting up I realize I know most of the basic driving laws at this point let's try this game out. I was hooked. The goals of striving for a new truck, or a new business upgrade kept the game alive. But a lot of fun wasn't the only thing that got me, I had gained the desire and confidence to drive.
I skimmed through the rest of the book, took the practice test, passed, and then went to the DMV and passed the real permit test first try (barely). At this point I still have my permit, but if it wasn't for Euro Truck Simulator 2, there is a very good chance I would still be slacking off and hardly touching the book, thank you Euro Truck.

Alright. Ahem...     UNDERTALE.
A game where you play as a kid name Frisk, who acidentally fell down a mountain, leading into "The Underground" filled with insane monsters (that are somewhat funny and friendly).
I knew this game when my friends (almost everyone) on skype recommend me to play undertale. I seen people play it like PewDiePie or JackSepticEye and people make songs out of it like DAGames. So after I see that there are alot of undertale on youtube, I might aswell play it. Did I waste my money on a crappy game? No, and its NOT CRAPPY. This game is worth your money.
I love playing games like these. I never fell in love with game characters other than this game. This game can really touch your heart. It has that kind of feel to it that makes you want to keep playing and not wanting to stop. You can always reset and start again or keep going and all. There are many theories and mysteries behind some of the characters in the game like Sans and theories about the underground and the game itself. Its crazy trust me. I tried to figure things out myself and it put my brain in a knot. But I do not want to talk about that. What I wanna review is the game characters 1 out of 10 and the story line 1 out of 10 aswell as the game overall (In a summary) 1 out of 10.
Characters:
Frisk: This character is who you are. Your a kid who fell down a mountain and is to find their way back but meets monsters on the way. I really have nothing to say but that this kid would not be me at all. If I was Frisk, I WOULD SO STAY UNDERGROUND WITH THE MONSTERS! 5/10
Flowey: The mystery creature. This flower has alot of dang problems I must say but he can be a badass at times. Flowey is a flower who can know you reseted the game at one time or another (But of course doesn't know after a true reset) and can actually CLOSE YOUR GAME BACK TO YOUR DESKTOP. He also gains a form known as OMEGA FLOWEY (Neutral Ending). And boy is he creepy or is it just me? 8/10
Toriel: The goat lady. Toriel was the queen of the underground but left his husband for the reason of taking the souls of humans that fell down (to break the barrier that keeps the monsters underground). Toriel, the guardian of the Ruins meets you after flowey attempts to kill you in the beginning of the game and make you welcome in her home in the Ruins. Sadly you leave her after her battle and of course yeah. Overall, 6.5/10
Sans: Sans is a skeleton that is a funny, joke loving... skeleton? I honestly dont know what to say other than this guy needs to be *pun*ished cause his puns are so *tear*able that we have to sit and do nothing but write down all the skele*tons* of puns he makes per day. Also he can cause you to have a bad time and all. 10/10
Papyrus: Papyrus is the brother of Sans who really badly wants to join the royal guard but attempting to capture Frisk but instead befriends you. He is a really fun guy I have to say. He isn't my favorite but hes on the list of awesome characters in games. 9.5/10
Undyne: Undyne is the leader of the royal guard who tries to kill you and steal your soul for the king of the underground. Later on you kinda befriend her. Friends with a fish? Never thought that was possible. Oh in Undertale you can be friends with a fish lady? Oh... makes sense. 8.5/10
Alphys: Doctor Alphys is the (royal?) scientist working for the king. You meet alphys who her lab and you be friends with her and... lets say she is insane on social media. As you walk around, you have to stop to read her spam of social media updates and all.    ... Honestly get twitter. That is where I get all my best trends at. 8/10
Mettaton: Mettaton is a robot made by Alphys. MTT is a the a popular person in the underground if somewhat. Its like... I dont know. You fight Mettaton and you fight them again but more intense and... I just gotta love Mettation for the legs. Im gonna get my arms removed and replace them with legs. 9.5/10
Asgore: The king of the underground. You meet asgore in his throne room and as he wants to have a seat with you and have a cup of tea with him, he says "You know how it is down here" pointing to the fact he has to kill you and steal your soul to break the barrier keeping the monsters underground. He is a nice guy and I just love his personality. I would so go for tea right now infact. Im going to QT now. 9.5/10
Asriel: The son of Asgore and Toriel. Asriel died and became a flower (Flowey) but returns in a form. Asriel tries to kill you but your soul refused to die. As your fighting Asriel, you save your friends from whatever curse they were under by Asriel and eventually, save ASRIEL. He turns back into a kid (Which is his main self ya know?). He eventually gave his souls up and all the souls he got broke the barrier. It was sad for Asriel to leave cause he would turn back into a flower without a soul. I love Asriel and his personality. This is my most favorite character in Undertale. 11/10
The Story Line:
You play as Frisk, a kid who fell into the undergound and try to return to the surface. Along the way, you meet friendly monsters. You face dangers, you make friends, heck... you can even date a skeleton. Will you make it out alive and return to the surface? That is for you to find out. I give the story line a 9.5/10
SUMMARY: Overall this game I would recommend to this to everyone I know and dont know. This game can really touch your heart and you can connect with some of the characters too. I never fell this much in love with a game EVER! Toby Fox did a really good job on the soundtrack aswell and the character ideas and stuff. Same props go to Temmie Chang.
Overall... This game is a 10/10 for me.

It's fun.
Guns, explosions. Lots of both. Multiply this times 4 and add synergies between items, skills and environment. Take 50 hours out of your life to become an unstoppable force and enjoy dropping enemies left and right. Your playing style is predetermined by your equipment, class and skills as in every action RPG. There are tons of synergy between those factors and developing your new hero is really fun.
It's stuck between Pandora and Mediocristan.

It's not a game that offers great depth to dive into and is like a pun based TV show. Between some easter eggs, innuendos, crazy NPCs and the occasional good drop you'll fight enemies whose sole difficulty lies within their hitpoints.

Is Euro Truck Simulator 2 fun? I'm not sure. What I am sure of is that I've spent more time playing it than any other game I picked up during the summer sale thus far. But why is it that when I should be riding techno dinosaurs in Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon or building a group of survivors in State of Decay I am instead carefully driving a load of logs through the English countryside, listening to French radio and checking my mirrors every time I want to change lanes? I have no real way of putting it into words. I guess because it evokes a sense of calm. If you've got the right music playing and you're in the groove on the highway, it suddenly becomes easy to fantasize about the simplicity and peacefullness that is being a trucker.
Maybe an easier way of putting it is to compare it to the game Zen Bound. Do you remember that game? It was an iOS game in which you turned a piece of wood around and around in an effort to wrap a paint covered string around it. The developers advertised it as a cathartic experience because while there was a "win condition," the game didn't time you or really penalize you for losing. It was all about focusing your brain without applying stress to it. That's what Euro Truck Simulator 2 is. Its funny that such a meditative experience hides behind something so apparently boring as driving a truck, and maybe the developers themselves didn't really understand the effect experiencing their game would have on the player. In that sense, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a happy yet unlikely twist of fate. After a busy day I like the idea of driving through a sun dappled countryside listening to the radio over stressing about whether or not I have enough ingredients for a fire before nightfall in Don't Starve.
Of course this is a assisted by the tremendous level of nuance applied ot the game that begins to expose itself the more you play (although these will all sound pretty dumb to someone who's not already on this game's level). Constructions sites will come out of nowhere, there will be heavy traffic in areas where there shouldn't be. The AI has its flaws certainly, but on the whole its extremely intelligent. One time I got to an intersection where another guy stopped to my right at pretty much the same time. I tried  to give him the right of way, but he just sat there waiting for me to go. I inched out, and oh he inched out at the same time. Inch, inch. Part of me wished I could just wave to my computer screen "go ahead, go ahead." The subtle realsim in a moment like that is incredible, and its compounded by the fact that the radio that you're listening to (if you're listening to one of the game's streams) is real. You're not getting some recycled GTA radio tied to the game, RTL 2 is actually streaming from France, including commercials, traffic updates (I think, I don't speak French), morning zoo bits making fun of politics and their very own jingle ("Rrr tee lll duuuuu!"). Its constantly changing with the times and feels current, and you have no idea what kind of spell that can cast in a simulation game. It actually makes me want to try it with the Oculus Rift, if the gods of Zuckerberg ever decide to grace the unwashed nondeveloper masses with it.

In these days of bad German simulators, European Truck Simulator 2 is a breath of fresh air. From the moment you load it up, you are greeted with a beautiful world. When you start to drive the trucks, you can really feel the weight and power that I imagine it must feel like to be a truck driver. The modelling of not only the trucks, but also the AI cars is outstanding. The sounds are almost spot on. The roads offer differing degrees of difficulty. You can imagine you are really behind the wheel of your favourite truck, whether it be Scania, MAN or Volvo, or one of the other trucks in the game. The design of the menu system is beautiful and simplistic. It is easy to use. The addition of a mod menu is another plus, even though SCS Software does not support them. There are many mods out there but I definitely recommend the Jazzycat Trailer mods. The world is absolutely gorgeous if you are fortunate enough to be able to run it at high settings. The only down side to this game (I feel) is that, in my opinion, there isn't enough road. So if you are a trucker at heart, I recommend this game. It is constantly being fixed and worked on, and you are usually lucky enough to find it on sale. So load up and get on the road! Happy trucking!

Undertale is technically a mediocre game in terms of its gameplay. It's simple and lacks much input, apart from the bullet-hell segments.
But if you're here for the characters, story and the overall world, then i can't recommend Undertale enough.
Every character just feels fresh and inspired, with every one of them (including minor NPCs and "enemies") complements each other to build a world full of thought and whimsy put into it.
There's definitely humor, but there's also heartwarming moments that i don't wish to spoil.
Also, it's worth noting that Undertale is the type of game that defies typical video game tropes and bends it to its advantage, much like the stanley parable and (debatably) jazzpunk.

Something about driving to new places and enjoying the scenery, gaining levels to unlock skillpoints, as well as saving up money and keeping your business going, is all weirdly addictive.
Most importantly, distances aren't true to scale, so driving from London to Poland would not take you a whole week in real life. Instead it will take about half an hour, but all the scenery is still there and feels true-to-scale.
I say give the demo a try to see if you like the gameplay. It's only for those with some attention span, though.

For those of you who enjoy a fast-paced action shooter, this is not your game. To perfectly sum up DayZ Standalone, imagine an apple-picking simulator blended with a hiking simulator, now throw in zombies, the inherent evil of man and a bunch guns... The main focus early on is surviving, to gather enough food and drink to be able to last. This is a truly brutal experience given the fact that nearly everything and everybody is either out to kill you, or rob you, or even both. More recently the developers had the fantastic idea of adding wolves in the recent update. That's all well and good, but when they take out vehicles, it makes life in this deadly Russian environment that much harder.
This being said, I love the game. I find the hours spent searching for a good rifle to be so worthwhile when it boils down to it. When your friends have accidentally drank from a pond and contracted a life threatening sickness, and die before your very eyes. Especially when my group is caught in the middle of nowhere and are eaten alive by a pack of man eating wolves. There is something to be said for the level detail already implemented, such as farming, fishing, and cooking. These aspects define this game as something with immense potential, and I so hope to see this game finished one day.
Apple-picking simulator: 10/10

As I have played Euro Truck Simulator 1 (retail edition) for ages, this review might be a little unfair, because I am likely to upvote this quicker than the average other player. At least it feels like that.
With over a hundred hours in this game, I can say that this game is absolutely amazing, the physics work well, but they are far from realistic (like the SpinTires realism), but hey, they work for what this game is made for, and that's driving. A LOT of driving.
Now a short list of what I think is good and bad about the game:
+ Good driving physics.
+ Large amounts of core customization available (extendable with mods).
+ Easy to install mods.
+ Custom radio/music player (you can link to a webpage player as well).
+ Good looking. The trucks look very detailed and the world feels more alive than in most other sims.
+ Easy to understand, there's only a 2KM drive tutorial to show you everything you need to know about the game.
+ Active developer team.
- The AI tends to glitch out sometimes (the developers are working on this).
- AI trucks don't have the same physics as you do, so AI trucks pull up way quicker from a traffic light than you do, even if you are maxed out or using an engine mod.
- BIG and old looking user interface, it becomes annoyingly big if you are on a screen smaller than 21".
- (Some) overpriced DLC. Asking 1.99 EUR for just 5 - 10 new skins/skin patterns seems a little bit too expensive to me.

Let me describe the gameplay first:
This game is a mix of a FPS and a crafting/building game and is strictly multiplayer (although some serves will be empty, so they're as close to SP as you can get). This game is correctly labelled as a survival game, but don't be fooled. Most survival games are about defeating monsters, or conquering your environment. Not Rust. Rust is about surviving other players. You'll spawn with a rock and torch, and you'll use your rock to gather resources to make better tools, and eventually a small base if you can manage it.
Making your first small base may take a while - especially on a well populated server. I recommend trying the game with a friend on a low pop server to get a feel for what it takes to get even the simplest base set up: it can be quite difficult on a good day, and impossible on a bad day. There is a steep learning curve to this game, but if you know someone who knows how to play it will make the experience a lot easier.
Once you've got your base set up, it's now about two things:
1) Defend your base, and all its loot
2) Raid other players' bases, and steal their loot
3) Possibly make friends along the way
There isn't really a proper end game in Rust, and I'm not sure if there will ever be one. But raiding and killing other players can be a satisfying experience. This isn't COD where there is no consequences for losing a skirmish: you could lose everything you've worked to achieve. That's what makes this game the
exciting game I've ever played.
Servers usually wipe weekly,
, which seems fair, given that most players come for the initial 'scramble' and after a few days the weaker players get weeded out from the server. It's a blessing and curse: on the one hand, you want servers to have wiped so that you can join and not instantly be at a disadvantage, but you might also want your hard earned work to stick around longer than a week.
Either way, I highly recommend this game, with all it's best and worst.

Addictive and engaging at first, but the community will get on your nerves fast.
Building your first house, crafting your first set of gear, and exploring the area for the first time feels great. The initial steps are rewarding and fun, but after a while you'll realize that you can't escape the fact that this is a PVP open world game. In terms of success, you get out exactly what you put in. And the average Rust player is putting more in than you. If you're picking up Rust just to play casually, you will get steamrolled by groups of people whose only source of enjoyment is in annoying other players.
I have a hard time connecting with anyone in game. I don't know if it's kids or just people who aren't the brightest, but you could even be giving stuff away and people would still try to kill you with a rock right after spawning in. The chat is a nonstop stream of slurs and posturing (e.g. "i just killed two geared f****ts with bow headshots kill yourself n****r"). I don't care what language people use, but it's symptomatic of a very immature playerbase.
The two observable goals of Rust are 1) Prove that you're the best, and 2) Make sure no one else is having fun. Two people once spent at least half an hour clicking on the wall of my hut. The chest I had inside was worth less than the 50 metal pickaxes they consumed breaking in. On another occasion someone waited at my doorway, staring at their screen for 20 min, until I came back from collecting resources. They didn't even end up getting anything, but it didn't matter. The real prize is undoing other people's progress. Clans will have people taking shifts so that they can raid people as they go offline and not get raided themselves, which makes casual play impossible.
You might think I don't recommend this game because of the toxic community. In part this is true, but ultimately I just didn't find a worthwhile goal to keep me playing.

That something I had lost was the concept of "determination," and Undertale reminded me it still exists. After a full playthrough, mind you a full playthrough in my mindset meaning a Pure Pacifist Run and leaving it at that, I haven't attempted to take my own life since. I've cried and laughed along with this game, made memories with the characters that I'll always cherish and never forget, and I have to thank Toby Fox and his fictional crew for reminding me I want to keep living and sharing smiles with my friends and family.

On side note about gameplay - it gets repetitive after time (or from start), but if you are worried about that, then driving or sim type games are totaly not for you.

I say give the demo a try to see if you like the gameplay. It's only for those with some attention span, though.

Great soundtrack, lovable characters, positive messages, good sense of humour, what's not to love? It made me laugh, and it made me cry, and it made me occasionally squeak in frustration. Let me explain:
1. Made me laugh
While the puns and references may not be many peoples' sense of humour, I loved it. You know a game's funny when it makes you laugh out loud at 11:30 PM with no regard for how loud you are. Also, the characters know when you reload to fix a mistake. That part is ingenious.
2. Made me cry
The characters have so much soul (hope you get that reference) that you can't help but feel guilt whenever you betray, harm, or (God forbid) kill any of them. I've accidentally killed a character that wouldn't get out of my way (blame the crits) and then regretted it later (if you call later five seconds after.)
3. Squeaks?!?
Okay, the squeaks are just my personal sound I make under stress. Please don't judge. But the bossfights (and some wandering monster fights) really are intensive. You must navigate your heart around a box while you are bombarded by bullet hell-style projectiles from all angles. If you don't get at least a bit of stress from that then props to you.
4. Great soundtrack
The soundtrack is pretty atmospheric, and somehow nostalgic AND fresh at the same time. Play through some of it on Spotify and tell me I'm wrong.
5. Random other tidbits about the game
-You don't have to kill anyone (bosses included).
-A flower tells you you're an idiot from time to time, then runs off.
-Lesser Dog is bigger than Greater Dog.
-Omega Flowey is creepy as hell. No matter how prepared you are.
I have no critiques about the game. If it's on sale, get it. I don't care who you are. Just do it.

This game is possibly one of my most loved games. It is definitely full of very many options that you can choose from, in the sense of variety in a singular route. This game also provides you the opportunity to not kill any of the characters in the game, which is definitely a spin on the RPG genre.
I recommend that you play the game through its entirety, not just the Neutral leading to True Pacifist route. There are so many changes to the story in each variation of the Neutral Route (Yes, there are actual variations in Neutral routes depending on who you kill, just don't kill all the monsters if you want to encounter a Neutral route. That's considered a Genocide/No-Mercy route.)
I've previously played through and completed the Pacifist Neutral and True Pacifist routes and I am currently playing through the Genocide/No-Mercy route. The story certainly does shift a significant amount from a peaceful run to a murderous one. I won't be posting spoilers but there are definitely some things to look out for when playing the Genocide/No-Mercy route. I've only gotten about halfway through the route and it is impressive the change(s) that you can experience in it.
The music for this game is very creatively placed and made considering some of these songs repeat leitmotifs in different rhythms or speeds to pass off as other songs in a certain way. It made me laugh at just how witty the creator was with composing those songs. I'm sure that when you play this game, you too will figure out what I mean by this. Aside from the lovely music, the story for the game is nicely made and very witty. There is always something in the dialogue or narrative text that is sure to make you smile or evoke curiosity.
All in all this game is certainly something that everyone should experience and in their own way. Don't let anyone tell you in what order that you should play the routes. Play in your own order. I do, however, recommend to play the game "blind" so you can immerse yourself even more in the experience.

Let me describe the gameplay first:
This game is a mix of a FPS and a crafting/building game and is strictly multiplayer (although some serves will be empty, so they're as close to SP as you can get). This game is correctly labelled as a survival game, but don't be fooled. Most survival games are about defeating monsters, or conquering your environment. Not Rust. Rust is about surviving other players. You'll spawn with a rock and torch, and you'll use your rock to gather resources to make better tools, and eventually a small base if you can manage it.
Making your first small base may take a while - especially on a well populated server. I recommend trying the game with a friend on a low pop server to get a feel for what it takes to get even the simplest base set up: it can be quite difficult on a good day, and impossible on a bad day. There is a steep learning curve to this game, but if you know someone who knows how to play it will make the experience a lot easier.
Once you've got your base set up, it's now about two things:
1) Defend your base, and all its loot
2) Raid other players' bases, and steal their loot
3) Possibly make friends along the way
There isn't really a proper end game in Rust, and I'm not sure if there will ever be one. But raiding and killing other players can be a satisfying experience. This isn't COD where there is no consequences for losing a skirmish: you could lose everything you've worked to achieve. That's what makes this game the
exciting game I've ever played.
Servers usually wipe weekly,
, which seems fair, given that most players come for the initial 'scramble' and after a few days the weaker players get weeded out from the server. It's a blessing and curse: on the one hand, you want servers to have wiped so that you can join and not instantly be at a disadvantage, but you might also want your hard earned work to stick around longer than a week.
Either way, I highly recommend this game, with all it's best and worst.

As I have played Euro Truck Simulator 1 (retail edition) for ages, this review might be a little unfair, because I am likely to upvote this quicker than the average other player. At least it feels like that.
With over a hundred hours in this game, I can say that this game is absolutely amazing, the physics work well, but they are far from realistic (like the SpinTires realism), but hey, they work for what this game is made for, and that's driving. A LOT of driving.
Now a short list of what I think is good and bad about the game:
+ Good driving physics.
+ Large amounts of core customization available (extendable with mods).
+ Easy to install mods.
+ Custom radio/music player (you can link to a webpage player as well).
+ Good looking. The trucks look very detailed and the world feels more alive than in most other sims.
+ Easy to understand, there's only a 2KM drive tutorial to show you everything you need to know about the game.
+ Active developer team.
- The AI tends to glitch out sometimes (the developers are working on this).
- AI trucks don't have the same physics as you do, so AI trucks pull up way quicker from a traffic light than you do, even if you are maxed out or using an engine mod.
- BIG and old looking user interface, it becomes annoyingly big if you are on a screen smaller than 21".
- (Some) overpriced DLC. Asking 1.99 EUR for just 5 - 10 new skins/skin patterns seems a little bit too expensive to me.
Sidenote: I would highly suggest getting the expansion DLCs for this game.
Another Sidenote: If you have all the expansion DLCs for this game, I would highly suggest checking out ProMods, since they make the biggest, most detailed map mod for this game. (but you need all DLCs in order to use it.)

Let me describe the gameplay first:
This game is a mix of a FPS and a crafting/building game and is strictly multiplayer (although some serves will be empty, so they're as close to SP as you can get). This game is correctly labelled as a survival game, but don't be fooled. Most survival games are about defeating monsters, or conquering your environment. Not Rust. Rust is about surviving other players. You'll spawn with a rock and torch, and you'll use your rock to gather resources to make better tools, and eventually a small base if you can manage it.
Making your first small base may take a while - especially on a well populated server. I recommend trying the game with a friend on a low pop server to get a feel for what it takes to get even the simplest base set up: it can be quite difficult on a good day, and impossible on a bad day. There is a steep learning curve to this game, but if you know someone who knows how to play it will make the experience a lot easier.
Once you've got your base set up, it's now about two things:
1) Defend your base, and all its loot
2) Raid other players' bases, and steal their loot
3) Possibly make friends along the way
There isn't really a proper end game in Rust, and I'm not sure if there will ever be one. But raiding and killing other players can be a satisfying experience. This isn't COD where there is no consequences for losing a skirmish: you could lose everything you've worked to achieve. That's what makes this game the
exciting game I've ever played.
Servers usually wipe weekly,
, which seems fair, given that most players come for the initial 'scramble' and after a few days the weaker players get weeded out from the server. It's a blessing and curse: on the one hand, you want servers to have wiped so that you can join and not instantly be at a disadvantage, but you might also want your hard earned work to stick around longer than a week.
Either way, I highly recommend this game, with all it's best and worst.

Addictive and engaging at first, but the community will get on your nerves fast.
Building your first house, crafting your first set of gear, and exploring the area for the first time feels great. The initial steps are rewarding and fun, but after a while you'll realize that you can't escape the fact that this is a PVP open world game. In terms of success, you get out exactly what you put in. And the average Rust player is putting more in than you. If you're picking up Rust just to play casually, you will get steamrolled by groups of people whose only source of enjoyment is in annoying other players.
I have a hard time connecting with anyone in game. I don't know if it's kids or just people who aren't the brightest, but you could even be giving stuff away and people would still try to kill you with a rock right after spawning in. The chat is a nonstop stream of slurs and posturing (e.g. "i just killed two geared f****ts with bow headshots kill yourself n****r"). I don't care what language people use, but it's symptomatic of a very immature playerbase.
The two observable goals of Rust are 1) Prove that you're the best, and 2) Make sure no one else is having fun. Two people once spent at least half an hour clicking on the wall of my hut. The chest I had inside was worth less than the 50 metal pickaxes they consumed breaking in. On another occasion someone waited at my doorway, staring at their screen for 20 min, until I came back from collecting resources. They didn't even end up getting anything, but it didn't matter. The real prize is undoing other people's progress. Clans will have people taking shifts so that they can raid people as they go offline and not get raided themselves, which makes casual play impossible.
You might think I don't recommend this game because of the toxic community. In part this is true, but ultimately I just didn't find a worthwhile goal to keep me playing.

So after playing 200+ hours here are my thoughts. Dayz has its problems. There are bugs, server wipes, and balance issues. It can be very unforgiving to new players, and the crafting can be obscure and confusing. Also there are similar games out there that deliver more features. The interface is a little dated and the controls can take time to master.
However, this game is still in Alpha, so such things should be expected and it clearly states this on the purchase page and in game. Yes it has been in alpha for a long time, but i do not believe a game should be judged on where it *should* have been in its development by now. Rather, I believe it should be judged on the playing experience as it stands at the moment.
The graphics are functional but at times it can look really good, as weather systems phase in and out. Some other similar titles have more stylised visuals, but i prefer Dayz's more realistic approach.
Personally I've had a lot of fun playing this game. It can be very atmospheric at times. But the real hook of the gameplay for me is in its tension. You never know what is going to happen. Death can come quickly at any time, with many players adopting a KOS attitude. This makes descision making and tactical thinking vital to survival. Gunfights can be amazing if expericed players are involved. Do you go in all guns blazing? Or do you track a player for while, watching their movement and picking the perfect moment to take them down? There can be periods of time where not much happens, but this game is not designed as a fast paced FPS.
Recent patches have made infected more of a threat with increased awareness and greater numbers. And though developement is slow, the wheel is turning.
In closing, i would recommend this game to anybody who is willing to look past its faults and see it for what it is. A tense, tactical survival game that can really have its moments.

At this point, Undertale’s reputation precedes itself. That’s too bad, because Undertale seems to inspire either absolute devotion from its fans or outright hatred from those who don’t like it. So you’d be forgiven if you didn’t want to approach such a controversial game.
I love Undertale, but it sure worked hard to earn that love from me. At first I thought I was playing a cute, strange homage to Earthbound: it looked like a Japanese RPG from the NES era, it was surprisingly tough, and it didn’t seem sure of where it was going. I couldn’t for the life of me fathom how it inspired such devotion from its fans.
After about an hour, Undertale finishes making its pitch to you. You start to understand the depth of the impact your choices have, and the cast of characters and sense of humor begin to mature. With each new section of the game, Undertale redoubles its efforts and portrays everything that came before with new significance. It builds and builds and builds until its poignant conclusion—a finale entirely of your own making.
I don’t really know how to sell a skeptic on Undertale. (If I did, this game would be in a very different position on this list.) But maybe it all comes down to this: Undertale has a real heart. It’s a warm game that wants to make you laugh and to have fun, and that devotion shows in every enemy encounter, every one-off snippet of weird dialogue, and every easter egg crammed into the game’s environments. It’s also the most genuine game I think I’ve ever played; the experience felt authentic, honest, and tonally consistent throughout. It probably helps that one person, Toby Fox, is the author of virtually every aspect of this game—the art, the programming, the music, the design.
Undertale feels deeply personal, and it succeeds at having an earnest dialogue with the player in a way that very few games in history ever have.

While I do recommend this game, first let me list a bunch of things I do not like about it, before telling you why it is in fact fun.
1.  No places to turn around.  The GPS in this game does not give you any audio clues as to when you are supposed to turn, so if you miss your turn due to the GPS not being obvious enough, expect to be driving another 3 hours down the road (5-10 minutes ingame) in order to find a place to turn around, or get ready to drive into oncoming traffic.  (Stupid.)
2.  The speed limit changes sometimes as often as every 50 yards, and the signs are very easy to miss, so expect to be getting a lot of speeding tickets for seemingly no reason.
3.  The headlight laws in the game are absolutely nuts.  You can be fined any time you don't have your lights on after 5pm, even though the world doesn't even start to get dark until 10pm, and isn't fully dark til 11pm.  (Really stupid.)
4.  Like I said, the GPS is bunk.  A lot of the focus in the game is on staying in your lane, not swerving into other cars (or players in the multiplayer mod).  So if you're really focused on that (and it can be quite difficult, even with a controller) you will often miss turns because the GPS gives you no cues at all other than you having to physically look at it.
5.  The physics.  Sometimes they're alright, and sometimes they're god-awful.  I have had instances where I've been going around a turn at speed and suddenly the truck is sliding - no warning at all.  No skidding of tires as they approach their shear limit, no onscreen traction warning - you just start sliding for seemingly no reason.  It would be really helpful if there were some kind of indicator for when you're getting too fast for a turn, because visually there's no way to tell.
Now, that being said...
The game is strangely fun and addictive.  There's something about driving down roads to make money and listening to your favorite mp3s or music stream that makes it really fun.  Not only that, the multiplayer mod is really what makes this game worth playing.  Currently there is no AI traffic in it, so the roads are clear save for the other players in the game.  And every truck you pass/run alongside is another person!  Not only that, people form truck companies (out of game - there's no ingame function in the mod to make a group company) and run convoys, which looks really fun (but I haven't been able to try yet).  So if you like driving (not racing, but driving), I definitely recommend it.  The fun of the game outweighs the annoyances to an extent. :)

So after playing 200+ hours here are my thoughts. Dayz has its problems. There are bugs, server wipes, and balance issues. It can be very unforgiving to new players, and the crafting can be obscure and confusing. Also there are similar games out there that deliver more features. The interface is a little dated and the controls can take time to master.
However, this game is still in Alpha, so such things should be expected and it clearly states this on the purchase page and in game. Yes it has been in alpha for a long time, but i do not believe a game should be judged on where it *should* have been in its development by now. Rather, I believe it should be judged on the playing experience as it stands at the moment.
The graphics are functional but at times it can look really good, as weather systems phase in and out. Some other similar titles have more stylised visuals, but i prefer Dayz's more realistic approach.
Personally I've had a lot of fun playing this game. It can be very atmospheric at times. But the real hook of the gameplay for me is in its tension. You never know what is going to happen. Death can come quickly at any time, with many players adopting a KOS attitude. This makes descision making and tactical thinking vital to survival. Gunfights can be amazing if expericed players are involved. Do you go in all guns blazing? Or do you track a player for while, watching their movement and picking the perfect moment to take them down? There can be periods of time where not much happens, but this game is not designed as a fast paced FPS.
Recent patches have made infected more of a threat with increased awareness and greater numbers. And though developement is slow, the wheel is turning.
In closing, i would recommend this game to anybody who is willing to look past its faults and see it for what it is. A tense, tactical survival game that can really have its moments.

At this point, Undertale’s reputation precedes itself. That’s too bad, because Undertale seems to inspire either absolute devotion from its fans or outright hatred from those who don’t like it. So you’d be forgiven if you didn’t want to approach such a controversial game.
I love Undertale, but it sure worked hard to earn that love from me. At first I thought I was playing a cute, strange homage to Earthbound: it looked like a Japanese RPG from the NES era, it was surprisingly tough, and it didn’t seem sure of where it was going. I couldn’t for the life of me fathom how it inspired such devotion from its fans.
After about an hour, Undertale finishes making its pitch to you. You start to understand the depth of the impact your choices have, and the cast of characters and sense of humor begin to mature. With each new section of the game, Undertale redoubles its efforts and portrays everything that came before with new significance. It builds and builds and builds until its poignant conclusion—a finale entirely of your own making.
I don’t really know how to sell a skeptic on Undertale. (If I did, this game would be in a very different position on this list.) But maybe it all comes down to this: Undertale has a real heart. It’s a warm game that wants to make you laugh and to have fun, and that devotion shows in every enemy encounter, every one-off snippet of weird dialogue, and every easter egg crammed into the game’s environments. It’s also the most genuine game I think I’ve ever played; the experience felt authentic, honest, and tonally consistent throughout. It probably helps that one person, Toby Fox, is the author of virtually every aspect of this game—the art, the programming, the music, the design.
Undertale feels deeply personal, and it succeeds at having an earnest dialogue with the player in a way that very few games in history ever have.
