EARLY ACCESS REVIEW POSTED: 30 DECEMBER, 2016
Is this game mind blowing? No. Is it fun and worth 5 bucks? Yes. Overall it is a decent survival/crafting game for the cost.
While it doesn’t break new ground, Fragmented hits all the right marks in the survival game genre and at the sale cost of 5 dollars, you get a decent amount of game per dollar. I would recommend it for the person who has never tried a first-person survival/crafting game before and wants to dip their toes in one that works relatively well and isn’t overly complicated.
Most the negative reviews here are from people who are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ about the devs previous early access project, The Repopulation, which is going through some very painful delays. As a backer myself of that game I am also bummed but this review here is focused solely on Fragmented gameplay itself.
Pros:
-Somewhat unique hybrid alien/earth world setting with nice graphics
-Large variety of cool weapons and armor, much more than most survival games
-Overall solid implementation of the standard survival /crafting game aspects
-Very good gamepad support
-Only 5 dollars
Cons:
-Limited features since it’s early access
-Low player base makes multiplayer a bit lonely and the game is mainly PVE for the moment
-Combat is on-par with other early access survival games, meaning it’s rather clunky
-While it implements the survival game basics well, it does feel rather repetitious to similar games and doesn't add much new to the genre
-A few poor UI and inventory management designs
Longer review:
Fragmented joins the fray of the numerous Steam Early Access survival/crafting games. At its core it seems inspired by what I consider to be the original and one of the best survival games, the Arma II mod DayZ (not the standalone version).
You start alone on the planet which you appear to have crash landed on. You then need to proceed to try and survive by staying fed, staying hydrated, staying warm, and of course staying alive. The graphics in Fragmented are nice and having played many early access survival games, it is better than most.
The one unique thing about Fragmented is the setting. It departs from the usual post apocalyptic/zombie environment found in many similar games. While much of the gameplay terrain looks very earthlike, there is a decent variation of alien looking plants and some rather interesting looking alien creatures you will be encountering and fighting. You can even get some as pets to help you.
You do all the basic things you would do in a survival/crafting game. You chop wood, mine stone, gather plants and then combine it all to make better stuff and keep surviving. The base building is modest so far and to clarify this is NOT one of those voxel based games where you can literally modify everything in game and make minecraft-like bases.
The combat is decent but nothing to rave about. Most survival games seem to have bad combat mechanics in general and even 7 Days to Die, which I own and is one of the best selling survival games, has combat that is pretty clunky and jarring. Combat is actually a bit smoother in Fragmented I think but could still use quite a bit of improvement. On the other hand Fragmented has the best variety of weapons and armor I have seen in this genre. From the plain ole stone weapons to sci-fi electro swords, flamethrowers, and laser rifles. It is a nice change of pace and gives you something to aim and progress toward.
I personally am big on gamepad support and Fragmented has done it well. Like many adult gamers I have a real job where I am in front of a computer all day. I want to be able to relax and game on my couch when I get home, and not keep hunching over in front of a desk. This has true gamepad support with inventory management, UI navigation, and hotkeys mapped to gamepad controls. It is almost 100% playable from a gamepad except for a couple functions you still need the mouse for and the radial wheel selector which glitches out occasionally requiring you to reset it with a mouse. Additionally the aiming and settings aren't quite optimized, but overall much better gamepad support than most games like it.
There is one feature most survival crafting games have which this one doesn't that threw me off a bit: the ability to craft or see info about crafting directly from your inventory. Inventory management is an issue in this game and unfortunately you can’t easily see what items can be crafted from the things in your inventory without closing it and opening the crafting menu and finding it in the recipes list there. This makes it more annoying than it should be when you are trying to make more room and figure which things are valuable for crafting and should be kept, and which aren't and can be ditched.
This game also has an annoying hotkey bar “feature”. The things you put on your hotkey bar still remain in your inventory, unless you are actually holding it in your hand. This can often result in the situation where you are holding a melee weapon, you kill something and pick stuff up, then you switch to another tool or weapon on your hotkey bar and your char tries to put his melee weapon back into inventory. But if there is no room since you picked stuff up in the meantime, he just throws it on the ground without warning. I died more than once when this happen since I got attacked right after my char inadvertently threw his main weapon on the ground. Seems like there is a better way to handle this, like just making the things on the hotkey bar their own separate inventory.
The biggest issue right now is the low playerbase. What makes survival games great is the moral dilemmas it puts you in with other players. Do I say hi to this other player I just met or kill him for his berries because I’m starving? Should I work with him which might be better in the long run or take his stuff for a short term one-time gain? Right now there isn’t much of this due to the low player base. Hopefully that will improve with time or you should consider playing it with a friend as I can see coop being rather fun.
Overall, if you have played other survival/crafting games there really isn’t much new here. If you haven't though this is probably one of the more decent games in the genre that has a low learning curve and which you can start playing and having fun surviving and/or dieing immedietly. While the overall game is limited due to its early development stage it has all the survival/crafting gameplay basics one would expect and at its current sale price is worth the cost. Given how early access this is and the unique sci-fi setting, there appears to be a lot of room up for this game to go. So at minimum I think you easily get your 5 dollars worth with the game in it’s current state, and at maximum you get something much better as it develops.

I bought Rust in the last Humble Bundle that was around. I've had my eye on this game for a while but I'm always hesitant in buying survival games that are in Early Access, not many make it out alive.
Me & my brother loaded up our own server to get the gist of the game, we didn't want to just keep getting mowed down by the experienced players while we had no idea what was going on.
20 hours later & we had our first ever house built & it was looking fantastic! (It took us a looooong time to even find each other as we were literally clueless, & then we had to contend with bears being local to our spawns every single time we spawned!)
The graphics in this game are much better than I thought they were gonna be, the menus are finnicky & sometimes a pain to find what you're looking for. Building houses is great, probably the best building mechanic I've used in a survival game so far. The gameplay itself is what you expect from this genre, start naked, smash trees, build, expand, ransack.
There are a couple issues that need addressing though, & I do feel the game may be a ways off full release.
- More variety in wildlife is much needed, it gets boring fast only seeing 2-3 types of animal.
- A better crafting menu system
- The game is prone to crashing, I'm not sure if it causes a memory leak like Ark can, but my PC constantly crashes because the memory used is sky high & constantly rising.
- Being assigned a gender based on your Steam ID. This is a rubbish idea, seriously. I understand the devs want people to recgonize other players on appearance only, but how about the first character you create is the one you're stuck with? I don't want to be some bald fugly woman! I never gender swap in games, so why am I being forced to here? In fact, why are most players female, I don't think I've seen a man yet!
So to summarize, this game is decent in it's current state, but still a while before full release. I wouldn't reccomend paying full price for this title until full release (If it ever comes), but if you can pick it up on the cheap or in a bundle, then 100% worth a shot.
For me it pales in comparison to my favourite survival game, Ark, & yet that games in Early Access & been on the market for less time but the amount of content offered in that game compared to this game is quite shocking.
7/10 - Good game with potential, but few too many issues for a full price purchas currently.

I may have, at this time, only 40 hours on record, but that is only since I have moved it to steam, that is, when patch 1.9 was released.
This game is surely the first in terms of trucking Simulator. It should be in Top 5 in terms of any driving simulator. I have been a fan of the trucking simulators, especially released by SCS and, I am happy to see, that the games improve from one to another. However, it is not perfect.
The trucks included are finally real life brands and, it with the announced Mercedes Actros being included; the big European brands are all coming together. You can choose from a variety of trucks with an extensive configuration possibility.
I especially would like to point out that, with patches, new trucks were added (i.e. new content), which is really nice. In terms of handlings, you can really feel the changes, depending on the trailer weight, which gives it a more real feeling.
There are, in each city, 3 to 8 (approximate) companies from/to which you can pick up and deliver a trailer with cargo. The variation is not too high here and you will immediately see the need of more. But, as always, there are enough mods on specialized sites that will fill in this gap. But still, what is missing in the game is the tandem truck & trailer. On the real road, you get, sometimes, some real nice colour schemes that start from the truck and continue to the end of the trailer. For me, this would have been a really nice feature.
This would be one of the disappointments, from my point of view. With the original game, you get mostly central Europe + UK, which is not really enough for a “Euro” road network. Although even here, more roads could be added, the ones that exist are nicely done.
With the DLC “Going East”, additional roads were added with 3(or 4) more countries. This was a nice addition, especially since the new roads/cities or really built and not reused from other areas.
But, I have to be honest: I am still waiting for Going South/West/North to be released.
On the other hand, there are some mods that you can find and will fill in the gap. But it’s always nicer to have the official part.
Not the main focus of the game, as it is, in the first place, a simulator. But you can build yourself a huge company with a maximum of 5 drivers/garage and 1 garage / city. In the beginning is a little harder but, after getting a couple of trucks and drivers, there is no longer a financial problem and too much money.
In conclusion, if you are looking for a trucking simulator, do not hesitate to choose this one. You will definitely not regret it.

Don't get me wrong, this is a pretty enjoyable game - When it works. Desperately in search for food and water as your hydration and hunger gets higher and higher, and you know you won't survive if you don't find it in time. And on the run, you pick up neat loot with a large variation of clothes from top to toe, vests, backpacks etc. while constantly keeping an eye out for zombies or other players who wish to gut you, lurking around in the shadows...
And then you just *POP* die. It doesn't necessarily have to be a sniper or your hunger level getting low (As if that wasn't enough), I've plenty of times found myself just dying out of literally nothing because of a bugged and broken game. Every hour or so, servers start lagging and desynching so much that you either fall off a cliff and die, or just quit eventually because it's unplayable. And those few times when you manage to stay alive for so long with no problems, that you actually quit the game because you've had enough for the day, your character is most likely to be reset (killed/dead) within the next time you start up the game.
It's a shame the game is as it is, because it has great potential to be amazing. The inventory system is amazing, with bullets that you actually have to load into magazines before loading the mags into your weapon, and you can even chamber single bullets if you don't have a mag. Wearables not only have appearance, but functions as well. You literally stack items into slots in your backpack/vest/jacket/pants. It's just such a shame that all this is in vain.
I like the fact that the developer has begun updating the game again; Decent hoardes of decent zombies, and even dangerous wildlife in the forests. But up until recently, it had been dead for a looong time with the complete absence of zombies. -Literally, no zombies. It just really shows how devoted the developer is with this game - It's broken and it's dead. It can be enjoyable at times, but it is not worth the time when those moments are
by bugs instead of ending in an acceptable way. It is not worth your money, it is not worth your attention.

I truly believe Rust to be one of the greatest games of all time, and it's by far my favorite game, ever - singleplayer or multiplayer. Rust combines the journey of self that is experienced in singleplayer games with the reward for discipline taught by multiplayer competitive games. There simply isn't another feeling like it short of going into real life and doing dope♥♥♥♥♥♥
Like other "hard" gaming feats - successfully raiding in WoW, controlling an island at the head of a coalition in Puzzle Pirates, getting a high rank in a moba or even figuring out how to log into the game in Eve Online, Rust has a steep learning curve which will punch you in the face repeatedly. But, unlike its facepunching peers, Rust allows you to define your own terms of success; it's almost the holy-grail-game of Eve without spreadsheets. You get to do whatever you want, and you'll innately know when you're winning or losing without a meter telling you your score, but the game retains the satisfactory feeling of "getting stuff done" that other casualy-sandboxy games like Battlefield or GTA lack.
And if you want to play the game the "normal" way, as a competitive long-form pvp match against hundreds of other people, it's better than Eve. The best part about Rust is the journey to riches, and every journey you learn more about the game and about yourself (#knowledge). Rust's combat is as visceral as DayZ or Eve and it combines itself with the feeling of accomplishment normally reserved for more arcadey games like LoL or csgo.
-------------
Yes, the game can be played casually for an hour a week and you will still have fun, contrary to what people who haven't played the game will tell you. No, you won't dominate a server, but you wouldn't expect to raid mythics in WoW with an hour a week or become Global in CS with an hour a week, but you can still have fun and find success the same way you can casually in WoW or CS
No, the game is not easy to be good at, but it's as easy to get into as Overwatch and the difficulty & burden of #knowledge creates the depth and replayability that Overwatch doesn't have but games like csgo and mobas do, while still being easier to get into than those games. You don't have to ask questions like "wheres dragon" "whats baron" "why cant i play nami mid", and you don't have to learn how to counterstrafe / what ct economy means / why dont my bullets go where my crosshair points, just to play Rust, BUT, similar mechanics are THERE, and you CAN learn them to get better.
The biggest reason I view Rust as one of the greatest games of all time is that it simutaneously allows people to play a different game within the same game. Just because I play it for the pvp and competition doesn't mean others can't play it like Stardew Valley, and have even more fun than I do. The stories and experiences you will have in Rust are reminiscent of WoW pre-crossrealm and pre-dungeonfinder, but told through a much more entertaining fps-shooter-builder medium than a clunky mmo, AND the #knowledge you gain (improvement) is so much more tangible than other games that it's just as much of a dopamine rush as seeing your level increase or getting a rankup.
Anyone that is able to try something without letting prior notions discourage them will enjoy Rust for what it is, simply because it can be so many different things. I would consider Rust a must-play if you enjoy multiplayer games.

After around an hour and a half of bad spawns, scarce resources, and short-lived ventures into the more inhabited areas of the map, I ran into the first friendly player I had met in Rust. I had initially spotted him pretty far away, but I paid no real notice to him as he had a rock equipped. Eventually he got close enough for us to clearly see each other and, upon the realization that neither of us were hostile, we both pulled out torches as a mutual sign of peace (or the highest possible level of non-aggression that can exist in Rust). I dropped my old hatchet for him as I had just finished crafting one with metal, and he gave me some food as a sign of good faith. After nearly 30 minutes of searching and scavenging, we had pooled enough resources to craft us each some minimally decent gear. We knew that if we wanted to progress any further we would need to mine boulders, and a lot of them. I used what remaining materials we had to put together a 9mm handgun and several bullets, though I reminded him it was only in case we really needed it. I had decided earlier during my many unwanted experiences with bullets to the face that I would try my hardest not to run around slaughtering every newly spawned player that I came across. A few minutes out from camp we had encountered a player with a hunting bow. I had been running with my hatchet out, so I quickly took out the handgun in my inventory and pointed it in his direction, attempting to scare him away. When the player was far enough away we continued up a road towards a few stones. The area was surrounded by trees so I opted to stand guard with the handgun while my friend mined. Just as we were moving on to the next boulder, I heard the gunfire start. I turned around to see a player with an assault rifle gunning down my friend, and before I could land any shots on him he had already begun shooting me. It was at that moment that I remembered I hadn't even crafted a sleeping bag for the camp, as that was one of the objectives of the trip we were taking. I typed into the chat, thanking the friend I had made for all of his help and asking the player who had killed us if we had been intruding in his area or something along those lines. He simply wrote "Sorry guys :D" This is the single problem that I have with games like this. Why does it have to be "shoot-on-sight?" That player had obviously taken us by surprise and was better equipped than us. Even if he had a justifiable reason for approaching two very poorly equipped players (which he really didn't considering we were in the middle of the woods and he had pretty much all of the gear you could need in this game) he could have easily told us to cooperate by either putting away our weapons or just leaving the area. But of course, he comes around, sees some players trying to gather enough supplies to get to a stable point in the game, and decides to go out of his way to approach us and use unecessary ammo for a hatchet and a handgun with four bullets. Then, to add even more of an insult, he adds an apology at the end, as if he had no choice but to shoot two unexpecting, half-naked, unprepared players.
All in all, though, I do see a lot of potential in this game, and the good in the community does shine through every once in a while. I just wish that people would realize that they don't need to go around killing players who haven't had the chance to experience the game. People like that are the single reason why so many players on steam feel that they wasted money on what would otherwise be a great experience.
It's a good & fun game, might take a while to know what the hell you're doing but once you get a few friends you can have even more fun than you would by your self.

I am rewriting my previous positive review.
DayZ is a game like no other, the idea behind it is such gold. DayZ is what I really believe inspired many game developers to make similar survival games. In DayZ players fight the enviorment, zombies, and players to gear up and obviously, survive. The feeling you get when you find ammo for your gun, or when you escape a huge gunfight is extraordinary, it's so rewarding to get what you need to progressively gear up. DayZ is what got me into survival games in the first place, and I love them to pieces. But, as much as I hate to say it, the grandfather of many survival games is among the worst. Even with only 70 hours on the game, I really love and hate it. I am going to go into details now.
PERFORMANCE: The golden question, "Will this game run well on my pc." The answer varies, but for the most part I will say No. The game glitches, it lags in cities, it looks half decent at the same time though. The engine NEEDS to be changed, I guarentee if they could handle performance issues, the game would have 10k+ daily players. But as of now 1/22/17, it does not run well.
GRAPHICS: They are alright. It's not going to be anything special, it's not going to look like the new Call of Duty, but it looks decent enough to get a good feel of what the enviorment is meant to be seen as.
GAMEPLAY: Like no other, if you enjoy taking long loot runs and surviving along the the way, you will love DayZ because that's all the game is.
GUNPLAY: If you ask me, it's horrid. In the middle of a gunfight players run in circles while dragging bullets into their magazines in their inventory. This game's gunfights are not tactical or realistic. It's all the strategy involved to not get hit and hit the other player before he does you.
LOOTING: The reason I can't love this game. The map is HUGE, unlike any other, but what happens is the good loot is 3/4 of the way on the other side of where you spawn. You will run for 30 minutes to reach the North-West Airfield to get an AK, or a gun that is worthwhile.
PLAYERS: The community is unfortunetely KOS no matter what. People will backstab you, people will trick you, people will snipe you. It makes the game real in the sense of everyone's for themselves, but it really sucks when you spend 4 hours collecting gear only to have a single bullet in the head end you. Not to mention how many people use lag and hacks to play the game.
BUGS/GLITCHES: For some games I'd say you MIGHT run into a few bugs, but for DayZ you WILL run into majot bugs and glitches, some gamebreaking, some just minor.
Pros:
Gameplay is unlike any other game
Graphics are good
Tons of items to collect and use
Hardcore
Cons:
Glitches
Hackers
Map size
KOS Community
Zombies are often more deadly than players (So buggy)
Updates are not very often

If Quentin Tarantino, a top-notch comic book artist, and a few drunken soldiers were to come together in a trailer park and develop a video game over a bottle of Jack Daniels, this would be the game. Yes! It is a Tarantinoesque revenge story, with all of the charming kitsch associated with his lovely films. A bit western, a bit sci-fi, tons of nonsense and vulgarity and non-stop violence. Aside form gratuitous sex (which this game does sadly lack) what more could one ask for? How do I love this game? Let me count the ways:
1.The animation is unique and charming; the characters are lovely and attractive and the scenery is top-drawer. I keep having lovely dreams involving Axton.....
2.The storyline is engrossing and lighthearted; I found myself very amused by the tongue-in-cheek dialogue. At one point the main antagonist names his diamond pony “Butt Stallion” in your honor. The voice acting is wonderful.
3.The controls are perfect. I never had any difficulty playing.  I normally am not a fan of first-person shooters as they tend to make me nauseous. I had no such issue with this game.
4.The game play does not become repetitive or boring in the least. You do not have to grind for levels at any point, nor do you constantly have to worry about upgrades. You will find better weapons and shields as the game progresses. The game has several quick-travel points throughout, so you will never find yourself running through miles of desert in order to get to your destination.
5.In terms of difficulty, the game is just right; not so complicated that you become frustrated, and not so easy that you are not challenged.
6.The soundtrack is brilliant and keeps with the fun Southern/Western U.S. theme.
This game will give you days, if not weeks of entertainment. Though I've only played with Axton thus far, I very much look forward to playing again with another character. The game has a bank system that allows you to twink your new characters using your more powerful ones.  If you are looking for originality, quirky fun, ridiculous humor, and carnage, this game is for you! Ten out of Ten!!

Undertale deserves all of the hype it gets. On the surface, it's the tale of a human in a hidden world of monsters. Looking deeper, it's simultaneously a love letter to classic RPGs, a digital poem about philosophy, and an interactive chiptune opera.
This game balances the elements of story, sport, and soundtrack in a splendid, if simplistic, style; the characters are compelling, the encounters are entertaining, and the music is magnificent. What other games accomplish through robust engines, breathtaking graphics, and other such modern conventions, Undertale achieves through a coherent narrative that blends well with the game mechanics.
If you're looking for a triple-A title that reinforces contemporary industry standards, look elsewhere. This game isn't remotely similar to the prolific first person shooters that dominate the market today; Undertale is a bullet hell of a different caliber entirely.

I'd like to start off by saying that no matter how much I like or dislike something I try to look at the situation from every angle possible and I try to not be narrow minded. I really want to say something good about this game but it's just so hard to find anything to compliment it on. I hope that I don't get attacked and downvoted to hell for saying my opinion as this has happened in the past when I got bashed by fanboys of another game. Now that I got that out of the way I can start my review. If you were too lazy to read it there will be a TL;DR at the bottom. Also don't be fooled by my playtime hours I have more on another account.
So I bought this game a few days after it was released back in December 2013 and boy was it lacking in features back then. There were just 2 guns, the M4A1 and FNX45 along with some basic melee weapons like the fire axe and kitchen knife. No vehicles, no animals, no base building. All we would do is get gear and kill each other. Sure it was lacking but it was a very ambitious project and it would surely get better in the future right? WRONG! Back then I was running the game on a laptop that barely covered the minimal requirements but I knew I would be getting a new PC soon so I decided to leave the game and come back in a few months when it would have been a little more polished. When I came back 5-6 months later everything was the same only there were more guns to kill each other with. I rolled with it but it quickly got boring so I decided to do the same thing and wait even more. Meanwhile the game had sold over 2 million copies by then meaning the dev's weren't lacking in the money department so surely they would use the cash to improve the game development right? Wrong again! I kept coming back every few months to check what was new and every time the game would run worse and worse on my new PC which was way above the recommended specs for the game. With every new patch the game would become more unstable and buggy and feature less and less content. Even the creator of the mod Dean Hall cut and run at a certain point abandoning this abomination. Bohemia promised this game would be released by the end of 2016 and here we are at the start of 2017 and the game is still in early alpha. Nowadays the developers seem more focused on adding stuff like more clothes and guns rather than fixing the sh*t AI of zombies or improving server connection. At one point they even removed zombies from the game because they were causing so many problems. Even with zombies you can go for hours without seeing even one. The game is so lacking at this point that the only way I could get any fun out of it was by bullying everyone who was dumb enough not to get away from me. Since there is so very little to do other than to shoot at each other you will barely have an interaction with another player that doesn't end with one of you dying. I guess you could have more fun with friends but you are still limited to killing/harassing other people after getting good gear in an hour or two after spawning. That is about the only good thing I can say about this game. You can have fun for a short while with friends. Maybe in 3 more years the game will be finished and will be much better but I somehow doubt it. The game was already sold to the target audience which gave up on DayZ a time long ago. From the 3 million+ people who bought it about 10-12K still play it. L4D2 which is 8 years old gets 18-20K players a day at its peak. That alone should tell you how dead this game is. The sad truth is that this game promised more than it could ever deliver and the devs were way in over their heads. This entire project turned into one big cash grab and we were all played. I can only hope that people won't get suckered into buying this and that I can save someones money from being wasted. If you want a realistic zombie survival game go buy Project Zomboid. While Project Zomboid has been stuck in alpha too for many years at least it is making progress and is stable enough to enjoy. If you still want an FPS survival game and PZ isn't your cup of tea just buy Rust instead. It's better than DayZ anyway. It seems like there's a simulator for literally everything now. Personally, I'm not a big fan of most of them either. It takes a lot of fine tuning, especially for this genre, to really sell me on it. Euro Truck Simulator 2, however, is something of a rarity. The graphics might not be A+ for 2014, but for what this game offers otherwise, make no mistake that it's one of the best driving games on the market. The map is massive, you can play your own music (and even internet radio stations) for that authentic highway feel, traffic behaves pretty similar to real life, and the actual controls on the trucks themselves are pretty intuitive. You can control the turn signals, warning lights, handbrake, horn, and practically everything else that matters on a vehicle. I noticed you can't roll your windows up or down, however. Nor do your drivers hands actually appear on the steering wheel, which seems a little odd to me. On the larger scale of things, however, only minor grievances. And once you get into it, hardly a game changer. You're gonna be more concerned about not destroying that load of Dynamite on a crowded freeway after awhile, rather than if your hands are properly positioned on 10:00 and 2:00 anyway.
Of course, there's the other amenties of life as well, no matter what you're hauling. Keeping gas in the tank, pulling over at a rest stop whenever you get tired, keeping the other drivers for your firm satisfied so they don't call it quits - all of these little things, as silly as some of it might seem, really do add to the simulation. Especially the part about not falling asleep at the wheel, since you can actually end up wrecking your truck if you're not careful to take heed to it. Of course, in real life you may be looking at police intervention, legal action from the survivors of the crash, punitive damages, unemployment, welfare, alcoholism... but that's water under the bridge. This is still a good game without that level of realism :P. And each truck has its own level of customization attached to it. So there's that too, without spoiling every detail of the game for everyone...
Now, for the TL;DR people:
* Massive, detailed Map, not even counting the Going East expansion
* Impressive amount of features in the trucks, and decently detailed customization
* Custom MP3s and Internet Radio help stave off the boredom, and make driving fun
* Various amenities such as Gas and Sleep are paramount, and aren't just there for vanity
* The graphics are a little dated, and aren't as impressive as other driving games
* The driver's hands and feet are invisible, which just seems odd
* Controlling the windows would be a cool touch, even if it is a little gimmicky/easy to forget
* Driving on the left side of the road for Americans, such as myself, can be strange. But it is Europe.
All in all, however, while I think $24.99 might be just a little steep of a price, if you can even score this game on sale for half that, you're gonna make out pretty nicely (I got it on sale for $4.99 last month, but I certainly wouldn't have complained). I give ETS2 a 9 out of 10, and highly recommend it to anybody who's reading this.

I don't write reviews normally, but, I'm making an  exception for this game because I think it's actually a worthy game and truck sim.  First off, this is the first time owning such a game so I didn't know what to expect.  Just configuring controls for my xbox 360 (pc) pad took a while and it's at this very first step that many will press quit.  Persevere though, with some trial and error along with keyboard assignments (a must in this game) and you will slowly discover this game has more than meets the eye.  For example, this game can stream real european radio-stations and living near Birmingham it's nice to see Kerrang represented which makes it even more real.  Yes, this game is briming with realism, this really is a proper simulation.  Details like excellent realistic rain-on-windscreen effects coupled with working windscreen wipers.  Toggable realistic head-lights (the options are literally the same as on a real vehicle).  Did I mention signalling?  Yep, just like real driving you've got to signal in this game.  Red lights?  Check, you've got to stop!  Speed-limits?  You better drive by the rules or you're going to be fined on every job you complete.  There's even rest locations, re-fuelling, toll-roads etc.  They crammed as much of real-life into this as possible.  Ok, so the roads aren't actually 100% A-Z accurate, but, that's why this is still a game.  Heck, delivering from Uk to Paris would take many real hours so the level of realism is completely acceptable for a game.  As you build-up your finances  and discover dealers and agencies you can grow your company which, then, deals with even more of the business-side of trucking.  Plenty to do in this game, trust me.  Graphics-wise this game isn't the best-looking in the world, but, there's plenty of options to get the most out of it.  The graphics are firmly based on the real-world, down to signs and set-pieces.  As you go abroad you also have to learn to drive on the correct side of the road and obey those countries road rules.  A solid game for trucking or realistic driving fans, there's nothing else like it on the market!  Have fun!

Undertale is a hard game to review.
That's not to say I can't define what makes it good. It's rather that I shouldn't. As popular - insanely popular - as it became, Undertale was, and is, a game best experienced blind. It's a game about simultaneously defying and meeting your expectations. It's a game about surprising you, not just with what it does, but in how it does it. It's a game that is self-aware of the nature of being a game, in which gameplay and story segregation is almost nonexistant.
While it may not be for everyone, anyone will enjoy it less with spoilers. To really see the magic of Undertale, you have to experience it for yourself. You have to make your own choices, see how things play out for yourself, and engage with it on a personal level. It's an RPG whose inventive mechanics go way beyond just the battle system. If you just try to go through beginning to end for the "best" of its multiple endings, it may seem a bit short. Get lost in its world, however, and it can stick with you for a long time, even after the game is turned off.

Rust is a game where you lose. And then you win, and sometimes both at the same time. Rust is a good go-to for evicting children from a hovel made of twigs and broken dreams, midnight swordfights against legions of russians with rocks, or some good ol' fashion divination through the scabs of your most recent encounter. In my opinion, if you want to play rust, there isn't really an alternative. Rust provides it's own experience that - once - was excruciatingly cancerous, groups of 70 with unlimited firearms and impenetrable bases; no longer, no more. With blueprints gone, there is no quarter for zergs, the game has come into it's own, firearms are a chance luxury, and playing on high population servers means everyone is on edge and jittery, you
kill that dude with the AK so long as you have something sharp to poke them with. Rust is most enjoyable in the early, pre-wipe stages where guns are an extreme rarity, or on medieval/primitive servers where meme magic wins most fights. No roof-camping - nobody has a roof. The playing field is level, and for those first 24 hours the game plays like DayZ but replace the survivors and guns with Zulus and spears.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a genuinely surprising game.
If you want to just get to the hard facts of the review, scroll down a bit.
After playing the demo of the original Euro Truck Simulator over a year ago now, I was very satisfied with what I saw. However, I later went on to try the demo of ETS 2, and have never looked back since. Don't be fooled by my mere 48 hours (at the time of writing) game time; I owned the game for ages before buying it with the DLC through Steam on discount. When I first started playing, the game was v1.2.5.1, which had the attraction of a newly aqcuired DAF license. You have to bear in mind that SCS used to be (and still sort of is) a tiny company, which didn't have the most outrageous budget to create a game.
That is why Euro Truck Simulator 2 is even more remarkable; from producing a mediocre game (harsh but true in terms of graphics, physics and sounds) in ETS 1, SCS has worked its proverbials off to deliver a game that has been improved and added to in literally every aspect. Since its 'birth' 18 months ago, ETS 2 has grown a gigantic amount. When it was released, there was only a license for MAN, Renault and Scania trucks. After the DAF license of 1.2.5, 1.3.1 saw the aquisition of IVECO and Volvo licenses, 1.4.1 saw the introduction of the IVECO Stralis Hi-Way, 1.7 saw a new Volvo implemented, likewise 1.8 a new Scania. 1.9 completely re-wrote the AI. ETS 2 has grown a huge amount, adding detail updates like fuel economy, adaptive automatic transmission, the list goes on.
Amazingly, all these crucial updates have come in just over a year after release, meaning they happen quite regularly, more than can be said for most games. Like Mendeleev's Periodic Table, SCS knew that gaps would be left by them when they made the game, so they also made the game easily moddable. Thousands of mods have been distributed on great sites, like the one second from top after you type 'ETS 2' into google, so players can easily choose what they want to make their game suited to them. I currently run around 40 mods, from everything such as real logos for AI cars to more realistic weather.
So what's it like to actually get behind the wheel?
Gameplay:
- There's no denying that the concept of ETS 2 is boring to an awful lot of people; You find a job, drive to it on your satnav, pick up a trailer of some yoghurt or organic logs, drive a thousand miles, park up awkwardly and recieve a seemingly small paycheck for your hard work. However, by following the "If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen" proverb, if you don't like truck driving, don't buy a truck driving game!
- However, you don't neccesarily have to enjoy truck driving or be an ex-trucker to like this game, although a lot of players are. ETS 2 has been designed with at least some thought of enjoyment to players; with many customisation options for your truck, trucks to buy, sights to see etcetera. Generally though, you can't avoid the sole purpose of the game for too long, as you will get bored of the customisation very quickly and some customisation mods will crash your game. However, some are genuinely a nice touch. Also, you do sort of have to drive to see the sights anyway.
- ETS 2 offers a large map area to explore, the default stretching from Aberdeen in Scotland down to Vienna (Wien) in Austria. You can buy the Eastern Expansion DLC, which I highly recommend, letting you explore a whole lot more of Poland and Hungary/ Czech Republic (In my opinion, they could have expanded the latters slighly more for the £9.99 price tag). I also run a well-known map mod which I don't care to name but let's it works with the "quality not quantity" idea ;)
- The timing in ETS 2 allows day/ night cycles to pass quickly; a minute in game is about 3 real life seconds. This means you don't actually have to drive a thousand miles, as the scale is shortened too; a mile takes just a couple of seconds to cover at full pelt. (90km/h or 55mph)
- The detail in ETS 2, such as fuel consupmtion, fuel tank, headlights, indicators, hazard warning lights, and the like, really adds to the realism.
Trucks:
- Truck physics are 1 billion times better than the first game and actually feel right, although I've never driven one in real life
- Huge variety to choose from when you take mods into account. Most people who play (40%) tend to drive a Scania mostly but I'm a Volvo guy myself. Engine choices aplenty.
- Truck engine sounds are to my taste but some say they are too quiet or wrong. Again, mods fix this.
Menus and discoveries:
- ETS 2 has a single-screen interface from where you can easily manage your trucks, garages, drivers, buy trucks online or in dealers, change you settings, configure your controller, free drive across Europe, etcetera.
- You can get jobs in new cities by driving into them and discovering them, you can also access the city's truck dealer and recruitment agency, but you can also do this 'online'.
Environment:
- Graphics are very good inside the truck and of the truck exterior but lack somewhat on AI cars and distant landscapes. Generaly higher than most simulators though.
- AI re-write as of 1.9 claims to have improved the God-awful previous AI a lot, but some areas I still think could be improved. However this could be due to my running of complicated map mods.
- In-game trailers and companies are incredibly dull, not that many default colour schemes or loads, no oversized or heavy trailers (ignore what the game says). You will want to install trailer mods as soon as you can.
Education:
- You learn a surprising amount about European geography as well as trucks from this game!
Lasting Appeal:
- If you can get into the mindset of the owner of an enterprising truck company, the appeal is already there for you: Buying trucks, upgrading them, earning money, garages all across Europe, cities to discover, drivers to hire and fire.
- However, if you don't think you will like driving lots of things a long way, then no, it isn't. My advice is to then buy the game on a £5-£10 deal, or $12 deal on Steam, then you can't really be disappointed.
Verdict:
- Good things
- Big map
- A must for truck lovers and drivers
- Lots of things to do
- Detail
- Regular updates with actually useful content
- Never known a game quite so moddable
- Not-so-good things:
- Hard to control with keyboard, reccomend at least an Xbox Controller, however not worth disreguarding if you don't      have one
- Useless content in terms of trailers and companies without a couple of decent mods
- Customisation of truck gets boring quickly
- Can be repetitive in some cases
Overall:
Gameplay: 8/10
Trucks: 9/10
Menu accessibility: 10/10
Environment details: 5/10
Driving feel: 10/10
Value for money: 8/10
Map: 8/10
Mods: 10/10
How many bugs and glitches?: 2/10
Final Score:
8.5

Riding virtual trucks turns out to be a surprisingly relaxing experience!
Unlike most simulations, this one looks polished and not outdated at all. The only point of the game is driving cargo from city A to city B and there is very little to do besides that. You can upgrade your truck and hire other people who you will never see in-game, but this gives little satisfaction. Driving, on the other hand, is very pleasant. Just watch out for traffic lights, speed limitations and other drivers, keep your lane and enjoy the soothing scenery!
My biggest problem is the diversity of road elements, buildings and cargo that you come across. Eventually you'll start noticing that some of them are duplicated across the whole map and that can somewhat shatter the illusion of a huge game world, though there was still enough diversity to keep me seeing something new once in a while after 30 hours of gameplay. Another issue is that the radio player in Linux is broken and the developer doesn't seem to care (though you can always play the stream you want from a browser).
In conclusion, it's a nice and relaxing game where you can forget your worries, turn off your brain for a while and chill behind the wheel. Just don't forget to tune in to your favourite podcast, or else you're risking to lose too many brain cells in the process.

Riding virtual trucks turns out to be a surprisingly relaxing experience!
Unlike most simulations, this one looks polished and not outdated at all. The only point of the game is driving cargo from city A to city B and there is very little to do besides that. You can upgrade your truck and hire other people who you will never see in-game, but this gives little satisfaction. Driving, on the other hand, is very pleasant. Just watch out for traffic lights, speed limitations and other drivers, keep your lane and enjoy the soothing scenery!
My biggest problem is the diversity of road elements, buildings and cargo that you come across. Eventually you'll start noticing that some of them are duplicated across the whole map and that can somewhat shatter the illusion of a huge game world, though there was still enough diversity to keep me seeing something new once in a while after 30 hours of gameplay. Another issue is that the radio player in Linux is broken and the developer doesn't seem to care (though you can always play the stream you want from a browser).
In conclusion, it's a nice and relaxing game where you can forget your worries, turn off your brain for a while and chill behind the wheel. Just don't forget to tune in to your favourite podcast, or else you're risking to lose too many brain cells in the process.

So I downloaded that demo and tried out for myself.
Intro screen : Monster get sealed under a mountain, and a child fall into their caves years later.
Classic.

But suddenly, there's some talking sunflower greeting me. Oh it's a tutorial? XP, LV, HP. Nothing unusual there.
Huh, I have to run into the pellets? I thought the gameplay was based around dodging stuff, but oka- OH ♥♥♥♥!
I HAVE 1 HP LEFT AND THAT WAS ONLY ONE ATTACK WTF?! OH♥♥♥♥♥♥ THERE'S MORE PELLET'S. Mmmh, you can't escape those ones. It must mean it's all part of the story and I'm going to get rescued at the last second? Yup, called it.
Hello, uhm... goat? Her name is Toriel, uh?
Anyway, more tutorial and some shenanigans, and I am eventually free to roam around a bit.
Not much to say here. I decide to go the pacifist route, because that's just what I usually do in those games that allow it. It's usually a nice extra challenge, but here the way to spare a monster is entirely different than to kill it. More interesting too, because you have to solve a little puzzle, that is different for each monsters.
Moving on. I find goatmom again and I'm going to... live in her house forever or something? I'm the hero of this RPG, so, of course, that's just not going to happen. Uh, she went into the basement that she specifically asked me to not go into. So obviously, I follow her. We end up at a door and she tell me it's the only way out and she want to destroy this tunnel. Come oooooon, don't be that way...
So, to proceed, I have to prove I can fight her? Damn, I don't want to. I try to spare her, but it doesn't seem to work. I guess I'll have to reduce her health until it's low enough and th- OH♥♥♥♥♥♥ WTF IS THAT DAMAGE NUMBER?! NO PLEASE DON'T DIE! PLEASE DON'T CRY! FUUUUUUUUCK...
I exit the game.
And start it up again.
I'm at the last save point, in Toriel's house. Thank god. Everything is back to normal.
I go fight her again, and this time, I figure out I have to keep sparing her. I didn't need to attack her at all.
Toby! You tricked me again!
So I get a phone, a hug and the way out. Farewell Toriel.
I move through the dark corridor and... Damnit! You again?
Yep, that's Flowey alright.
So He proceed to blow my mind, by telling me he knows I killed Toriel.
Whaaaaaaat?!
He had the ability to savescum before I arrived here.
Whaaaaaaaaaaaat?!
He eagerly await the moment I will give up on not killing anyone.
...
Challenge accepted!
Thus, this is the end of the demo, and I immediatly proceed to buy the game and have my mind blown even more.

I saw this game was the Deal of the Day about a week ago, and so I checked it out. It appeared to be one of those forgettable games with a generic name that was just trying to cash in on based on just the picture from Steam's store page, but I was intrigued anyway because I love all things cars and trucks, though I've mostly been stuck as a car hobbyist and racing genre fan, and never played driving simulation games. Based on the reviews I saw, this one was worth checking out--so I bought it and the Going East DLC.
Short summary: this game is awesome in so many different ways. You start out as a low tier leveled business owner, and they don't give you any benefits of the doubt--you have so little money, you don't even get your own truck (yet). You can work for other companies, using their trucks to deliver cargo to a handful of cities across Europe. You have to obey all traffic laws (I made the mistake of rolling through a red light because I hadn't noticed they were there to be obeyed, and was charged a fine), and you have to deliver the cargo in a timely manner. If you damage the truck you're working with, the repair cost is deducted from your pay. The time you have to finish the job is also pretty relaxed--this is no Crazy Taxi, though they do have skill upgrades that allow you access to more time sensitive jobs that pay more for the benefit of a quick job.
Speaking of which, yes, you level up in this game, and this is also great. You can level up in different ways such as in fuel conservation, where you use less fuel and therefore save more money, or you can unlock a number of different jobs by leveling up your training in different areas. High valued cargo? Check. Fragile cargo? Yep. All of these give you access to even more jobs from the extensive list you already had, and you're able to pick the jobs that pay more (it's also great to pick jobs where the delivery is in a city you've never visited, so you explore more of the map and see new sights).
Control-wise, this game also plays extremely well. At first, my time with the controls was chaotic. I've been using a 360 controller to play, and I tried to mess with too much at once, and ended up getting stuck in parking lots because I couldn't figure out how to reverse (ha). If you want to use a controller, I'd suggest not changing the controls from the standard they pick for you at first. Drive around a bit before you decide to change anything.
Moving on, as you make money doing jobs using another company's truck, the bank will eventually contact you and let you know they're offering you a loan. It's enough to buy your first truck, but you'll have to be diligent in making sure you make enough money each day to make your loan payments. With your own truck, you're free to explore the map without a time limit (though you do pay for gas!), finding new truck dealers, farms/factories/cargo drop offs, recruitment agencies, and even future garages that you can buy to expand your grasp in the truck business industry across Europe. Once you work hard at that, the bank will increase your credit limit--allowing you to upgrade your garage if you wish, allowing you to buy additional trucks and hire drivers for you.
Driving simulation now gives way to business management, and this is pure enjoyment of the genre here. You have a number of garages you can obtain later on in the game once you have enough money, but at first, you'll just be buying another truck and assigning it to the additional space in your garage, where you can hire a driver to use. You can use any recruitment agency you've found to hire a driver, and from there you can hire them based on their skills and rating. Not only do they also level up, you can choose how you want them to work. For example, I chose to have my first hired driver focus on long distance jobs, since I myself was focused on shorter jobs that dealt with fragile or valuable cargo. Your hired drivers will also improve their rating over time, as they constantly are driving and working to improve their skills, though you have the authority to fire them if you so wish.
Last but not least--part of the charm in this game is just driving. It felt great to be driving a truck pulling 16 tons of cargo down the highways of Europe, discovering new cities and fulfilling contracts. I knew that with each job I completed, I was a tiny bit closer to paying off my loans, proving my worth in the industry, and making enough for that next truck or next upgrade. Also, the game has a radio feature, which lets you listen to live streams of a great selection of European radio stations--yes, real stations in real time while driving in a Euro truck simulation--and this is awesome. Last night while playing this game, I was driving my truck to a city I'd never seen before, pulling tons of cargo in the dead of night. Only once in a while would another car drive by because of the time, so I was mostly alone on the road. The radio station was playing some older American rock hits between commercials in another language. I was able to zone out. It was simply beautiful to just drive alone on a highway at night, listening to classic rock. I've never played a game that makes you feel so relaxed, so in awe of everyday things...and I've played thousands upon thousands of games. This game does it right.
I can't really say this game surprised me--based on the list of positive reviews, this game is a hit with many. But to think a game named Euro Truck Simulator 2 could be one of those games where you're watching the time get later and later and you think to yourself, "Just one more, then I'm done, I swear!" If you like trucks, you will love this game. If you like driving simulation, you will love the game. Heck, if you just enjoy driving like I do, you'll love this game. If you like business management games, you'll love this. If you love games where you start off dirt poor and actually have to work hard toward proving yourself, this game is one of the best you can buy. If you're looking for something you can pick-up-and-play to relax, yeah, this game is that, too. When I bought this game, I hoped I made a good choice, and my husband kind of made fun of me for the purchase since he knows anything with cars or trucks makes me weak, but when I played it, he kept looking over and saying, "Wow. I guess I can see why that would be interesting." And he has zero interest in automobiles and rarely plays simulation games!
So, with that said, the long summary comes down to this: this game is awesome for pretty much everyone.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 might come as a boring, "what's the point really?" kind of game to many folks. And it may actually be true. However, this game isn't meant to appeal to the masses. If you've ever seen a truck, specifically, a trailer, and wondered "Hmm, I gotta get me one of those!" or "I'll be king of the road if I was inside of those trucks", then you'll be more than pleasantly surprised with this game.
To cut the story short, playing this game actually feels like having a second job. Your purpose is to do the evil corporations' bidding and send goods from point A to B. Along the way, you'll traverse past many different Europe countryside. It's straightforward really, but the fun is in the details and technicalities. You'll try to build up your delivery empire while comparing jobs to see which one pays off better [Usually, it's more of which job is less boring].
The fun really starts once you incorporate the many wonderful mods that the community has pumped out. Real companies, incredible parts and tuning accessories, a gigantic world with more cities and landscapes and best of all, more truck models.
For me personally, I enjoy this game for the sense of realism, the Scania trucks, the trailers and admittedly, using it as a sort of simulator to train my driving awareness [Though driving 140kph in a fully-loaded truck is not recommended in real life].

Riding virtual trucks turns out to be a surprisingly relaxing experience!
Unlike most simulations, this one looks polished and not outdated at all. The only point of the game is driving cargo from city A to city B and there is very little to do besides that. You can upgrade your truck and hire other people who you will never see in-game, but this gives little satisfaction. Driving, on the other hand, is very pleasant. Just watch out for traffic lights, speed limitations and other drivers, keep your lane and enjoy the soothing scenery!
My biggest problem is the diversity of road elements, buildings and cargo that you come across. Eventually you'll start noticing that some of them are duplicated across the whole map and that can somewhat shatter the illusion of a huge game world, though there was still enough diversity to keep me seeing something new once in a while after 30 hours of gameplay. Another issue is that the radio player in Linux is broken and the developer doesn't seem to care (though you can always play the stream you want from a browser).
In conclusion, it's a nice and relaxing game where you can forget your worries, turn off your brain for a while and chill behind the wheel. Just don't forget to tune in to your favourite podcast, or else you're risking to lose too many brain cells in the process.

I personally have a love/hate relationship with this game
It can be a really fun and intense game to play, and I had plenty of hours of entertainment out of this game. It always has had its large share of bugs and issues that need to be fixed and it generally takes way too long for the devs to fix even a really simple issue, but I usually have overlooked these and ignored them.
Recently however, a new patch (0.61 to be precise) has completely ruined the game for me and others as well. Instead of fixing genuine bugs and issues with the game, they just made the game brutally hard, making worthwile loot extremely rare, making just about every spawn point garbage, and also even seemingly adding bugs that weren't previously there. An example of this in which has affected me quite a bit, is the fact that zombies hitting you almost always cause you to become sick/have infected wounds. Now maybe this wouldn't be too big of a problem if this was something that wasn't hard to overcome, but the item needed to heal this (alcohol tincture) is extremely rare. It used to be rare that you would ever get sick from getting hit by a zombie, but now it is overwhemingly easy to become sick from a zombie, in which is a huge problem.
There are more examples of bugs that seemingly were added in such as vehicles becoming essentially impossible to find; in fact, i'm fairly certain they don't spawn in at all.
On top of all of these issues, the optimization for this game is very poor. A lot of the optimization issues were fixed in patch 0.60, but it still needs a lot of work. This game has been in early access for almost 6 years now, and it was even stated by the developers that we would see a full release of DayZ by 2016. As of right now, in 2017, it is nowhere close to that benchmark. That is very disappointing.
At the very least, if they fix the issues with the current patch in the next one, I will start to support the development of this game once again. But as of right now, this new patch is just horrid.

I saw this game was the Deal of the Day about a week ago, and so I checked it out. It appeared to be one of those forgettable games with a generic name that was just trying to cash in on based on just the picture from Steam's store page, but I was intrigued anyway because I love all things cars and trucks, though I've mostly been stuck as a car hobbyist and racing genre fan, and never played driving simulation games. Based on the reviews I saw, this one was worth checking out--so I bought it and the Going East DLC.
Short summary: this game is awesome in so many different ways. You start out as a low tier leveled business owner, and they don't give you any benefits of the doubt--you have so little money, you don't even get your own truck (yet). You can work for other companies, using their trucks to deliver cargo to a handful of cities across Europe. You have to obey all traffic laws (I made the mistake of rolling through a red light because I hadn't noticed they were there to be obeyed, and was charged a fine), and you have to deliver the cargo in a timely manner. If you damage the truck you're working with, the repair cost is deducted from your pay. The time you have to finish the job is also pretty relaxed--this is no Crazy Taxi, though they do have skill upgrades that allow you access to more time sensitive jobs that pay more for the benefit of a quick job.
Speaking of which, yes, you level up in this game, and this is also great. You can level up in different ways such as in fuel conservation, where you use less fuel and therefore save more money, or you can unlock a number of different jobs by leveling up your training in different areas. High valued cargo? Check. Fragile cargo? Yep. All of these give you access to even more jobs from the extensive list you already had, and you're able to pick the jobs that pay more (it's also great to pick jobs where the delivery is in a city you've never visited, so you explore more of the map and see new sights).
Control-wise, this game also plays extremely well. At first, my time with the controls was chaotic. I've been using a 360 controller to play, and I tried to mess with too much at once, and ended up getting stuck in parking lots because I couldn't figure out how to reverse (ha). If you want to use a controller, I'd suggest not changing the controls from the standard they pick for you at first. Drive around a bit before you decide to change anything.
Moving on, as you make money doing jobs using another company's truck, the bank will eventually contact you and let you know they're offering you a loan. It's enough to buy your first truck, but you'll have to be diligent in making sure you make enough money each day to make your loan payments. With your own truck, you're free to explore the map without a time limit (though you do pay for gas!), finding new truck dealers, farms/factories/cargo drop offs, recruitment agencies, and even future garages that you can buy to expand your grasp in the truck business industry across Europe. Once you work hard at that, the bank will increase your credit limit--allowing you to upgrade your garage if you wish, allowing you to buy additional trucks and hire drivers for you.
Driving simulation now gives way to business management, and this is pure enjoyment of the genre here. You have a number of garages you can obtain later on in the game once you have enough money, but at first, you'll just be buying another truck and assigning it to the additional space in your garage, where you can hire a driver to use. You can use any recruitment agency you've found to hire a driver, and from there you can hire them based on their skills and rating. Not only do they also level up, you can choose how you want them to work. For example, I chose to have my first hired driver focus on long distance jobs, since I myself was focused on shorter jobs that dealt with fragile or valuable cargo. Your hired drivers will also improve their rating over time, as they constantly are driving and working to improve their skills, though you have the authority to fire them if you so wish.
Last but not least--part of the charm in this game is just driving. It felt great to be driving a truck pulling 16 tons of cargo down the highways of Europe, discovering new cities and fulfilling contracts. I knew that with each job I completed, I was a tiny bit closer to paying off my loans, proving my worth in the industry, and making enough for that next truck or next upgrade. Also, the game has a radio feature, which lets you listen to live streams of a great selection of European radio stations--yes, real stations in real time while driving in a Euro truck simulation--and this is awesome. Last night while playing this game, I was driving my truck to a city I'd never seen before, pulling tons of cargo in the dead of night. Only once in a while would another car drive by because of the time, so I was mostly alone on the road. The radio station was playing some older American rock hits between commercials in another language. I was able to zone out. It was simply beautiful to just drive alone on a highway at night, listening to classic rock. I've never played a game that makes you feel so relaxed, so in awe of everyday things...and I've played thousands upon thousands of games. This game does it right.
I can't really say this game surprised me--based on the list of positive reviews, this game is a hit with many. But to think a game named Euro Truck Simulator 2 could be one of those games where you're watching the time get later and later and you think to yourself, "Just one more, then I'm done, I swear!" If you like trucks, you will love this game. If you like driving simulation, you will love the game. Heck, if you just enjoy driving like I do, you'll love this game. If you like business management games, you'll love this. If you love games where you start off dirt poor and actually have to work hard toward proving yourself, this game is one of the best you can buy. If you're looking for something you can pick-up-and-play to relax, yeah, this game is that, too. When I bought this game, I hoped I made a good choice, and my husband kind of made fun of me for the purchase since he knows anything with cars or trucks makes me weak, but when I played it, he kept looking over and saying, "Wow. I guess I can see why that would be interesting." And he has zero interest in automobiles and rarely plays simulation games!
So, with that said, the long summary comes down to this: this game is awesome for pretty much everyone.

I played the hell out of this with friends in the legacy days. Though not as good as it was with friends, it was playable alone as well. Even after the frustrating desync issues and seemingly regular denial of service attacks on servers, over all rust legacy was a lot of fun... and its never coming back, and i respect the developers for wanting to keep in line with their original goal. I think i payed like 10 bucks back then for it, and, well, i feel bad for paying so low given the hours i put into it with friends.
But on to the game in its current state....
When rust "experimental" was released it looked cool, i gave it a good attempt, kinda missed the zombies, but i had known that they weren't planned to be a permanent fixture. I liked it enough to sink a few more hours into the game.
Since then my feelings towards this game have deterriorated.
While i still think it would be good for a few evenings of play with friends, it just hasn't hit the spot for me like legacy did, or even the earlier releases of experimatal/2/non-legacy.
The developers seem to be in some sort of creative flux:
+ Content and visual design seems to be improving
+ Introduced a XP, then removed it again. Good move, but...
- Removed blueprints too, which IMO removed some of the competitiveness over rad towns and landmarks
- Resources enough aren't enough to spur on competitiveness, i was on a 100 player server and found plenty... except animals (which after circumnavigating the map, didn't see a single one the other night)
- While bear attacks suck, i don't feel like i'm under constant threat, apart from other players with better equipment who kill on sight.
- Servers now end up completely littered with empty and broken into bases, even 1 or two days after a wipe.
- Their aim to encourage exploration doesn't quite hit the mark. I have very little reason to now. While the proc-gen is impressive, then only reason i have to for exploring is finding an un-colonised space to begin seting up a base that i've got very little reason to since i don't have to compete for diddly-squat.
While it can still be fun having raiding wars with friends against other groups, its pretty boring played alone (aside from treating it as an fps), and there are plenty better FPS games out there, even within the survival and crafting genre,
TL;DR: Was fun, then got weird, then got boring,
But it does look pretty good.
5/10 - Maybe I will throw spears while naked at other players yelling 'ooga booga' at them again.... time will tell.
Edit: FYI I got my moneys worth in legacy and have no regrets.

I've never played a game that makes you feel so relaxed, so in awe of everyday things...and I've played thousands upon thousands of games. This game does it right.
I can't really say this game surprised me--based on the list of positive reviews, this game is a hit with many. But to think a game named Euro Truck Simulator 2 could be one of those games where you're watching the time get later and later and you think to yourself, "Just one more, then I'm done, I swear!" If you like trucks, you will love this game. If you like driving simulation, you will love the game. Heck, if you just enjoy driving like I do, you'll love this game. If you like business management games, you'll love this. If you love games where you start off dirt poor and actually have to work hard toward proving yourself, this game is one of the best you can buy. If you're looking for something you can pick-up-and-play to relax, yeah, this game is that, too. When I bought this game, I hoped I made a good choice, and my husband kind of made fun of me for the purchase since he knows anything with cars or trucks makes me weak, but when I played it, he kept looking over and saying, "Wow. I guess I can see why that would be interesting." And he has zero interest in automobiles and rarely plays simulation games!
So, with that said, the long summary comes down to this: this game is awesome for pretty much everyone.

At it's current state, this is by far, at this moment, one of the best games I have ever played on Steam besides CS-GO. If you choose a server that multiplies the amount of resources given when you hit a tree or rock it's quick to get started. I don't like to sit around and churn on those mundane tasks. I like the fact Rust allows you to mod and create your own server. Playing solo the majority of the time, I can build on a non-decay server and start raiding with very little work and actually not have to log in each day to keep everything active. Over time you learn how to build to prevent full blown raids, and at least keep them out of your loot or make it extremely hard to get to it. The funnest part about this game is the PVP and raiding action. I like raiding a base, seeing the owner sleeping and then slashing him/her with a pick axe or something. I like being able to put up signs and canvas drawings in my base. I seriously spend 20 minutes sometimes drawing on them. Sure the graphics in the cities isn't all that great and the fact you can't really see yourself via looking around (arms only), but I absolutely love this game. I like seeing people around the map. One time a player came up to my base and over the mic he asked if I wanted a chocolate bar. I then shot him from the roof and stole his chocolate bar :) Later on we became friends. I like being able to chat via text too. I like skinning things too like the armored doors on the base, clothing and storage containers. The building in this game is truely amazing compared to other games, and Rust gives you the ability to pretty much build what you want, any way you want, quickly. I like the fact that the bears and wolves are quite deadly if you happen to run up on them without any fire-power. I have not noticed any bugs, but I do think sometimes people may use ESP to know where things are. You just have to build in a way to prevent them from actually getting to those things. The game gets updated and they seem to be doing a really good job improving it. Overall I personally give this game two thumbs up ;)

Rust is by far, my favorite FPS. Lots of action, plenty of modded options to suit your available free time, and there's a competition for everything. Some days you find yourself laughing at your neighbors poor accuracy, while other days you log into an offline raided base, with nothing left -- you never know what's coming.
I've played since Rust left browser, aka legacy, and I've always known this to be an FPS/Crafting/base builder, and NOT a survival game. For those of you looking to trade, create towns, or play peacefully alongside your neighbors, you'll be hardpressed to find a server with any kind of roleplaying, or friendly players at this point. They do exist, but there are usually a lot of rules to follow, and these can be interpreted many ways, apparently.
Most players will simply bait you into your own death, which can be worth a laugh or two, or kill on sight. Personally, I strike first, and negotiate a truce once my opponent has been run into the ground. You can retain allies, or even make friends in this way, I've come to find. Rust is very difficult to play solo, but can be very rewarding if you're a capable shot, even while outnumbered.
Learn to shoot accurately with each weapon, and make sure you shoot first.. and remember: dont be greedy when you loot a kill, or you'll soon be looted too.

Undertale is a must play for everyone who has ever thought to themselves, "Do these creatures I relentlessly kill in other games have a life beyond getting destroyed?" Undertale looked at that question, saw it as an idea, and then to drive the point home, made sure that the player would find out about the life of each and all of the enemies.
Every creature, from the wimpiest frog to the final boss has a life. Each creature has it's own thoughts, life goals and other things.
If Undertale were just that, it would be good. But what really sells the game to me is how deep it is. If you decide to kill anyone, it will affect the ending. Go on ahead, try it. Try killing one of the bosses and then finishing the game. The ending will change depending on what bosses are alive and which ones are dead.
Undertale promotes peace and being friendly rather  heavily. But not in such a way that the game forces you to be mr. nice guy to everyone. If you want to kill everything (and litterally everything, not just what comes on your path), the game will allow you to do so, but also forces you to see the consequences of it.
Go play it. Just go plau it.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 might come as a boring, "what's the point really?" kind of game to many folks. And it may actually be true. However, this game isn't meant to appeal to the masses. If you've ever seen a truck, specifically, a trailer, and wondered "Hmm, I gotta get me one of those!" or "I'll be king of the road if I was inside of those trucks", then you'll be more than pleasantly surprised with this game.
To cut the story short, playing this game actually feels like having a second job. Your purpose is to do the evil corporations' bidding and send goods from point A to B. Along the way, you'll traverse past many different Europe countryside. It's straightforward really, but the fun is in the details and technicalities. You'll try to build up your delivery empire while comparing jobs to see which one pays off better [Usually, it's more of which job is less boring].
The fun really starts once you incorporate the many wonderful mods that the community has pumped out. Real companies, incredible parts and tuning accessories, a gigantic world with more cities and landscapes and best of all, more truck models.
For me personally, I enjoy this game for the sense of realism, the Scania trucks, the trailers and admittedly, using it as a sort of simulator to train my driving awareness [Though driving 140kph in a fully-loaded truck is not recommended in real life].
