I bought this really cheap on a flyer a few sales ago and I've got 94 hours in it now. Wasn't expecting that, at all. Don't want to make more of it than it is, but for what it is, it's just about perfect. I drove a truck (53' trailers and all) long-haul for a couple of years, just for reference, doing ~3000 miles a week.
At speed, time passes at about one minute per second, maybe two seconds, but the driving is apparently at normal speed, they do a really good job of blending the different scales. The traffic's reasonable though it's obvious those aren't people driving, they're not nearly so smart nor nearly so stupid as the real ones. Weather's well done, the visuals are rewarding.
You can get KB+M set up properly, though it's real work to do it. I've got a gamepad and don't use it for this game, this setup works that well for me.
For me, getting the steering usable means turning off the system's mouse acceleration ("enhance pointer precision" on Windows), set the in-game steering sensitivity at near minimum, steering non-linearity dead minimum. There's some weirdity about getting the initial choice of controls set properly, I have to go in and manually pick keyboard+mouse a second time no matter what I do in the initial setup.
Then: view control, the mouse buttons are entirely given over to that. Get to its "keyboard" control settings (that should be spelled "buttons") and set
Rotate Camera (in Mouse Control): Right Button
Interior Look Forward: Wheel Up
Interior Look Up Right: Wheel Down
Interior Look Up Left: Left Button
Interior Look Up Middle: Middle Button
I've got a M510 mouse, extra buttons on the side, I have them set on Interior Look Left and Interior Look Right which means I need the RMB only rarely. The LMB/RMB/Wheel asymmetry wasn't my first choice, it's something I arrived at.
Then the rest of the buttons, non-defaults are Q and E as the turn signals, parking brake on B, exhaust brake on the spacebar, Hazard Warning F, Light Modes N, High Beam H, Beacon X, Horn V, Light Horn Z, Y is the wipers (visual onomatopoeia). (edit: engine start is ]).
Set the transmission type to "Real Automatic" unless you're a masochist. Don't use the "Simple Automatic", it's just wrong. The airbrake simulation mode is a bit annoying, mine never got in the way that much, the rest of the realism options I like.
Truck physics does lack a certain feel to it, but there's enough there to demand real attention to payload.  Don't go trying to deliver a heavy load to Zurich until you can afford a decent motor, for instance.

This pixelated game by Toby Fox was made entirely in RPG Maker (a special program allowing you to create simple role-playing games without too much coding) and funded by a Kickstarter campaign. Apart from the excellent characters, on-point humour and the utterly amazing soundtrack, the game also features a very interesting story. You play as Frisk, the gender-neutral, silent protagonist who falls into the underground by accident and discovers it’s inhabited by monsters. Now he has two options: either he tries to befriend everyone or he slaughters them all. The protagonist, although he has an official name, is supposed to resemble you, so the game becomes extra personal. If you go as a Pacifist, by not killing anyone, you’ll experience a very humorous, emotional, heart-warming adventure. Go Genocide, by killing everyone, and the game will constantly remind you that you are a horrible person and you will start to feel bad.
The game’s technical side is also quite impressive: the fourth wall gets broken sometimes and when it does, it does so extremely well; to the point where you start to feel like this is not a game anymore. The combat system is also quite refreshing: it’s a combination of a top down arcade shooter and other mechanics e.g. a platformer. Your soul is represented by a little red heart trapped in a box that has to dodge the different attacks coming at it. It can be tricky at some times to pull it off and, especially in the genocide run, you will grind your teeth on some of the boss battles. This game sets the new standard for future games to achieve and shows that you don’t need a publisher to make a masterpiece. It took us by surprise, much like Minecraft did back in the day and it feels like this is the return of something we had to miss for a long time. I highly encourage you to play it, because seeing how such a small game can have such a great impact, fills you with DETERMINATION.

At it's current state, this is by far, at this moment, one of the best games I have ever played on Steam besides CS-GO. If you choose a server that multiplies the amount of resources given when you hit a tree or rock it's quick to get started. I don't like to sit around and churn on those mundane tasks. I like the fact Rust allows you to mod and create your own server. Playing solo the majority of the time, I can build on a non-decay server and start raiding with very little work and actually not have to log in each day to keep everything active. Over time you learn how to build to prevent full blown raids, and at least keep them out of your loot or make it extremely hard to get to it. The funnest part about this game is the PVP and raiding action. I like raiding a base, seeing the owner sleeping and then slashing him/her with a pick axe or something. I like being able to put up signs and canvas drawings in my base. I seriously spend 20 minutes sometimes drawing on them. Sure the graphics in the cities isn't all that great and the fact you can't really see yourself via looking around (arms only), but I absolutely love this game. I like seeing people around the map. One time a player came up to my base and over the mic he asked if I wanted a chocolate bar. I then shot him from the roof and stole his chocolate bar :) Later on we became friends. I like being able to chat via text too. I like skinning things too like the armored doors on the base, clothing and storage containers. The building in this game is truely amazing compared to other games, and Rust gives you the ability to pretty much build what you want, any way you want, quickly. I like the fact that the bears and wolves are quite deadly if you happen to run up on them without any fire-power. I have not noticed any bugs, but I do think sometimes people may use ESP to know where things are. You just have to build in a way to prevent them from actually getting to those things. The game gets updated and they seem to be doing a really good job improving it. Overall I personally give this game two thumbs up ;)

'Why on earth would i find it fun to deliver things in a big, heavy, and slow truck?' - This is the question that I and many people asked when looking at Euro Truck Simulator 2. Hell, when i told my brother that I'd racked up 9 hours on the demo alone, he thought i was mad... Until he got his hands on it and ended up putting in over 10 hours himself! You see, ETS2 is a sim like no other. Just by the loading times, it sets itself above all simulator games that I've ever played. Most take minutes to load, but this, from launch to drive, takes a matter of seconds. A nominal point perhaps, but it really does show off how well polished and awesome this simulator really is! Then comes the graphics, which are quite simply beautiful. Shadows dance across beautifully modeled truck cabs, cars on the road, whilst not liscenced, look realistic and behave very well within the stunning environment. Never before have i found the M1 so beautiful! But of course, its not the graphics that make the sim - its the gameplay! The driving experience is sublimely crafted, with the vehicles behaving differently depending on the brand, chassis layout, engine type and weight of trailer (among other factors). While it can sometimes become monotonous on long haul deliveries, there are plenty of things that keep on your feet when driving. With the ability to travel through different towns and countries, you have to adapt to different road laws and watch out for traffic. Not doing so will result in penalties, and damage, and can affect your performance rating. On top of having to constantly  stay focussed, the game also has real, live radio intergration which not only adds to the immersion, but also makes for more fun travles! (if you ever get this game ,you need to listen to '80s hot mix radio!'. The sim isn't only about you and customizing your trucks however, as your aim is to build a trucking empire! Not only are you allowed to name your company, but you are also given the responsibility of buying garages across europe and hiring different drivers to carry out jobs. Sometimes you might need to take out a loan to keep your business going, or you might end up in some trouble! This is only covering a minute amount of what this game offers, but the bottom line is that it really is fantastic fun, and unlike any other sim out there. If you're on the fence then try the demo, and i can almost guarantee that you will love it. The experience is totally customizable, with added support for actual driving wheels such as the Logitech G27. simply? GET THIS GAME!

Welcome to Europe,
You are now a truck driver, the most unknown driver of the world.
A driver with smelly and hairy armpits and a poodle on the passenger seat. (Close your eyes and imagine this! I KNOW YOU WANT TO!)
No matter who you are, how smelly you are you want and WILL be the biggest and the most popular truck driver of Europe.
You shall face the adversity of the others drivers, the ones that zig-zag, the ones that DUI, the one that sleep. – Oh and, just saying, you’ll be the one that sleep too, say thanks to the best sleeping simulator inside a truck simulator you’ll ever see, so good it will make you reconsider to have a regular sleeping schedule (the one that no gamers have) – and your counter-attack for this is a BIG, LONG AND POUNDING truck to penetrate you a way down the road.
But WAIT, your truck will be small, mildly menacing and rusty at start, but don’t worry, the more you’ll play with, the more you’ll be able to get a big one.
The best part of this is how gradually it will be.
With the help of a hand draw map – That will remind you the classic dungeons game with an absent map, so absent you have to draw your own card on a grid paper sheet – Your first truck will be a rented one, that come with no extra wheel in case you roll over some nails or some very acid skunk impregnated of pee – so acid that you’ll feel that salty onion vaporized taste ON EVERY SINGLE taste bud on your tongue – crushed on the road.
The truck with the most damaged seats you’ll ever sit on. – More holes in it than a Swiss cheese – with that nice “squishy feeling”, so sweaty smelly squishy that at EVERY single move, that you will feel that cold sweat water impregnated in the remaining foam on the seats. (I know you want some “squish-squish” cheese now!)
You always have to start somewhere huh?
You’ll slowly but surely becoming wealthy enough to buy your own truck with the most fancy GPS in it, with some fancy memory foam leather covered seats. The same leather of the brand new leather coat you just bought for your dog.
You’ll slowly have bigger contract some that you will like, some that you won’t like. But… c’est la vie!
This game is more than a simple truck simulator. It will get you very emotional. You will have to take heartbreaking choice – should you take this detour and deceive yourself for not seeing a squirting show due to water main breaks? – this game is going to be tough on your mind, but very enjoyable on the outcome.
This is the most deep and biggest simulator you will ever play in your entire life.
It will make you thinking about a career change, and you will never see your social environment the same way after.
Have a happy journey in Europe and be ready for the adventure of a life!

About the game:
------Gameplay------
The game consists in a truck driver career with RPG mechanics like Exp and Perks. You start as freelance driver selecting cargos to deliver from different companies, you receive Money and Exp by type of cargo and distance travelled. The money you save you use to buy your first truck and then save more money after to buy your first truck depot who allows you to buy more truck and hire drivers for your company. As you gain level with  Exp you upgrade your driver skills with perks allowing transport more valuable cargos.
------PROS------
-Graphics (7/10) Truck interior and exterior fully detailed, nice sky and weather transitions.
-Controls (10/10) as a simulator game, the controls responds like a real truck should be.
-Music (10/10) The game allows you listen your mp3 or a online radio.
------CONS------
-Bad IA traffic (3/10) The IA traffic is really bad, turning lights don't cause any effect, the other drivers are just zombies who only stop on red lights or in eminent collision.
-No physical damage (0/10) Despite the damage the truck or cargo can receive, there's no visible damage, the truck not even get dirty.
-GPS (4/10) The GPS in the game is speechless and don't alert about radars, i just don't understand why a modern truck like these don't have a decent normal GPS like in real life.
Cities (4/10) Cities are almost the same: just have a truck dealer and/or job agency, hotel and some industries nothing special.
OVERALL RATING [ 6.8 ]

Yes the game still has lots of bugs, but that's mostly due to the old engine features, that are beeing replaced with the new Enfusion engine, step by step.
First we got the new renderer which changed the graphics engine to a more modern standard, beeing DirectX 11 -> better Optimization, while looking better and adding new graphical features (only downside is people with potato gpus that don't support DX11, got left behind, but well, time for an upgrade huh?).
After that we got the new Eden sound engine, that completely overhauled the way audio works, being able to hear gunshots up to a few kilometers and beeing able to assess if they are close or far away. In the same update they introduced the dynamic infected spawns, increasing their base number, and adding more in certain areas if there are more players (a bit like in the mod). Infected are far from perfect, but at least they now are a threat to players if you're not careful (if you shoot in a city, prepare to get swarmed by lots of them). They push players around and are difficult to hit sometimes, because they are using the new physics engine while the players are still on the old legacy one, which is going to change with the new player controller. In the last update they also introduced new network optimizations and I haven't died to a stair or rock glitch since then.
In the next update we will see an overhaul to the forests making them thicker, better looking and more optimized. After that it's time for the new player controller, which will hopefully get rid of most of the quirks regarding clunkiness of movement and how the player interacts with objects and the world.
IMO, theres no other open world survival game like DayZ. Many have tried, but never reached it's toes, even beeing incomplete and buggy (Miscreated is the only game on a good track, which has a lot of updates, so check that out , it's pretty good!). I'm not even going to adress the "It's been 3 years in development *foams from mouth* " crowd, because if you have any idea how game development works, with complicated engine changes, you wouldn't go on the hate bandwagon like everyone else.
The dev's biggest mistake was the roadmaps they put up and couldn't realize, creating high expectations for the player base and then failing them.
To finish, It's been a bumpy ride, and theres still some pot holes ahead, but we're getting closer and closer to beta.
So, I recommend this game right now, if you don't mind a somewhat buggy (not gamebreaking) game and have patience (keyword!). If you don't, move on with your life and come back later! (Or not)

Some Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- The preformance has improved greatly. Lag spikes rarely occur like they did in older versions and I don't get rubber-banded as much anymore.
-- The menu looks like an actual menu, with functioning buttons and actual response to them. No more clicking repeatedly to make sure you clicked that one button.
-- The in-game UI works better too. The redesign is more pleasing to the eyes, and simpler to use in the inventory screen.
- Textures have gotten a facelift too
-- Your character now actually looks human instead of a wax mannequin. There's also more playermodel options, although these may just be randomized skins, like in Rust.
-- The zombies especially look actually scary now. Like actual people turned infected. When you see one up close you can see every detail in good resolution (assuming your computer can handle it, but mine's not the best either if you're stressing.)
-- Not to mention there's some nice variety in zombie models.
-- Item textures are improved, such as guns, etc.
- Controls are more responsive
-- I haven't had as much trouble with falling down stairs and breaking my legs as i used to do before. I have fallen off cliffs but mainly that was user error and not poor control response.
Cons:
- Melee is AWFUL
-- You can't hit feces with it. You pretty much NEED to go into first-person and pray to almighty Raptor Jesus that you'll hit something HALF the time with whatever weapon you have. It ensures that almost every close encounter you have with a zombie, you'll die, and if it's another player, you two will look like real-life Mount and Blade: Warband players swinging wildly to try and hit something whilst also not getting hit.
-- And don't get me started on the responsiveness there.
- Swimming is pointless and will kill you.
-- There's a neato island to the southeast, if I recall correctly. Has a castle, a lighthouse, a few houses, and GUNS. Many guns. However, you'll get drenched swimming there (understandably) but you'll also get cold. Every piece of clothing you put on will ALSO get wet because your body is wet. However... there's no real way to dry YOURSELF off. Only wring out water from clothes (which doesn't really work.)
-- So you'll be cold, wet, and trying to find food or fire to survive. Well, thanks to the ever-present law of "♥♥♥♥ you, you need this? You'll NEVER find it!" applies, and so you die on a high-loot island of the cold, or bleeding if there are zombies there.
- This game is still Running Simulator 2013-- er, 2017.
-- Yeah, vehicles were added. With the ability to fix them. But good luck finding a working vehicle, getting ALL the parts to fix it in the same town, successfully fixing it, filling it up with gasoline which could be anywhere, and driving it. I've seen players do it, and if you see one, don't shoot them. Let them enjoy their effort. They worked hard on it.
-- I'm not an idiot when it comes to theoretical zombie apocalypses but something tells me that not every car on Chernarus has to be totalled, or have the car battery, 2 tires, a spark plug and headlights taken off of it for no reason. It also asks why bother adding vehicles and bugifixing them if nobody's going to actually find one and keep it? I doubt it's a private vehicle that logs off with you when you log off. Anyone could come along and take it on a joyride. So all effort would be wasted anyways.
- The guns are even more vague than before.
-- Never have I had to look up things in this game more than "what ammo type does [GUN] use?" There's virtually no description. "Oh but it's realistic." Know what else is realistic? Fall damage after 5 feet only if you faceplant.
-- I swear, I don't see any reason why the devs would take away descriptions that included ammo type for the gun the player was holding. There isn't even any inscription on the lower-tier guns that gives any indication.
Decide from there.

I drove trucks for 10 years part-time and I have to say that I am blown away by this simulator. I became an airline pilot and didn't have any great expectations to this game versus flight simulation, but this is a very accurate simulation to trucks equally as FSX is to aircraft. It's very fun as well and the I have a Titan card and this game maxed out looks very great and very smooth on three monitors. I actually use my flight sim yoke and rudder pedals as a gas and break combo and it works fine. You can also place your favorite music in the folder and the in cab radio plays your music crisp. It has everything imaginable and even simulates clutch and shifting with all kinds of shifting patterns and transmissions available. If I owned a trucking company and bought the steering wheel, shifters and pedals, this would be a valuable tool to use for evaluation. All kinds of options for the trucks. The most hardcore survival I've played, as with other survival games that are hard (dayz for example) the biggest opponents are other players. The game is a bit taxing on the computer but considering it runs maps with the size of 5x5 km and holds up to about 400 players on some servers it runs pretty smoothly.
The game is constantly updated with a big update hitting every month, items have skins with player created (workshop) skins, there are community and official servers with enough capacity that you don't have to worry about not having a spot.
The learning curve is steep and you will need about a month to get the hang of things, for me the biggest difficulty was learning to use alt look, spotting players and getting used to recoil and sights of weaponry at which I am still terrible at. As far as building part goes it's easy if you aren't stupid, but if you are the latter then boy I feel sorry for you.
Now for some downsides: Official servers tend to get laggy in the last week of the 5-ish week wipe cycle, community servers have to wipe every week because population doesn't hold out and there are hackers. As far as hackers go I haven't had much problems on official servers where it happens less but doesn't get banned as fast, on community there seem to be more but the admins react to it faster.
I've heard the community being accused of being toxic, which really depends on which server you play on, where on the server you make a base and how you play it. If you play the right way you can avoid a large part of toxicity to the point where you aren't aware of it after which I would argue that toxic players aren't really an issue many players make it to be.
The game is just unforgiving and punishes you for mistakes greatly. HTFU or GTFO basically. Good game 9/10, great value for cash definitely 10/10, developer-consumer interaction 10/10, probably the best I've seen over the years.

DayZ is easily the best game I have played. In three months, I have dropped almost 340 hours into this game. I disliked it at first when I realized that is isn't COD and getting gear takes time. I later came back when a friend taught me to play it. Here's why I think it's the greatest game ever.
PROS:
-Amazing graphics
-Rarely laggy/glitchy
-Large selection of weapons to use
-Player interactions are adrenaline filled and amazingly fun
-Every weapon can be good, I've seen and done squad wipes with simple weapons such as a Glock.
-Roaming the map never gets old, there are so many places to go
-Different challenges to try every day, for example, the pistol only challenge
-Bases are amazing to create, and even better to find
-Hold-Ups
CONS:
-Sucks to get killed
-Running for hours, but is is part of the reason why the game is fun
I'm not sure why people always mention bugs and glitches, as I've never experienced any of them. Also not sure what the issue is with this game being Early Access if it's a good game, don't know why people complain. 0.61 was truly revolutionary, it took away the chance of getting a Bolata spawn, running up to Pavlovo, Myshkino, and Zelenogorsk and getting geared within an hour. It instead focuses on northern pvp, with most of the spawns being by the North Western highway area. The idea of adding a small military checkpoints between a lot of the towns is a good idea now, it's an easy way to get prepared to go to the larger military bases where players will have more gear. Tisy is amazing! If you're able to get a Svetlojarsk spawn, you can work your way up to Novo, then the Kamensk base, and then Tisy, if you survive all of this, you WILL be very geared! People complain about the run to Tisy, but honestly, it takes about the same amount of time to run to Tisy from a Svetlojarsk spawn as it did back in 0.60 and other versions by getting a Bolata spawn and running to Myskino tents. The devs want us to focus more on northern pvp instead of coastal pvp. This is a much needed change and one that I personally believe will carry DayZ to go on as one of the best games in history.

I bought this really cheap on a flyer a few sales ago and I've got 94 hours in it now. Wasn't expecting that, at all. Don't want to make more of it than it is, but for what it is, it's just about perfect. I drove a truck (53' trailers and all) long-haul for a couple of years, just for reference, doing ~3000 miles a week.
At speed, time passes at about one minute per second, maybe two seconds, but the driving is apparently at normal speed, they do a really good job of blending the different scales. The traffic's reasonable though it's obvious those aren't people driving, they're not nearly so smart nor nearly so stupid as the real ones. Weather's well done, the visuals are rewarding.
You can get KB+M set up properly, though it's real work to do it. I've got a gamepad and don't use it for this game, this setup works that well for me.
For me, getting the steering usable means turning off the system's mouse acceleration ("enhance pointer precision" on Windows), set the in-game steering sensitivity at near minimum, steering non-linearity dead minimum. There's some weirdity about getting the initial choice of controls set properly, I have to go in and manually pick keyboard+mouse a second time no matter what I do in the initial setup.
Then: view control, the mouse buttons are entirely given over to that. Get to its "keyboard" control settings (that should be spelled "buttons") and set
Rotate Camera (in Mouse Control): Right Button
Interior Look Forward: Wheel Up
Interior Look Up Right: Wheel Down
Interior Look Up Left: Left Button
Interior Look Up Middle: Middle Button
I've got a M510 mouse, extra buttons on the side, I have them set on Interior Look Left and Interior Look Right which means I need the RMB only rarely. The LMB/RMB/Wheel asymmetry wasn't my first choice, it's something I arrived at.
Then the rest of the buttons, non-defaults are Q and E as the turn signals, parking brake on B, exhaust brake on the spacebar, Hazard Warning F, Light Modes N, High Beam H, Beacon X, Horn V, Light Horn Z, Y is the wipers (visual onomatopoeia). (edit: engine start is ]).
Set the transmission type to "Real Automatic" unless you're a masochist. Don't use the "Simple Automatic", it's just wrong. The airbrake simulation mode is a bit annoying, mine never got in the way that much, the rest of the realism options I like.
Truck physics does lack a certain feel to it, but there's enough there to demand real attention to payload.  Don't go trying to deliver a heavy load to Zurich until you can afford a decent motor, for instance.

STORY: Taking place after the events of the first Borderlands, the story bares striking resemblance to the one that came before it. Once again, four characters (conveniently distinguished by combat class) have come to Pandora in search of a second vault. Yes, a second vault. From the moment the absolutely incredible opening cut-scene plays, you’ll be roaring with laughter. The sheer absurdity that after all you experienced in the first game, a new set of four will have to go through it again, and it’s genuinely funny. Not video game funny; genuinely funny.
However, I feel I’m almost doing Borderlands 2 a disservice here, because the entire story is so much more fleshed out than its predecessor. The characters you grew attached to in the first title return, but they aren’t bit-part players. Sure, you can’t take over Roland again, but he’s a major player in the story, and he’s not the only one. Some of the story beats (that I wouldn’t dream of spoiling here) are genuine punch-the-air moments, and there has been a tremendous amount of effort put in to making the side-missions just as fun; with some wonderful characters there too.
Handsome Jack is the antagonist for Borderlands 2, a pretty-boy who runs Pandora by force, destroying anyone who stands against him. Jack wants what is inside this second vault, because he believes it will give him the power to do pretty much anything. By opening the first vault, the hunters unleashed Eridium onto the world, a rare material that is worth a fortune, yet also holds mysterious powers. Your job is simple, stop Handsome Jack, and have plenty of fun and games along the way.
GRAPHICS: It’d be a lie to say that the visuals had been completely overhauled for Borderlands 2, but they do look far crisper and cleaner, with a slight design change in terms of art direction. Thicker blacks surround people and places, making them stand out even more. Of course, Pandora is full of colourful characters like the sultry Moxxi, or the crazy-violent gun merchant Marcus (among many, many others) and they all look brilliant. They also have so much more life to them, and when they give you an item they will literally hold their arm out for you to take it from them.
Even during battles where elemental damage is littering the screen, damage numbers are flying everywhere and loot is spraying out of dying foes, the frame-rate is pretty solid and there are very few noticeable moments where it chugs, though it happens mostly when you’re playing with others. The action is fast, frenetic and rendered beautifully, with luscious vistas and locations to visit. There are absolutely no complaints in the visual department for Borderlands 2.
SOUND: If you’ve played the first Borderlands then you’ll find that not much has changed in terms of the music you’ll hear. Despite the kick♥♥♥♥♥opening, the moment-to-moment gameplay has that same Borderlands feel to it, twanging country-style acoustic guitar for the desert areas, a chilling soundtrack to fill the ice-caverns, that kind of thing. When the combat ramps up, music will kick in to get the adrenaline flowing. It all works as it should, playing largely second fiddle to the voice acting.
GAMEPLAY: It’s tricky to know where to start when discussing Borderlands 2’s mechanics, because Gearbox have so completely upgraded them, that it’s astonishingly impressive. As with a lot of games containing loot, currency in Borderlands became pointless after a reasonable amount of progress had been made. The player had so much cash it was a worthless commodity. So, to fix this, Borderlands 2 has an additional currency called Eridium which ties nicely into the storyline. If you want to buy the really important things from the black market (more inventory slots for example), you’ll only be able to do so with Eridium. Whilst you still pick up cash at an alarming rate from the richest bandits you’ve ever come across, Eridium is far rarer and seeing some drop, or finding some in a lock-box is a hugely satisfying event.

Synopsis: This is a first-person perspective truck driving simulator that also includes the ability to purchase multiple garages from which to base multiple trucks and hire drivers to drive them for increased income. The simulation takes place in parts of Europe.
As far as the truck simulation itself is concerned, you never get a perspective that allows you to be on the ground. You are either in your driver's seat, or you manipulate the other parts of the simulation from control windows; you cannot get out and walk around.
There are multiple control schemes includng mouse&keyboard as well as controller and wheel support. Controls can be remapped. I find using mouse and keyboard takes a little getting used to, though there are choices to be made here as well. For example, you can steer with the keyboard or with the mouse. Keyboard steering snaps back to center when you aren't depressing a key where mouse steering allows you to maintain a certain amount of steerage constantly, but might feel contraining as any mouse movement results in input to your truck's steerage.
The graphics are decent to excellent depending on whether certain kinds of detail are important to you. The rendered roadways and accompanying scenery are very nice, but several of the vehicle models you will see and buildings are reused throughout the simulation. I find that driving at night is harder on my framerate than daytime driving. Rain is simulated pretty effectively. Windshield wipers, horns, and auxilliary lighting are all modeled. There are multiple camera angles as well. The interior of the trucks also has excellent modeling.
The AI drivers you hire will  run routes in the background. You have no control over this part of the simulation other than to try to level them up in certain areas. For example (and the most important hint for the AI drivers) is that I level them up in their long distance driving first as this opens up more jobs to them faster than any other choice. This is important because if there are no jobs in the town they are in that the drive is capable of taking, they will run bob-tail (without a paying load) back to their home garage, costing you fuel and their salary without income. For the most part, this part of the simulation results in a slow trickle of income that increases as your drivers level up and as you add more garages, trucks and drivers.
Which brings us to the goals of the game. You spend your income either on truck upgrades and vanity items, or in expanding your business. Otherwise it is an open-ended simulation of driving a truck. There is a built in radio function that pulls in European radio stations that you can listen to or play your own music. It can be quite relaxing to just drive your simulated truck and listen to tunes, and this is the appeal for me. Especially once you have a decent business up, you can drive your truck bob-tail all over the game's roads just for fun and never run out of gas or repair money, which is only important in so far as you aren't required to run jobs for this income yourself if you don't want to. Note that although I speak of relaxation, the driving can be demanding if you are driving a heavy load in a hurry.
Overall, this is a must buy game for this type of activity. Obviously, not everyone enjoys a relaxing game or perhaps some only relax when they are overstimulated. But, for those that do like a relaxing simulation, this is recommended. As always, look for it on sale.

Super enjoyable game... under a few conditions.  You have to be willing to lose everything and be okay with it.  The enjoyment from this game is not to look at your player after months of grinding to see all high level stats, but rather I find enjoyment in this game from simply being able to survive.  The first few weeks are rough, you will continuously die, and literally make no progress after hours of work.  But with persistance, determination, and a little bit of luck, you'll start getting better and better, slowly surviving for longer and longer periods of time.  The true beauty of Rust is that literally ALL of your progress can be destroyed and wiped from you instantly, it just makes the progress that you make feel 10000x more rewarding.  Graphically, this game is extremely impressive, realistic shaders and high quality textures, with very widely varying landscapes that I never realize are randomly generated.  Every island truly feels unique and has its own personality.  There are flaws with this game (bears are way too strong at almost any point in the game they can just come and kill you, not being able to delete destroy or otherwise remove a wall after having placed one, etc) however the benefits outweigh the flaws tenfold.  Would most definitely recommend.

I bought this really cheap on a flyer a few sales ago and I've got 94 hours in it now. Wasn't expecting that, at all. Don't want to make more of it than it is, but for what it is, it's just about perfect. I drove a truck (53' trailers and all) long-haul for a couple of years, just for reference, doing ~3000 miles a week.
At speed, time passes at about one minute per second, maybe two seconds, but the driving is apparently at normal speed, they do a really good job of blending the different scales. The traffic's reasonable though it's obvious those aren't people driving, they're not nearly so smart nor nearly so stupid as the real ones. Weather's well done, the visuals are rewarding.
You can get KB+M set up properly, though it's real work to do it. I've got a gamepad and don't use it for this game, this setup works that well for me.
For me, getting the steering usable means turning off the system's mouse acceleration ("enhance pointer precision" on Windows), set the in-game steering sensitivity at near minimum, steering non-linearity dead minimum. There's some weirdity about getting the initial choice of controls set properly, I have to go in and manually pick keyboard+mouse a second time no matter what I do in the initial setup.
Then: view control, the mouse buttons are entirely given over to that. Get to its "keyboard" control settings (that should be spelled "buttons") and set
Rotate Camera (in Mouse Control): Right Button
Interior Look Forward: Wheel Up
Interior Look Up Right: Wheel Down
Interior Look Up Left: Left Button
Interior Look Up Middle: Middle Button
I've got a M510 mouse, extra buttons on the side, I have them set on Interior Look Left and Interior Look Right which means I need the RMB only rarely. The LMB/RMB/Wheel asymmetry wasn't my first choice, it's something I arrived at.
Then the rest of the buttons, non-defaults are Q and E as the turn signals, parking brake on B, exhaust brake on the spacebar, Hazard Warning F, Light Modes N, High Beam H, Beacon X, Horn V, Light Horn Z, Y is the wipers (visual onomatopoeia). (edit: engine start is ]).
Set the transmission type to "Real Automatic" unless you're a masochist. Don't use the "Simple Automatic", it's just wrong. The airbrake simulation mode is a bit annoying, mine never got in the way that much, the rest of the realism options I like.
Truck physics does lack a certain feel to it, but there's enough there to demand real attention to payload.  Don't go trying to deliver a heavy load to Zurich until you can afford a decent motor, for instance.

For a game that has been in development for as long as it has, you'd probably expect a little bit more. At this point, it's kinda difficult to pinpoint exactly what direction they're taking this game considering how they're constantly swapping out/rolling back features that are long overdue. In any case, there is a very clear 2-steps-forward-1-step-back feel to its journey towards completion.
Having said that, I have, for the most part thorougly enjoyed my time spent playing DayZ. It can be tedious at times, and there is definitely a valid argument for it being a "running simulator" because so much time ends up being devoted to gathering/exploring. However there is a great deal of depth here, not so much in mechanics or gameplay, but in the potential for social interactions that to me are very much unlike any other multiplayer experience. I say that because the nature of this game invites for some truly dynamic encounters with other players. There are no rules to the world or laws to abide by, which in this case seems to prove that people are ruthless. Scarcity breads uncertainty, and you find yourself cautious of everybody you come across. I have spent many a late night in heated standoffs with other players simply because the intentions of either side weren't clear. In cases like that, it's usually safest to shoot first and ask questions never.
In addition to PVP, the cooperative experience is by and far one of the most satisfying and enriching that I've ever had in a game. Because of DayZ's survival-centric nature, relying on others is imperative to lasting a worthwhile amount of time in the wild. Not only are you defending yourself against other players, you are also pitted against the elements, and your chances of suviving both are much higher when you have a few buddies to help you out.
All-in-all, my personal experience with DayZ has been mostly fulfilling and from it I have gained some really great memories. The type of comradery that can come out of a chaotic social experience like this is easily the most unique and satisfying aspect of this game, which I think makes for the biggest selling point. However, for me the "golden age" of DayZ was when it was at its earliest stages, and as time has gone by the updates have not done much to keep it a compelling experience.
I would encourage anyone who is interested in DayZ to watch gameplay videos prior to purchasing, as they typically do a good job of illustrating the overall experience and what you can expect from the current build.

This is an apt description of the development process of DayZ. I write this review having followed and observed the progression of development since it came out in 2013.
For the most part Dayz is STILL an empty barren map with nothing of any interest, there are no zombies, no items, no players and offers nothing to do except run around a spartan forest region.
There is no indication the developers(BI) have any interest in working on the game anymore and have likely given up all efforts to continue game development. Stable branch updates are sporadic at best(1 per year) each delivering nearly zero fresh content or change to existing assets and a few supposed bug fixes which never seem to ever work.
I have the belief that after 4 years players are starting to wisen up and understand BI as the studio that delivers more empty promises than software development.
This is a perfect example of studios abusing early access status, I hope games like this stay off steam.

STORY: Taking place after the events of the first Borderlands, the story bares striking resemblance to the one that came before it. Once again, four characters (conveniently distinguished by combat class) have come to Pandora in search of a second vault. Yes, a second vault. From the moment the absolutely incredible opening cut-scene plays, you’ll be roaring with laughter. The sheer absurdity that after all you experienced in the first game, a new set of four will have to go through it again, and it’s genuinely funny. Not video game funny; genuinely funny.
However, I feel I’m almost doing Borderlands 2 a disservice here, because the entire story is so much more fleshed out than its predecessor. The characters you grew attached to in the first title return, but they aren’t bit-part players. Sure, you can’t take over Roland again, but he’s a major player in the story, and he’s not the only one. Some of the story beats (that I wouldn’t dream of spoiling here) are genuine punch-the-air moments, and there has been a tremendous amount of effort put in to making the side-missions just as fun; with some wonderful characters there too.
Handsome Jack is the antagonist for Borderlands 2, a pretty-boy who runs Pandora by force, destroying anyone who stands against him. Jack wants what is inside this second vault, because he believes it will give him the power to do pretty much anything. By opening the first vault, the hunters unleashed Eridium onto the world, a rare material that is worth a fortune, yet also holds mysterious powers. Your job is simple, stop Handsome Jack, and have plenty of fun and games along the way.
GRAPHICS: It’d be a lie to say that the visuals had been completely overhauled for Borderlands 2, but they do look far crisper and cleaner, with a slight design change in terms of art direction. Thicker blacks surround people and places, making them stand out even more. Of course, Pandora is full of colourful characters like the sultry Moxxi, or the crazy-violent gun merchant Marcus (among many, many others) and they all look brilliant. They also have so much more life to them, and when they give you an item they will literally hold their arm out for you to take it from them.
Even during battles where elemental damage is littering the screen, damage numbers are flying everywhere and loot is spraying out of dying foes, the frame-rate is pretty solid and there are very few noticeable moments where it chugs, though it happens mostly when you’re playing with others. The action is fast, frenetic and rendered beautifully, with luscious vistas and locations to visit. There are absolutely no complaints in the visual department for Borderlands 2.
SOUND: If you’ve played the first Borderlands then you’ll find that not much has changed in terms of the music you’ll hear. Despite the kick♥♥♥♥♥opening, the moment-to-moment gameplay has that same Borderlands feel to it, twanging country-style acoustic guitar for the desert areas, a chilling soundtrack to fill the ice-caverns, that kind of thing. When the combat ramps up, music will kick in to get the adrenaline flowing. It all works as it should, playing largely second fiddle to the voice acting.
GAMEPLAY: It’s tricky to know where to start when discussing Borderlands 2’s mechanics, because Gearbox have so completely upgraded them, that it’s astonishingly impressive. As with a lot of games containing loot, currency in Borderlands became pointless after a reasonable amount of progress had been made. The player had so much cash it was a worthless commodity. So, to fix this, Borderlands 2 has an additional currency called Eridium which ties nicely into the storyline. If you want to buy the really important things from the black market (more inventory slots for example), you’ll only be able to do so with Eridium. Whilst you still pick up cash at an alarming rate from the richest bandits you’ve ever come across, Eridium is far rarer and seeing some drop, or finding some in a lock-box is a hugely satisfying event.

My whole experience with this game amounts to starting up, wandering around, seeing a zombie, now there are 5-10 zombies running at me, running for my life with nothing but a can of beans and whatever stock items I have on me, summoning up the courage to fight and kill a zombie, learning that basic attacks i.e. punching suck in this game, dying. The next play through (6 months later) I decided to play sneakier. So if I saw a zombie I'd just try my best not to pull aggro, and continue searching for some kind of weapon. Welp, that would eventually just lead to dying. My 3rd and final try at the game was the exact same experience as the 2nd, with that I quit, uninstalled for the 3rd time, and never thought about it again until now, when I am writing this review (2 years later).
What can I say about it, when it has such a high learning curve, no initial thrust into it's environment, and no real goal at hand? I didn't expect a story, or anything of Minecraft proportions, but I did expect to at least shoot a gun or two, or maybe even play with other people. That's one thing I forgot to mention, every time I played, I never ran into anyone on the servers. I saw people online in the servers, but never saw anyone playing in game. Another thing to mention is how bland the world is in this game. It's boring, the houses have nothing going on in them. there is nothing to do at all except die, die, die.
I even gave this game a huge chance seeing how it was early access. I see people complaining about how it still is early access even after 3 years. Personally, I don't mind because it makes it feel like it's still 2013, which is nice.

is arguably the best PvP out there nowadays.
is a game in the open world, here you create your world through a complete system of crafting. Probably the best survival game these days.
The design of the game is very interesting - basically it functions as the beginning of life in society - by collecting resources, hunting wildlife, and crafting tools. The character starts naked and only with a wood stick and a rock that serves to collect resources (wood and stone). From there, collect the necessary materials, make your clothes, build your tools, your house, your bed (functions as the game checkpoint), enhances the protection of your home, and later makes weapons, explosives, etc.
is a realistic survival - players, animals, and the elements compete to kill you. Survive by being cautious and relying on strategy over brawn.
However, in my opinion, it's very difficult to survive in this game playing alone. It's practically impossible. In 80% of cases you are killed by other players without knowing the reason (only by the instinct to kill), and the other 20% are killed by bears. It's frustrating. Unless you get on a server that has been recently wiped and have lots of time to put into the game to build up your base, I would not bother. If you just start out on a server that has not been wiped, prepare to have your base raided to no end. Also if you plan on playing by yourself, you will also have almost no chance as most servers have been basically claimed by a group that just go around and raid everyone.
You need to be careful and attentive that even when you log off you are still in-game, and able to be killed. So, you need to have enough time to build a stable base before leaving the server. In other way, you'll take the risk being killed and stolen. And r*ped too.
All in all, though, I do see a lot of potential in this game and, coupled with a good community increasingly committed in the evolution of the game. It has constant introductions of characters and new tools by the players themselves.
However, is the best PvP game that I've played to date.

Every element of your truck can be modified, from the engine, to the chassis, to the paintjob, to the lights that sit on top of the cab.

But despite the minor problems, I'd give this game an 8/10, an awful lot of fun with a lot todo but not without its flaws.

I love this game. This is the very game that got me into simulators (til I found out 90% of them is crap), If you are to buy any simulators get this. Its more than just driving around in a truck. Theres a whole management side to it with hiring drivers, buying garages, and buying trucks. It gets updates every once in a while, but they are always big updates, the traffic AI is the best of any game yet. On the minimap it tells you the speed limit of the road you are on which is helpful as speeding tickets are rather expensive. It is very realistic, the trucks feel like trucks and trailers affect the trucks performance based on the weight of the trailer, the road you are on and the damage of the truck itself. There is loads of mods you can get for this game and has a huge map, To get from the UK to the very opposite edge of the map will take a good 3 hours, and thats straight across. Even after a few hundred hours of playing, you'll find there are still roads you havent driven yet the map is so big. Graphically it is amazing, and is very well optimized, and the trucks are very well detailed. The trucks are mostly licenced, from the Scania R Series to the Volvo FH, with the only unlicenced truck being the Majestic Across (Mercedes Actros). There is a load of customization, plus there's new paint DLC's that really enhance the look of your truck. I really recommend Euro Truck Simulator 2 at full price, but this game isn't for everyone so take a look at the demo (its essentially the start of the full game) and if you like it, buy the full game. 9.5/10

This game will pull at your heartstrings, if you allow it to. As I'm sure most people who have heard of this game know, the less you know about the plot going into it, the better.
It is a dynamic game, and can change depending on the choices you make. Granted, like all games, there are certain limitations to that freedom of choice in this as well, but Undertale is unique in the sheer variety of impact your choices have on the world around you. There are certain things that will simply change how characters or enemies interact with you, and there a few, seldom acts that change the entire course of the game. And best of all, it encourages replaying if only to see those different outcomes (you monster. Players who have tried a few different routes will understand what I mean).
Further, this game has depth. the previously mentioned variety is only possible because of the diversity of characters and their personalities. Granted, this is somewhat limited in terms of in-game mechanics due to the game's deliberate style that seems to be an homage to the 8-bit golden-oldies of previous generations, but for those willing to use their creative imaginations, this actually becomes a doorway to a whole new level of personal investment into the characters.
Since I've brought it up, the game's graphics are nothing special. Everything is pixelated, and while the sprites for the characters aren't much in detail compared to today's triple-A titles, they are still able to convey a sense of individuality that is refreshing after the many generic hero and villain archetypes we run into today. Even the first adversary you run into is someone you wouldn't expect, and simply bleeds personality!
By now you can probably see that I love this game. I love its characters, I love its story, I love its mechanics (especially the save and reset mechanics), and I absolutely adore the game's soundtrack. This is a game worth checking out. Just... beware of the fanbase. They can be scarier than the mightiest of foes that you'll encounter in the world of Undertale. Don't get me wrong, though: I do appreciate the community this game has created. However, they can be a little over-zealous in trying to "protect" it from critics that may not enjoy the experience; a pursuit that, in my eyes, is unnecessary. This game can stand on its own merits, and critics that don't enjoy it simply have different tastes. But if anything I've said up to this point resonates with you, then by all means. Give Undertale a chance. Just make sure you're kind to any flowers you come across. :)

I'm not a simulation player at all, and I resisted playing this for ages. Its truck driving FFS. Boring. WRONG.
This has me hooked. As well as relaxing you in its stunning environments and bathing you in the rich lather of learning and refining a genuine skill, ETS2 will more than satisfy any gamer's loot craving by allowing you to pimp out beautifully modeled real world, hundred-thousand Euro trucks. Fancy an IVECO or SCANIA truck with more bling than The King? Watch the AI crash as it cranes its robot neck to take a look at your awesome paint job.
In fact, watch the AI behave exactly like road users anywhere in the world - from kindly Transit van drivers flashing their lights to let you out, to idiots in Skodas cutting in on you at the last minute. Expect all the challenges of real roads, with all the gravitas and focus-demanding presence that 40 tons of high-speed steel commands. It may not be a super-high fidelity simulation like OMSI2 or MS Flight, but let yourself get immersed and you'll be surprised how many times you catch your brain doing EXACTLY what it does when you're behind the wheel in reality.
The empire building is just yet another compelling and addictive element - this game just keeps pulling you back in for another go and gives the constant sense of progress, both in an abstract gamey sense as well as a real world skill sense. I can well understand how people have 500+ hours in it. A tremendously active and dedicated mod scene means you are unlikely to ever run out of road, or new sexy metal to purchase and upgrade.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a driving simulator where you're driving trucks delivering cargo from one place to another. You can drive around most parts of Europe delivering cargo.

There are tons of garages to be bought all over Europe and you're also able to hire other truckers to drive for your company which will generate a nice extra bit of income while you're doing your own jobs.
Great simulator and a nice experience, even more so if you have a steering wheel to get an even more immersive gameplay experience.
Definitely recommend this game if you like driving and simulators.

Miscreated, another alpha I took a break from to try Dayz  is certainly a more polished game and if you are stuck trying to decide  between the two go with the latter. After I purchased Rust it quickly became one of my favorite games ever, but at its current state I can't recommend it and am probably going to quit playing soon myself. The devs are slowly killing every desire I had to play this game and are turning it into a shell of what it once was and is supposed to be: a survival game.
Here is a list of the current problems in the game:
- Lack of progression/servers dying off and losing population way too fast. As of now most servers (excluding officials and a small percentage of community servers) start to die off 2 or 3 days after a wipe. This is due to both lack of progression and poor game design. What happens is players can run around radtowns and streets breaking barrels and opening crates and recycle all the components they get to craft a full set of gear and weapons. They then can go around killing and raiding everyone starting out and trying to build a base, causing them to quit the server. This goes on for a couple days until the server starts losing its population and the raiders leave and do it all again on another server that has recently wiped, leaving the people who actually play the game as if its a survival game and not PUBG alone on an empty server. Once people get raided they have absolutely 0 reason to stay on that server because there are 50 others that have just wiped that they can join. These are their two choices: they can remain on a server where they have nothing, but others have everything or they can switch to a server where nobody has anything. The second choice is obviously the wisest. The community has asked the devs countless times to address this issue, but they don't seem to care and would rather Tweet out pictures of genitalia with the caption "get ♥♥♥♥ed reddit."
- Gunplay is awful. With the addition of the infamous aimcone, gunplay has become a joke. Bullets do not go where you aim them and PVP has turned into an RNG fest. There is no skill involved in fights. Again, the community has asked the devs to do something about this, but all they do is reply with emojis making fun of the feedback.
- So many things are unbalanced in this game. The devs will add new content that is almost always extremely OP, then they will ignore the feedback and won't touch it for a month's time, then finally they will nerf it into oblivion and nobody will use it anymore. As an example, they added heavy plate armor, which was cheaper and stronger than the previous high-tiered armor, making all other armor obsolete and turning players into tanks. This problem was ignored by the devs for about a month until they made it so you can no longer see your entire screen while wearing it, you're slowed down significantly, and you cannot aim down your sights. After this nerf I have not seen a single person wearing it in game ever. It hasn't been touched or mentioned since. This has happened time and time again and the devs just keep moving on to new broken content.
- The game is confusing and lots of information about it is outdated or just flat out wrong. The wiki gives out wrong information, there are hardly any in-game tips about things, descriptions for items completely lie about their features, and armor/weapon values make no sense. Pretty much you're on your own if you want to learn how to play this game, and you'll be doing things wrong for weeks until you accidentally learn that no, your cooked bear meat isn't actually burnt and won't hurt you if you eat it, it's just labeled wrong.
I realize the game is in early-access, but the entire point of letting players play a game before its release is to listen to feedback and make changes to improve the game. It seems like the reason this game is in early-access is because Garry likes to make fun of people who give feedback and tell them to get ♥♥♥♥ed. Some people may think the way he acts is funny and charming, but to me its extremely unprofessional and disrespectful to the people who gave his game a chance and have supported it through its development. And Helk can say "I want to make one thing absolutely clear. Rust is a PvP game." as justification for all the stupid changes he's made, but the first line of the game's description says otherwise.

Rust is primarily a PvP game, and secondarily it is a survival game. I'm interested in it for its survival elements, ideally aiming at team survival against weather changes, failed crops, dangerous fauna and flora, and maybe some kind of overall encroaching threat (maybe a military takeover or something. idk). None of those elements are in Rust. It is a game about base building, racing to dominance, and pillaging other players' bases although that means ruining hours of their hard work. I am not at all a fan of this.
PvE (Player vs Environment) mode salvaged this game for me. This mode is available in community servers, and is great for learning the mechanics of Rust without being murderated repeatedly by little pubescent monsters. It is a survival game with promise, but clumisly handled. It's definitely visually appealing, but the vanilla game encourages players to be psychopaths. Raids are an accepted part of the game (where in other games like minecraft, they are usually misdemeanors), and they can be very traumatic to the party being raided. All of your hard work can be dashed by a group of hostile teenagers who don't see the damage they're doing. Dying can be very traumatic in this game, specifically dying to other players. You are literally naked when you start out, and to die repeatedy to better-equipped players is excruciating and frankly not worth your time. Wouldn't recommend this game in its native form to anyone, as I think it has a bad effect on players.
Pros:
+Visuals are nice
+Some interesting survival mechanics
+Fun items and some exploration
+Innovative
Cons:
-Not terribly well fleshed-out, as it is developed by, as far as I can tell, two people
-The building mechanics are pretty awkward, you cannot easily destroy something you have placed
-You can reach endgame pretty quickly, and the only real boss of the game is an attack helicopter
-As such, most players find the game to be more of a survival arena game, in which it is a race to dominance, one which is hard to win if you are not in a group or, say, have a job that prevents you from devoting all your waking hours to this game
-The idea of sleepers is cool in theory, I like the idea of having to build a suitable dwelling to protect yourself from the environment and bears and the like, but again the developers have chosen to make this a PvP game. This means that the sleepers mechanic just leaves you vulnerable to someone slowly chipping away at your base, finding and killing your sleeping avatar, and then stealing all of your hard-grinded goods. It's not terribly fun, to say the least.
-The community can be nice (in PvE servers especially), but it can also be extraordinarily toxic (PvP servers). You lose trust in pretty much every other human player, as backstabbing is something the game practically encourages. It's incredibly socially stressful. (If you have the social skills in the first place that is.) I think many players are not yet old enough or mature enough to possess sensitivity, or are so given to toxic masculinity that there's no point trying to hold a conversation. Many view the events in rust as simply happening in a game, but the results can have real-world impacts on players. I have stopped playing because of the interactions I have had with toxic players.
In short, I don't recommend you get this game in its current form. If you do get it, I recommend starting out on PvE servers, as at least you won't be repeatedly murdered and harassed by other players.

As well as relaxing you in its stunning environments and bathing you in the rich lather of learning and refining a genuine skill, ETS2 will more than satisfy any gamer's loot craving by allowing you to pimp out beautifully modeled real world, hundred-thousand Euro trucks. Fancy an IVECO or SCANIA truck with more bling than The King? Watch the AI crash as it cranes its robot neck to take a look at your awesome paint job.
In fact, watch the AI behave exactly like road users anywhere in the world - from kindly Transit van drivers flashing their lights to let you out, to idiots in Skodas cutting in on you at the last minute. Expect all the challenges of real roads, with all the gravitas and focus-demanding presence that 40 tons of high-speed steel commands. It may not be a super-high fidelity simulation like OMSI2 or MS Flight, but let yourself get immersed and you'll be surprised how many times you catch your brain doing EXACTLY what it does when you're behind the wheel in reality.
The empire building is just yet another compelling and addictive element - this game just keeps pulling you back in for another go and gives the constant sense of progress, both in an abstract gamey sense as well as a real world skill sense. I can well understand how people have 500+ hours in it. A tremendously active and dedicated mod scene means you are unlikely to ever run out of road, or new sexy metal to purchase and upgrade.

There are tons of garages to be bought all over Europe and you're also able to hire other truckers to drive for your company which will generate a nice extra bit of income while you're doing your own jobs.
Great simulator and a nice experience, even more so if you have a steering wheel to get an even more immersive gameplay experience.
Definitely recommend this game if you like driving and simulators.

I really thought I wouldn’t like Euro Truck Simulator 2. I thought it was in the same vein as Farming Simulator, Street Sweeper Simulator, Snow Cat Simulator, etc. It’s not. This is a quality game with effort put into its design and I actually do enjoy it.
ETS2’s biggest positive is that it’s very relaxing to play. If I have a free hour and want to chill out, I will fire this up and do a quick trucking job or two. It also does a fair job in presenting you with different landscapes and varied scenery.
The downside is that the landscapes are not quite varied enough. The devs made a decent effort but after playing for a while, you will recognize all the reused set pieces such as highway interchanges, exit ramps, maintenance garages, and branches of companies where you accept jobs. And aside from driving on the left hand side of the street in England and some different background scenery, the experience on every highway and inside each city is virtually the same. Driving in Stuttgart is the same as driving in Paris is the same as driving in Rome. You won’t see the Eiffel Tower or Coliseum in the background nor any other famous streets, bridges or landmarks from any particular city. Likewise, every toll booth and rest stop are exactly the same, whether in Austria, the Netherlands or the Czech Republic.
It’s also missing visual damage to vehicles. Your truck can get damaged by accidents but none of it will show on the outside. Neither will it show up on any car you hit. Every once in a while I like to cause chaos by getting up a head of steam & swerving into oncoming traffic. It’s very unsatisfying when nothing much happens aside from traffic stopping. I know that sort of thing is more reserved for a title like GTA or Saints Row, but still.
The option of playing your own MP3s over the truck’s “radio” while driving was a great idea. Unfortunately, I found this to be a buggy feature. The game won’t play many of my MP3 files and I don’t know why.
To make up for these shortcomings, there is a very engaging career mode. The more deliveries you complete, the more experience you earn. This allows you to gain levels which in turn allows you to build up your driving skills to make more money, unlock new types of delivery jobs and unlock new options & upgrades you can buy for your truck.
Speaking of buying trucks, there are a lot to choose from, based on real life models from manufacturers like Volvo and DAF. They are expensive, but you can take out a loan from the bank if you want to get things rolling early on. You can also buy & upgrade various garages around Europe, buy more trucks, hire drivers to drive them, and all of this will end up earning you even more money.
I’m still in the early stages of the game as I only have the one truck of my own and am working on repaying a loan, but I’m looking forward to continuing to play this. It’s more of something I will progress in gradually rather than sitting down and trying to grind away at. It’s a very nice change of pace.

After I purchased Rust it quickly became one of my favorite games ever, but at its current state I can't recommend it and am probably going to quit playing soon myself. The devs are slowly killing every desire I had to play this game and are turning it into a shell of what it once was and is supposed to be: a survival game.
Here is a list of the current problems in the game:
- Lack of progression/servers dying off and losing population way too fast. As of now most servers (excluding officials and a small percentage of community servers) start to die off 2 or 3 days after a wipe. This is due to both lack of progression and poor game design. What happens is players can run around radtowns and streets breaking barrels and opening crates and recycle all the components they get to craft a full set of gear and weapons. They then can go around killing and raiding everyone starting out and trying to build a base, causing them to quit the server. This goes on for a couple days until the server starts losing its population and the raiders leave and do it all again on another server that has recently wiped, leaving the people who actually play the game as if its a survival game and not PUBG alone on an empty server. Once people get raided they have absolutely 0 reason to stay on that server because there are 50 others that have just wiped that they can join. These are their two choices: they can remain on a server where they have nothing, but others have everything or they can switch to a server where nobody has anything. The second choice is obviously the wisest. The community has asked the devs countless times to address this issue, but they don't seem to care and would rather Tweet out pictures of genitalia with the caption "get ♥♥♥♥ed reddit."
- Gunplay is awful. With the addition of the infamous aimcone, gunplay has become a joke. Bullets do not go where you aim them and PVP has turned into an RNG fest. There is no skill involved in fights. Again, the community has asked the devs to do something about this, but all they do is reply with emojis making fun of the feedback.
- So many things are unbalanced in this game. The devs will add new content that is almost always extremely OP, then they will ignore the feedback and won't touch it for a month's time, then finally they will nerf it into oblivion and nobody will use it anymore. As an example, they added heavy plate armor, which was cheaper and stronger than the previous high-tiered armor, making all other armor obsolete and turning players into tanks. This problem was ignored by the devs for about a month until they made it so you can no longer see your entire screen while wearing it, you're slowed down significantly, and you cannot aim down your sights. After this nerf I have not seen a single person wearing it in game ever. It hasn't been touched or mentioned since. This has happened time and time again and the devs just keep moving on to new broken content.
- The game is confusing and lots of information about it is outdated or just flat out wrong. The wiki gives out wrong information, there are hardly any in-game tips about things, descriptions for items completely lie about their features, and armor/weapon values make no sense. Pretty much you're on your own if you want to learn how to play this game, and you'll be doing things wrong for weeks until you accidentally learn that no, your cooked bear meat isn't actually burnt and won't hurt you if you eat it, it's just labeled wrong.
I realize the game is in early-access, but the entire point of letting players play a game before its release is to listen to feedback and make changes to improve the game. It seems like the reason this game is in early-access is because Garry likes to make fun of people who give feedback and tell them to get ♥♥♥♥ed. Some people may think the way he acts is funny and charming, but to me its extremely unprofessional and disrespectful to the people who gave his game a chance and have supported it through its development. And Helk can say "I want to make one thing absolutely clear. Rust is a PvP game." as justification for all the stupid changes he's made, but the first line of the game's description says otherwise.
added note : 4.1 million in game return pay back yet this game has "very Positive" ....... yeah not true. this game is beating a dead horse .

Believe the hype.
I'm not a simulation player at all, and I resisted playing this for ages. Its truck driving FFS. Boring. WRONG.
This has me hooked. As well as relaxing you in its stunning environments and bathing you in the rich lather of learning and refining a genuine skill, ETS2 will more than satisfy any gamer's loot craving by allowing you to pimp out beautifully modeled real world, hundred-thousand Euro trucks. Fancy an IVECO or SCANIA truck with more bling than The King? Watch the AI crash as it cranes its robot neck to take a look at your awesome paint job.
In fact, watch the AI behave exactly like road users anywhere in the world - from kindly Transit van drivers flashing their lights to let you out, to idiots in Skodas cutting in on you at the last minute. Expect all the challenges of real roads, with all the gravitas and focus-demanding presence that 40 tons of high-speed steel commands. It may not be a super-high fidelity simulation like OMSI2 or MS Flight, but let yourself get immersed and you'll be surprised how many times you catch your brain doing EXACTLY what it does when you're behind the wheel in reality.
The empire building is just yet another compelling and addictive element - this game just keeps pulling you back in for another go and gives the constant sense of progress, both in an abstract gamey sense as well as a real world skill sense. I can well understand how people have 500+ hours in it. A tremendously active and dedicated mod scene means you are unlikely to ever run out of road, or new sexy metal to purchase and upgrade.
You know what? This actually makes me wanna be a Trucker. Hell, bring on ICE ROAD TRUCKERS SIMULATOR!
